Resident Evil Revelations was a solid experience, especially as someone who’s recently become a bigger fan of the Resident Evil series. Seeing Jill Valentine again was easily one of the game’s biggest highlights, and the episodic chapter structure gives it a unique mini-series feel that keeps things moving with short, digestible segments. While the atmosphere and classic survival horror charm are definitely there, the gameplay can feel a bit rough around the edges compared to stronger entries in the franchise. It’s not particularly difficult, but some mechanics feel dated enough to hold it back. The story does its job, but it never really reaches anything especially memorable or impactful. 

Overall, this feels more like a game made for existing Resident Evil fans who simply want more time with familiar characters rather than a must-play standout on its own.

[i]A decent side mission for fans—more enjoyable for returning to Jill than for the adventure itself.[/i]

It's fun, even Raid Mode is, but it doesn't surpass Revelations 2. The atmosphere and horror are there, but the problem lies with the characters. They add cliché humor with Keith and Quint, and Jessica's lustful relationship with Chris in life-or-death situations, which disrupts the game's atmosphere and seriousness. Even so, I recommend it; it's a good Resident Evil game if you can overlook these issues or don't mind them too much. The overall pacing is slow compared to RE4, RE5, or RE6, but that's because it was originally a Nintendo 3DS exclusive. I must admit that the looting is very slow.

To start off, I do like this game and believe that it is enjoyable. However, I can't think of a world where I would recommend this game to anyone but dedicated Resident Evil fans. While I enjoyed the episodic aspect of the game, it definitely ruined the pacing. I enjoy the characters in this game, Jill, Chris, Keith and Quint, Jessica, Parker, O'Brian... Everyone was cool to see on screen, and each twist really made this game feel like a thriller/drama show, which I enjoyed. The problem is thinking about the fact that we probably wont see these characters again. One of my biggest issues with the RE Franchise is how they prioritize which characters to return. Sure, Jill and Chris make appearances later on, but what about Jessica and Raymond? There is still clearly more to be told with this cast and yet we only see TWO of the characters return. And from my knowledge, Jill is only in RE5 after this (maybe 6?) and Chris is in 5 and 6, with minor appearances in 7 and 8. What about his story with the BSAA? What about Parker? Anyways, I also liked the Genesis device. It wasn't very plot relevant but it had its moments. I like the idea of it and it was something new. The final boss being similar to the classic tyrants was cool. But a big problem I had with that boss was how inconsistent the teleportation mechanic was. It really seemed like that the boss would just change up his attack, despite the starting move being the same as any other. It was kind of hard to predict what he would do next. And every single boss in this game LOVES to eat your ammo. It was seriously crazy how often they wanted me to fight someone, but I wouldn't have the ammo to fight them because they'd tank it all anyway. And this is coming from someone who understands that you're not supposed to fight every enemy, SO I would pass some by to preserve my ammo. It really feels like the bosses are programmed to die only when you are drained of all of your resources. The dodge mechanic is also really inconsistent. The map is confusing. The lack of inventory management and puzzles sucked. The camera was annoying to move and made it hard to aim. Now, I know this is a lot of negativity, so I'll give the game this: The aquatic theme with the ocean, the boats, sea creatures, and water as a whole was honestly pretty cool. I was hesitant at first with the other games (like 4) straying away from the traditional zombies, but I've grown to like the idea more. They take the traditional enemy type and put a new spin on them to fit the theme of the game.

Overall, I had fun. I always love seeing Jill on screen, the side characters helped elevate this game, and the story really felt like a tv show. But I just cannot recommend this to anyone unless you're dedicated enough to the series where you wouldn't mind the wonky controls, and the fact that most of these characters don't return.

Resident Evil Revelations is criminally underrated, and honestly it’s getting old seeing people trash it just because “it’s a 3DS game.”

Yeah, it started on 3DS. So what? That doesn’t magically make it bad. In fact, it does more right than a lot of the bigger Resident Evil titles from that era.

It actually brings back some tension, the ship setting works really well, and it’s not just nonstop brainless action. Jill is great here, the atmosphere hits, and even if the story gets a bit messy (as usual), it keeps you hooked.

But of course, there’s always some idiot going “nah it’s just a handheld port” like that automatically invalidates everything. Most of those people probably barely even played it.

Is it perfect? Not even close. Some parts drag, the episodic structure can feel weird, and yeah, you can tell it wasn’t built as some massive AAA blockbuster. Still, it holds up way better than people give it credit for.

If you skipped it because of that dumb “3DS game” excuse, that’s on you.

I’ve seen people online being quite kind to this game, and I understand why: it’s a spin-off, and it was originally developed for the 3DS, so expectations were lower than for mainline entries. On top of that, it was released during the franchise’s weakest period, which makes it seem better in comparison.

The problem is that, if you judge it outside of those redeeming factors, the game is very flawed:

- Probably due to its portable origins, the campaign reuses the same environments repeatedly, not only through backtracking, but also by having you replay sections multiple times with different characters. It feels redundant and cheap. Even with this method of padding the runtime, the game is still quite short (around 8 hours).
- Exploration feels off. Even with all the backtracking, there’s little to discover outside of your current objective, so the game ends up feeling quite linear. This is a shame, because the cruise ship is a perfect setup for a Resident Evil game, almost like a Spencer Mansion at sea, but it never fully takes advantage of that potential.
- The game’s only original mechanic, the Genesis device (used to find hidden items and farm healing items by scanning enemies), feels like a chore. In my opinion, the game would have been better off without it.
- Both the gameplay (mostly derived from RE5) and character progression are extremely basic. A dodge mechanic was added, but it feels unreliable since it doesn’t have a dedicated button.
- The story is forgettable. It leans more toward political intrigue, but some events are too far-fetched to fit the tone. It also presents key events in a way that feels too detached from the player, making it hard to care about them. At the beginning of the game, I assumed the events of Terragrigia must have been covered in another spin-off or animated film, because they are introduced so matter-of-factly and with such detachment that it feels like we’re expected to already know them. The story also seems unsure about how it wants to treat certain plot points.
[spoiler]For example, Parker has a stereotypical death scene but then randomly survives.[/spoiler]
- The original characters created for this game feel cartoonish. There are two completely superfluous joke characters that you actually have to play as, during a couple of short segments. Chris’s partner also looks like a supermodel, which feels extremely out of place.
- Boss battles are underwhelming.
[spoiler]The mutated girl is framed as an important fight, but we never actually get a proper final showdown with her. The final boss also comes out of nowhere.[/spoiler]

In the end, after having played all the numbered Resident Evil titles and considering myself a fan of the series, the only game I would rank lower than this one is RE6, which says a lot. In my opinion, for someone who doesn’t care much about the series, this game is likely to be even less enjoyable, so I can’t really recommend it.

No, I can't recommend this. Coming straight off RE4 (2005), it feels like night and day, though I probably should have expected that, considering Revelations was originally a 3DS game made by a different team.

The structure doesn't help. Twelve episodes, each with a "Previously in..." recap that feels both lazy and pointless, especially when some episodes can be cleared in 30 minutes or less. The objective markers are also contradictory: you're told to fight a boss while actually needing to keep exploring first, otherwise you're wasting time underequipped and destined for failure. Have fun figuring that out on your own.

The gameplay has several issues on top of that. Plenty of the "hurry" situations have no time limit, so it's impossible to take them seriously. And when a time limit does show up, they put a bunch of weapon upgrades in your face with no clear indication of whether you can come back for them later. In most cases you can, but you won't know that. The mouse-struggle QTE (when grabbed by an enemy) is horrendously implemented. It fails to register left-right movement properly, so you can easily die to a control problem. The dodging mechanic is inconsistent too: sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. Bodies despawn when you leave an area - probably a technical limitation of the original platform - but it means that if you didn't scan in time, tough luck, those points are gone. Your companion serves basically zero purpose beyond maybe acting as a small distraction for enemies, in the best-case scenario. The developer's main goal was to bring back the content and horror of the Resident Evil roots while at the same time modernizing the gameplay... they didn't do a good job considering this felt 2 different games mashed together sometimes.

The story has some cool moments, but it feels convoluted and too dramatic. The dialogue is poorly written and questionable. It also appears that the writers are scared of having a moment of quiet because the characters just keep on talking, saying obvious and filler phrases at every opportunity. Let's not even get into Jessica's wetsuit design choice. The music and initial ambience are genuinely the most memorable parts, both put together well.

Checking Steam achievements, 76.6% of owners scanned an enemy (the most basic thing in the game), yet less than half of those (45.3%) bothered to finish it. Not a nice look. Maybe worth it on a discount if you're a massive fan of the series, but that's about it.

You don't really manage your inventory anymore for example moving items or combining herbs, which kinda take away the classic RE element which is juggling herbs. But on the other hand the game feels faster as you don't think about problems like no inventory space, which to me was a plus.

As for movement improvements, you can finally properly strafe and aim, plus you can move while aiming, although there is a classic controlls option which makes it similar to RE4 and RE5 stationary turret aiming and shooting. But the new action controls is a great improvement although still not perfect but huge improvement again comparing to RE4 and RE5.

Resident Evil Revelations is a spinoff game for the 3DS, meaning you shouldn't expect the quality of a mainline game. However, the package here is surprisingly robust with a Campaign and a Raid Mode (The Mercenaries type of experience). 

Let's start with the Campaign, which I think is certainly nothing extraordinary. You will find in the beginning that the setting of the Queen Zenobia is quite cool and unique with different distinct areas, like the casino, but as the campaign progresses there is quite a lot of recycling and tracking back to already explored areas. Now, this wouldn't be a problem as it happens in every RE game, but this game takes it to the limits. Honestly, storywise I can't even remember to tell you what happened , I didn't care for it, I found it quite dull. The enemy variety and gun variety does seem lacking at first but it gets better as you progress. You do get to play with Jill Valentine again which is nice. Oh also the scanning mechanic is absolutely useless, it get's introduced as this important thing in the intro but no it's useless.

In conclusion the Campaign for me is a 2.5/5 , I'd say it ranks towards the weaker side of the Resident Evil Campaigns not unplayable but also not really worth it if that's only what you are looking for.

And now we get to the meat and potatoes of this game, where you will be spending most of your time, (if the middling Campaign didn't put you off the game entirely) the Raid Mode. This gamemode is just so much fun! You get put through all the areas from the campaign again, but now you have to reach the end of each linear level by killing anything that stands in the way. The genius part is in the leveling system and getting better weapons with unique abilities that radically change how you play each level. There are a total of 60 levels (20 unique but with 3 difficulty settings) and I know you maybe thinking, how is this not going to get repetitive, revisiting these levels so many times, but it somehow doesn't because of the bonus challenges that the game requires to get 100% completion. These can be quite the gauntlet at times, but when you beat a level and see all bonuses pop up, it's a genuine triumph. The weapons you unlock at higher levels are crazy, from snipers that deal massive critical damage, to revolvers with giant muzzles providing massive damage and submachine guns with massive fire rates and on top of all that, you can customize them with unique abilities, like auto-shot where the gun fires itself as you aim at the monsters, (basically aimbot!), or full burst, where you basically mag dump the enemies with just one trigger pull. They are really fun and OP and bring something fresh that shakes up the gameplay. The gamemode is Co-op so you can grab a buddy and grind with them if it gets too repetitive on your own. Fully completing this mode is a tall task, for context, I already have 40 hours recorded and I'm just about halfway through the levels and bonuses. 
Final note, this gamemode is perfect for the Steam Deck as you can quickly pop in, complete a couple levels and go on with your day. 

Final verdict: If you are looking for a great story or overall Campaign experience there are definitely better games in the series for that. The true magic is in Raid Mode, where levelling up and fully completing a level is addicting and most importantly fun, with a wide selection of characters to choose from with unique attributes, vast amounts of weapons and gun mods to provide a lot of ways to tackle each level and a genuine challenge present for platinum hunters. 
Overall Rating: 8/10, worth buying, especially on sale!

Overll it a decent port of a great handheld game that lost a bit of it charms from the transition but still remains a good entry in the series.

Additionally, the game has abhorrent pacing and completely ruins any atmosphere it's trying to setup. The early game Jill sections are pretty cool, only to be interrupted by a generic action flashback where you fight the same enemies in a generic office building, or flip to another character fighting the same enemies on a snowy mountain. The constant flipping back and forth ruins the atmosphere and pacing setup with Jill's section.

The game also gets pretty boring towards the end, and I was just ready for it to be over. You're running back through the same sections over and over, which, in a normal Resident Evil game like the first, or 2, isn't a bad thing, since you're able to unlock new areas or solve new puzzles. One last thing, is there is literally zero inventory management. The only decision you have to make is which three weapons you want to bring.

I didn't hate the game, and it is a cool concept, but the story and dialogue is truly awful, and it constantly shoots itself in the foot. RE Revelations was definitely one of the best for its time. The mechanics in this game are insane to think about; even the remakes don't have these mechanics. Now I do think the game is fully into the action part of it and less survival with no real scary moments, just scary enemies due to the truckload of damage they deal. But back to the mechanics, the swimming part of the games is done wonderfully with having to explore underwater areas in most parts of the game, though I did not like the idea of having enemies be able to stun lock/Insta-kill you underwater and you having no way to fight back other than maybe like 2 grenades they gave you before the areas; I think if we were able to shoot underwater or even punch/kick the enemies away, the underwater areas could've been better. The concept of turrets was so cool to me, being able to just spray and pray away at the Queen Zonobia and just destroy the boss; it was one of the best parts of the game. The scanning system was incredibly cool to me, as it's so innovative and just makes sense for this type of game. Having a scanning system in a biology-based game where all the enemies make no sense is just so cool, with the game also rewarding you with heals if you scan enough enemies and fill up a bar. The concept of also scanning hidden items and them having herbs, ammo, or gun parts is fantastic. More on the gun parts: another incredibly innovative system for its time, being able to add upgrades to your guns adds so much variety and keeps the guns fresh no matter where you are. One example is the charge upgrade for the shotgun, being my favorite, which makes the shotgun stronger and helped incredibly for the final fight against Morgan. The bosses in this game were nothing short of incredible, with every boss feeling fast and action-paced and giving you a sense of urgency to kill them quick. My favorite boss had to be Morgan's T-Abyss tyrant; it's so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool. The fact that it has 2 weak spots on the back if you're forced to dodge and when it attacks the front heart area to stun him is fantastic. The teleporting and mirages he uses for the fight are awesome, and it's such a cool idea to change up the tyrant so it's not the same old, same old fight. One thing I want to brush up more on is the punch mechanic, with all 4 characters you can play as having a different animation too. It's essentially the punch mechanic from RE4, but you can hold it to do a ♥♥♥♥ ton of damage. The mobs/enemies in this game are a little faulty, with most of them being reskins and having little to no variety. For example, we have ooze, shooter ooze, tank ooze, and boss ooze. 4 of the same mob, basically, and later on in the lab they just reskin them to be more shark-like, but they still just ooze. Definitely one of the weaker parts of this game but nonetheless still great. Finally, the story was amazing; for an episodic game, it really does do a great job with building tension and having you guessing and wondering what's next. At first, the game tricks you into thinking that O'Brian was the mastermind behind the "new Veltro," but in reality, at the end of the game, we learn that he built the entire situation up—the 2 boats, the fake bombings, everything—all to take down the head of the FBC and the real owner of Veltro, who was still alive under the hidden 3rd ship. It also does an amazing job at keeping you guessing on who the "mole" is until they reveal it's Jessica, which was crazy to me. I had no idea it was her at all. Some things I didn't like were the way they left everyone alive; I know it sounds dark, but at certain points of the game we see multiple people who should've died, died. Except no, they didn't; they kept Quint and his friend alive even though they literally got nuked. And with Parker, even though he's the GOAT, he clearly shouldn't have lived that lmao. I also don't fully love the idea of Raymond being nice, then evil, then nice, then at the end of the game he was just being nice to Parker for saving him at Terragrigia, but he's still evil. Confusing character, and I never got why they did that. Pros and cons aside, this game was fantastic, and it might be in my top 3 of RE games; the story was great, the characters had meaningful connections, the combat and action were fun, and overall it was an amazing game. If I had to give a rating, this would definitely be on the same scale as RE2, sitting at a 8.5/10. If a remake ever gets made for this game, I will be playing immediately.

A solid intermission between major titles, offering a unique detective romp and expanding the worldbuilding of the Resident Evil universe.

Resident Evil: Revelations (2012) is a side installment to the main franchise, canon to the story, but taking several liberties with the existing formula. The events take place in 2005, this time you take the role of several characters, all BSAA operatives, returning mainstays Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield, each accompanied by their work colleagues Parker Luciani and Jessica Sherawat respectively, as well as support agents Keith Lumley and Quint Cetcham, as they uncover the mystery of the 2004 bioterrorist attack on Terragrigia, an island city in the Mediterranean noted to be the first fully solar-powered metropolis (dubbed "aquapolis" due to it being on an island), and bring to light the players behind the attack. The BSAA is tipped off that their answers lie on a derelict cruise ship, the Queen Zenobia, and they do not end up disappointed, as a new threat aiming to infest all the oceans of the world rears its ugly head.

Revelations for the most part takes the gameplay systems introduced in the action trilogy (RE4-5-6), though with a noticeable nerf on the weakpoint melee finisher system, now needing to properly stun an enemy to even get the prompt, which may or may not happen at all. You are also equipped with a scanner tool, which you will use to scour around environments to find hidden items, as well as scan the unique bioweapons situated on the Queen Zenobia, fulfilling a 100% scan quota giving you a free healing item each time. Scanning the same enemy type repeatedly gradually lowers your score, however. The game also introduces part kits, which can be used at a workbench to equip onto weapons, giving them different upgrades depending on what you found, like firing rate, damage, clip size, etc. The BOWs this time are afflicted by the new T-Abyss virus, an offshoot of T-Virus that gives both marine lifeforms and others aquatic attributes. The game is split into chapters, like the last three major games, letting you pace yourself. It's rather long for a spinoff, at 12 chapters, averaging at around 10 hours, with a few setpieces and mechanics to mix up any possible monotony you might feel if you play for too long, as well as the constant back-and-forth perspective swaps between characters. Rev 1 is second on the list of most playable characters in a single Resident Evil game, right behind RE6, and I think that provides it a lot of value. While light on puzzles, it maintains an atmosphere at least somewhat more akin to the survival horror titles, being quieter on average than the very loud and boisterous tone of 5 and 6.

Visually, it may not hold up in some places as well as, say, RE6, though that might be due to it being originally a 3DS game ported to console, namely UI elements are somewhat fuzzy, however it boasts support for modern resolution scaling, as well as 120hz refresh rate, helping the in-engine visuals age better due to the 2013 HD port. The lavish decks and flooded hulls of the Queen Zenobia, and the snowy mountainous regions hold up fairly well, as well as most of the character models, maintaining more or less the same artstyle since Resident Evil 1 Remake, with an almost painted-on aesthetic. 

RE: Revelations is a fun reprieve from the usual formatting of the core games, and is worth the money, especially on sales, if you just want to experience a bit more Resident Evil. I wouldn't quite put this as a must play for newcomers, it's more a supplementary material for those already deep into the series. Wait for sale.

Resident Evil Revelations deserves way more love than it gets.

The atmosphere alone makes it special. The Queen Zenobia is an incredible setting, bringing back the claustrophobic corridors, darkness, and tension that define classic Resident Evil. Exploring the ship genuinely feels unsettling, and the sound design and lighting do a great job of keeping you on edge the entire time.

Jill is amazing in this game. Calm, professional, and composed, she feels like the perfect survival horror protagonist. Playing as her brings back that classic Resident Evil feeling where survival and awareness matter more than pure action. The story is intriguing enough to keep you invested, slowly unfolding its mystery without overstaying its welcome.

Gameplay strikes a great balance between action and survival. Ammo management matters, scanning for resources adds tension, and combat feels more deliberate in tight spaces. Enemy designs are creepy and fit the horror tone really well.

Raid Mode adds a ton of replay value and is surprisingly addictive. Even after finishing the main story, there is still plenty of reason to come back.

Resident Evil Revelations feels like a true return to survival horror roots. It is not flashy, but it understands the core of Resident Evil and delivers an atmospheric, satisfying experience that stands out in its own way.

[h1] A Mixed Bag [/h1]

Resident Evil Revelations has some things I really like, but there's also a lot I don't like. To start off with the good, the game can be genuinely scary at times. It definitely got me with a couple jump scares and the overall setting is pretty scary, with a lot of tense moments. The combat is good enough, especially for what was a 3DS game, and I enjoyed how you play as a variety of characters, figuring out the different pieces of the story from their perspectives and seeing it all come together. I also thought the story was decent. Nothing too memorable but not bad. There's also a couple really good boss fights and some absolutely stellar set pieces. I like the setting of a cruise ship, although I don't think it lived up to its potential. The customizable weapon parts was a really cool addition as well, allowing to tweak the weapons to your preference, and giving you a sense of getting stronger as the game goes on. There's also decent enemy variety. and there's some cool designs as well. Lastly, the soundtrack is amazing. There's some area themes that are incredible and the music really stood out to me.

Now for the bad. The awesome setting of a cruise ship felt absolutely wasted. Very little of the places you explore feel like an actual cruise ship. You spend way too much time in boring grey, dark hallways, that could be absolutely anywhere. The few times the game really leans in to the cruise ship theme are the best areas in the game in my opinion. Something about shooting zombies in a fancy stateroom or in a grand dining hall, or a casino really appealed to me, and I thought these were the best areas. The writing can be atrocious at times. Characters will be in a serious situation and crack awful jokes or just have really corny dialogue that took me out of the moment. I didn't love the episodic aspect of the game although can appreciate why they went that route for a 3DS game, and it better allowed them to have multiple different campaigns to play through much more easily so I don't hate this, it was just kind of annoying. There's also a lot of back tracking, which was probably due to the 3DS' limitations but it doesn't change the fact that the game can get repetitive and it leads to a lot of down time where nothing is really going on. Another thing that adds to this is that the ship can be difficult to navigate. The map is terrible, and all the hallways look exactly the same, making it very easy to get lost in some of the episodes. Lastly, I hate the stupid scanner thing. Scanning enemies can get you healing items and allows you to find hidden items which are pretty necessary to keep ammo in stock and it gets extremely annoying having to pull out the scanner every 30 seconds to see if there are any items to collect, or dead enemies to scan. 

Overall, Resident Evil Revelations was a fine enough game, that I think is worth getting if you're a fan of the series.   I would recommend getting it on sale, especially if the raid mode doesn't interest you at all, like me. I solely played the campaign, and I had a good enough time with it. So far I'm two hours in and it feels more like House of the Dead than RE. I've played nearly all the RE and this one seems action oriented without save points or safe rooms, but rather it autosaves at key periods and you finish chapters each of which focuses on different characters and settings (levels). This gives it an "arcade-y" feel. You have an AI companion who is basically useless, but at least you can shoot at/through them without hurting them. This is helpful because you will get swarmed often. Feels kind of like Doom (2016), although it pre-dates Doom so maybe Doom copied the format where you make your way through a claustrophobic level (RE Rev adds cheap jump scares which...aren't scary) fighting off isolated baddies and then end up in a locked "arena" where they throw continuous waves at you. Not sure why they added this but it cheapens the experience with throw away enemies that are also annoying in their level of tenacity, attacking from multiple directions. This is where your companion is slightly useful in becoming both bait as they seemingly cannot die nor have to heal, and they also attack the baddies though not nearly as often as you would like. This reminds me of a watered down RE5 or 6. More to follow, but so far I do not recommend....

Update: After exploring the ship some more I can faithfully say that it is total ass. The map, as others have pointed out, is completely useless even though it is 3D. I can see where to go, but have no otherworldly clue how to get there. Now I'm backtracking through the ship....going to take a while. I have considered uninstalling at this point but cannot refund, so sunk cost fallacy being what it is I will probably continue for a little while longer to see if I can make meaningful progress without looking up a walkthrough. I really want to like this game, but so far I cannot bring myself to do so.

Update: Almost 6 hours in and it has improved somewhat, but you have to get to episode 4 to actually enjoy it. It still plays more like a third person shooter, and being surrounded by enemies it becomes impossible to maneuver even with the quick turn mechanic. Enemies will often get behind me and attack, or spawn behind me. The dodge mechanic is almost worthless and has led to significant damage and "You're dead". Map is still difficult to use and it would have been helpful to have a way-finder mechanic similar to other games like Deadspace to at least point me in the right direction. Your location is depicted as a blue dot, and the objective a yellow dot. Problem is very frequently your objective won't appear until you have met conditions, which require a trigger point - generally this means you have to proceed in your mission until it shows you where to go but this can take a while and you end up in the wrong direction or don't hit the right "trigger" to show the objective location. Also, for some reason your objective itself is pretty vague and only appears when you hit the pause menu but not the map, which makes no sense. There aren't sub-objectives or conditions checks either. The whole thing feels very superficial and simplistic, which makes it very difficult to navigate. Sometimes enemies will also spawn out of a vent or even directly from the floor in front of you. I appreciate a jump scare as much as the next RE fan, but when it spawns and attacks leading to an unavoidable hit this causes undue frustration - like give me a friggin chance. This is worse in the "water" levels as when you are wading through waist deep water you will be attacked spontaneously, and without warning, by a multitude of creatures who will eat your face off and you can't avoid it. Grenades work well for these enemies as the grenade detonates as soon as it touches the water (you don't seem to take splash damage and for some reason your worthless AI partner is also invulnerable) - but grenades are few and far between. I still don't really recommend unless you are a hardcore RE fan. I feel like the setting is neat, but the frustrating controls and dynamics make it not worth it unless you are a completionist and "have to" play every RE game (which is why I am playing this for the first time > 10 yrs after it was published.

Update: Finally finished the game. It was a slog toward the end with a lot of navigating underwater areas, backtracking, and enemies jumping out at you. Never figured out the dodge mechanic exactly, which is necessary to avoid taking huge damage. Basically you can get killed in two or three hits, and some areas you get killed instantly if you cannot avoid attacks. The story was forgettable, along with most of the ancillary characters. If this was less an arcade style shooter and more survival horror then I would have been more forgiving. Save yourself a lot of time and skip this one. There is nothing here you haven't already seen elsewhere, but done better.

I played this when it was first ported over to Xbox One and was pretty underwhelmed by it. Going back in 2026 and the campaign for this one is just a forgettable(and sometimes frustrating) Resident Evil game. 
I can appreciate those that got to play this when it originally came out on 3DS, as having a full fledged Resident Evil game on the go would be awesome. But on home console/PC, there is a lot to be annoyed with. 

The game starts off promising, giving very much vibes of a fun survival horror game. However, you will quickly find that this isn't really survival horror, and is just a weak action horror game. The weapons all lack punch and the enemies do not give much feedback so you will constantly waste a couple bullets on enemies when they die. It gives the illusion that is like classic RE with different keys to find and whatnot but you actually just get everything linearly.  You have to fight many bullet sponge bosses that are very frustrating to deal with, especially since they have tons of other enemies in the fight.  
The character control is off, with their base speed being too slow and they turn like they are the elderly. Aiming is loose and feels sloppy. The dodge mechanic is terribly implemented. Some sections really will test your patience with the weak movement/gunplay("Mayday" fight, a timed escape with a boss enemy hounding you that made me almost uninstall the game). 
The game also is broken up episodically, which may have worked for bite sized playing on the 3DS but here its tedious. The story is blah with some truly stupid characters(Jessica, the two "comic relief" characters that you play as in pointless sections), and a plot that is just not memorable. The pacing is all over the place, and any time you leave the ship with Jill, the game screeches to a halt.

TLDR - Competently made but overshadowed by other RE titles.

Revelations clearly has a respect for classic Resident Evil. Ultimately, it's limited by the simple fact that it was a side entry made for 3DS.

The game is structured as a chapter-based Metroidvania with Jill, occasionally interrupted by disconnected corridor shooter chapters that add to the story, It's a 6-ish hour romp if you don't dillydally or die too much. You always have a partner, but there isn't ACTUALLY co-op in the story like RE5 or 6? That felt weird to me. Might just be a consequence of them reusing a lot of RE5 assets.

The actual STORY part of the story mode... tries too hard to have a cliffhanger at the end of each episode, and I feel it hurts the storytelling. It was the kind of plot I needed to piece together after the credits even though it isn't ACTUALLY complicated when you lay it out.

Weapons and combat follow the RE4 skeleton, although this was the first RE to let you aim and move simultaneously, making it feel a little less special. On Normal difficulty, enemies don't feel like much of a threat, as long as you can figure out how they work and remember to take them seriously. You can't change difficulty in the middle of a Story playthrough and I reccommend most RE veterans to play Infernal.

The inventory is like a much less clumsy version of RE6's. That game would've been more fun if weapons worked the same way.

REV1 introduced modular upgrades in the form of Custom Parts. They're the focus of "Raid Mode", which is like if RE3 Mercenaries or RE2R missions were looter shooters. I prefer my upgrades to be non-random, but if you're into that kind of gameplay, REV1 Raid Mode is still overshadowed by REV2 Raid Mode, though.

Technical complaints: Default FOV is REALLY tight, and you need mods to change it. I played in a couch setup and still got motion sick every time I swung the camera.

[h1]Revelations Reveals Nothing but Disappointment[/h1]

[i]Resident Evil Revelations returns redefined for PC complete with high quality HD visuals, enhanced lighting effects and an immersive sound experience.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
The story takes place between Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5 and focuses on series veterans Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield. The game’s narrative centers around the BSAA (Bioterrorism Security Assessment Alliance) investigating a new bioterror threat involving a virus called the T-Abyss virus. The narrative unfolds in episodic chapters, giving it a TV-series feel with “Previously on…” recaps before each section.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil: Revelations is a third-person survival horror game. To progress, you have to complete objectives like solving puzzles, defeating bosses, finding keys, and reaching specific points. Revelations focuses more on survival, evasion, and exploration than fast-paced combat, offering limited ammo, health, and movement. You can carry up to three firearms, grenades, and a knife. Weapons include handguns, shotguns, SMGs, and rifles. Gameplay is primarily third-person but switches to first-person when using the Genesis scanner or sniper rifles. In this game you can also dodge enemies’ attacks.

The Genesis scanner reveals hidden items and rewards herbs by scanning enemies. Each scan adds a percentage, with closer scans giving more. Reaching 100% grants a herb and resets the meter, though repeatedly scanning the same enemy type reduces the percentage gained. Some enemies can be scanned multiple times, and if your herb count is full, the scanner holds at 100% until you use one.

Most of the game has you playing as Jill Valentine, though some sub-episodes let you control Chris Redfield and two other characters. Firearms can be upgraded with weapon parts, and a slightly stronger melee attack can be performed on stunned enemies. Ammo and health items are scattered throughout to help manage resources.

[b][u]Raid Mode[/u][/b]
Revelations also features Raid Mode, a more action-oriented mode for one or two players. It reuses campaign locations but with tougher, varied enemy encounters. Completing stages earns experience and battle points, which can be spent on new weapons and items. As players progress, they unlock harder missions, better gear, and additional playable characters.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
The main enemies, called the Ooze, are humans grotesquely mutated by the T-Abyss virus. Their erratic, unpredictable movements make them hard to hit. Variants include melee types that rush you, ranged types that fire projectiles, explosive types that detonate when damaged, and underwater-adapted forms that attack while swimming through flooded sections of the ship.

There are also several rarer enemy types that serve as mini-bosses, along with a handful of larger, more elaborate boss encounters throughout the game.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
The main setting of the game is the abandoned cruise ship Queen Zenobia, stranded in the Mediterranean Sea. However, some episodes shift focus to other characters in different locations, such as Terragrigia—a “floating city” or “aquapolis” constructed in the Mediterranean—and even snowy, outdoor areas in Finland.

The level design is mostly linear but interconnected, with shortcuts that make revisiting areas feel natural and give the ship a labyrinthine quality. Environments are mostly claustrophobic—narrow corridors, cramped cabins, and tight mechanical rooms heighten tension, while occasional swimming and diving sections add variety. Navigation is assisted by a minimap in the top-right corner.

The lighting is surprisingly bright and the environments are well-lit, which undermines the intended horror tone. The game was marketed as a return to the series’ survival-horror roots, but in my experience, it failed to deliver any real sense of fear or dread.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
The main enemies are pale, bloated humanoid creatures with twisted, elongated limbs and claw-like appendages—disturbing remnants of the people they once were. When defeated, their bodies collapse into a puddle of blood and dark, viscous ooze. The game reinforces its maritime theme through both environment and UI design, incorporating nautical elements throughout to remind you that you are trapped aboard a massive vessel at sea.

Distant waves, sloshing water, and the metallic groan of the ship’s aging structure constantly echo around you—a constant reminder of the oceanic setting. However, the Ooze lack distinct auditory cues between their different variants. Their moans when injured or killed provide some feedback, and the wet splatter as they melt into sludge is memorable, but more variation in their sound design could have helped build tension and differentiate encounters.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
Including an arcade-style mode like Raid Mode is fine, but the overall experience—even the campaign—leans too heavily on that arcade feel. It misses the signature atmosphere and slow-building tension that define the best Resident Evil games.

The Genesis scanner also feels awkwardly implemented. Items that only exist after scanning break immersion, and constantly stopping to scan enemies and the environment interrupts the flow of action. Worst of all, the rewards are underwhelming. Gaining only a green herb from scanning makes the feature feel almost pointless. A more rewarding system—such as scanning to reveal enemy weaknesses or provide damage bonuses—would have made it feel meaningful.

The mouse controls suffer from poor mouse acceleration, making precise aiming uncomfortable and unreliable. Clearly a result of poor port optimization, this makes the PC version feel like an afterthought.

Dodging is equally frustrating. Since dodge input is tied to the same movement controls, it often activates unintentionally during normal traversal—and sometimes fails entirely when you need it. When a core defensive mechanic is this inconsistent, combat quickly becomes irritating.

Backtracking is another major issue. The Queen Zenobia already lacks visual variety, so repeatedly revisiting the same narrow corridors and small rooms becomes tiresome fast. Sometimes you even backtrack to the area you just backtracked from. Some episodes also include replays of certain areas but with different characters in another point in time. Later in the game, large portions of the ship become flooded, forcing you to swim and dive through areas you’ve already explored. This adds another layer of repetition and makes the backtracking feel even more tedious.

The inventory system is fully streamlined, with green herbs stacking up to five and each ammo type having its own slot. While convenient, this removes a classic survival horror element: having to make tough choices about what to carry.

The enemies' designs lacked intimidation and their encounters became repetitive. Several boss fights and tougher foes lean more toward annoyance than tension, largely due to the poorly executed dodge mechanic.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil: Revelations delivers a serviceable story, bridging the gap between Resident Evil 4 and 5 with a few familiar faces. However, new characters lack depth, and most plot twists are predictable, making it primarily appealing to dedicated fans eager to explore every corner of the franchise’s lore.

The action and weapon systems are competent but not particularly thrilling. Weapon upgrades add a satisfying sense of progression, though the system is fairly basic in execution.

Originally developed for the Nintendo 3DS, the game was later ported to consoles and PC. The PC version, unfortunately, suffers from uneven controls. Proper mouse and keyboard optimization should be standard; players shouldn’t have to buy a controller to enjoy a game marketed as PC-compatible.

Resident Evil: Revelations — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Ah… Revelations.
A title that promises truth — though, as I’ve learned, humanity rarely knows what to do with the truth once it finds it. What Capcom attempted here was… ambitious. A return to atmosphere, tension, and claustrophobic dread. And yet… even ambition can rot when it’s left adrift at sea.

The Queen Zenobia — a luxury cruise ship converted into a floating tomb. A fitting metaphor for the state of the world: gilded on the surface, diseased beneath. Within its decaying halls, the remnants of yet another “anti-bioterror organization” flounder against yet another viral catastrophe.
How predictable.

Enter Jill Valentine.
Ah, yes — the ever-resilient thorn in my side. Even on vacation, she finds herself wading through corpses. She hasn’t changed — stubborn, resourceful, tragically noble. Watching her navigate the Zenobia’s corridors with pistol and flashlight in hand… it’s almost nostalgic. A pity she never understood that her greatest enemy was her own morality.

Her partner, Parker Luciani, is… functional. Gruff, loyal, fond of sandwiches — the usual human clutter. Adequate muscle, limited insight. A bodyguard masquerading as a co-protagonist.

And then there’s the BSAA. My, how far the children of S.T.A.R.S. have come — from local law enforcement to global anti-bioterror operatives. I must admit, the irony is delicious: they spend their lives cleaning up Umbrella’s messes, yet never question the hands funding their missions. Truly, ignorance is evolution’s most effective tranquilizer.

Now, let’s discuss the virus — the T-Abyss.
A marine variant of the T-Virus, designed for aquatic environments. Ingenious in concept, pitiful in execution. The infected creatures — ooze, fish, hunters — are grotesque, yes, but lack the elegance of my designs. They crawl, they lurch, they flop… an undignified breed of monster. If I were still in charge of Umbrella, I would’ve thrown the entire research team overboard.

The gameplay, however, shows promise. Tight corridors, limited ammunition, the feeling of isolation pressing against the hull — all the hallmarks of true survival horror. When the Zenobia’s lights flicker and the ocean groans outside, there’s a sense of pressure, of decay.
It’s almost… beautiful.

Yet, the illusion fractures whenever the narrative surfaces. Espionage, double agents, conspiracies — all tangled in melodrama. Terragrigia, the FBC, Morgan Lansdale — names and organizations that think themselves powerful, yet crumble under scrutiny. None of them understand the virus. They wield bioweapons like children playing with scalpels.

The enemy designs deserve some praise, however. The infected crew, their bodies warped into glistening silhouettes of their former selves, embody the fear of the deep — life adapting, mutating, surviving. Were I still pursuing bioevolution, I might have stolen a few of their samples. For refinement, of course.

In the end, Revelations is an oddity — a mixture of brilliance and mediocrity. It reaches for the grandeur of the classics but remains anchored by clumsy storytelling and inconsistent pacing. Still, it captures something that many of its successors lost — atmosphere. That delicate blend of beauty and dread.

Final Assessment:
An imperfect experiment, but one worth observing.

Third-person shooter set between Resident Evil 4 and 5. Posits itself as a survival-horror game like the Resident Evils title of old, but make no mistake: this is an action game first and foremost, and plays accordingly, with hordes of enemies, plentiful ammo/health, and minimal item management and planning.

The cruise-liner setting is a good choice here, but the large interconnected map is almost completely wasted since the game railroads you in a set path for almost the entire duration of the campaign, and what little atmosphere and tension the game manages to build is routinely vented with the regular character and location switching thrust upon the player with each passing chapter.

In the end, Resident Evil: Revelations tries to appeal both to old-school Resi fans and fans of the newer action titles at the same time, leading to a game that half-asses both of its inspirations and ends up being mostly bland and uninspired as a consequence. There’s nothing here that hasn’t already been done far better by the series, and you’d be far better off simply playing one of this game’s predecessors instead.

If you're into survival horror, this game is a must-play. Resident Evil: Revelations brings back that classic RE atmosphere, where you're always on edge, low on ammo, and constantly wondering what's lurking in the shadows.

What really stands out here is the atmosphere. The Queen Zenobia ship is creepy as hell, and it feels like something's about to go wrong at any moment. The whole game has this constant sense of dread that just doesn't let up. And while the story isn't anything groundbreaking, it's still engaging enough to keep you hooked. Plus, it's a nice bridge between RE4 and RE5.

The gameplay is solid. The balance of exploration, combat, and puzzle-solving is spot on. Jill is back, and she’s just as badass as ever, with a great sidekick in Parker. The Raid Mode is also worth mentioning – it's addictive as hell. It adds a ton of replay value, and you'll find yourself coming back just to level up your weapons and tackle tougher challenges.

That said, it’s not perfect. The episodic structure can feel a bit jarring at times, and some of the enemy types get repetitive. But these are minor complaints compared to everything else the game nails.

Overall, I’d say if you’re a fan of survival horror or the RE franchise, Revelations is a no-brainer. It's a fun mix of the old-school horror vibes and the more action-oriented gameplay of later RE games. Definitely recommend it!

Resident Evil: Revelations takes place aboard the luxury cruiser, The Queen Zenobia, a vessel which is said to have ties to the terrorist organization Veltro, who caused the destruction of oceanic city, Terragricia some months prior to the beginning of the campaign. Jill and Parker, two agents for the BSAA are deployed on mission to investigate the ship, and uncover any potential bio-terror threats. Meanwhile, Chris and Jennifer, two other BSAA agents, are deployed to recover information elsewhere. Together, their stories will overlap as they learn that the Veltro threat may be connected to a much larger game of chess, with The Queen Zenobia as its central piece.

Regarding the narrative of Resident Evil: Revelations, I think it's incredible that Capcom let a five year old write the story as part of a Make A Wish initiative. The little guy really put his all into the st--.... excuse me. I've just been informed that this game was actually written by fully grown adults, who were paid for their time, and the output was prior to the rise of generative AI. The story is comically bad, even by Resident Evil standards, with characters dropping action lines which fall flat more often than not. There are moments when it lends itself to the B-movie action aesthetic that the series is known for, without any of the more subtle undertones which often provide more depth for lore nerds of the franchise. The game is just a collection of episodes, twelve in total, with wildly dated story telling choices, like a "Previously On Revelations" flashback at the beginning of each episode, like we somehow forgot what happened in the last hour (since most episodes are only 30~60 minutes long). Previously on flashbacks in video games were cursed to a very specific time in video game history. Fake out deaths can be reasonable once, but get increasingly silly when it becomes nearly every character, more than once over the course of an eight hour story. If narrative is one's driving reason to play a game, I'd suggest Revelations is one to skip.

The gameplay of Resident Evil: Revelations is more akin to an action FPS than a survival horror game, with combat feeling more arcady than tense. The game is set up to provide co-op option, with most missions seeing the controlling character accompanied by a supporting NPC who lays down fire and eats hits. NPC allies are seemingly invulnerable, as players only need to focus on controlling their own characters in combat. Every character is equipped with three weapon slots, a medical items stack, and a couple of supporting items, such as grenades. Unlike most Resident Evil: Games, there one cannot mix herbs in their inventory, and there's seemingly no limit to how much they can heal. There's a rather strange gameplay mechanic, where the player is encouraged to scan corpses, which in turn build towards recoverable items; however, the rate at which you're granted the rewards for scanning is rarely worth the player's time. Thus, the game incentivizes a more aggressive gameplay, often sending waves of enemies at the player. The player can come across a rather large collection of weapons, each of which can be modified with a variety of customizable parts. Custom parts act as feats for weapons and can range from simple damage buffs, to changing how the weapon behaves, via burst damage, or charged shots. Overall, it was fun to mix and match different custom parts on weapons, to make stronger and stronger builds. The combat is, well... incredibly easy, with every level being trivial to obtain S-Rank on with 0 deaths. As one might expect, there are a lot of modes and ways to enjoy the game after beating the campaign; however, those tend to interest me less than the main stories, so I didn't engage with them as much.

Resident Evil: Revelations would not be a game I generally recommend to most, outside of the most fanatical of Resident Evil fans. The gameplay and writing are painfully dated, and people frankly have better games to play than this now.

Back in the day when RE: Revelations first came out for the Nintendo 3DS, It was praised. Nowadays however, the game is barely brought up. Playing this HD re-release for the first time, I can see why.

In 2012, having a Resident Evil game that felt closer to being a horror game after RE5 went full-on action was a breath of fresh air. Not to mention having a brand new game of the series that plays like 4 and 5 on a handheld was novel at the time. Playing this game in 2025 however, Revelations is a very bland and forgettable experience.

The gameplay as I said is the third person shooting of 4 and 5 but it's very dumbed down here. Combat just lacks that dopamine the other games provided. Most levels are also short and lack enemy variety if not enemies altogether and are more just borderline walking sections. People said it brought back horror to the series, it's true to a certain extent. You have sections that tries to remind you that indeed RE is a horror franchise but those are few and far between. Revelations is still mostly going for this cheesy action movie feel with a story that takes itself way too seriously.

Other than the roughly 6-7 hour campaign, you can play New Game+. Not a bad idea, many RE games gave you the incentive to do multiple playtroughs but given the game's linear and repetitive nature, I just dread even the idea of replaying this. There is also Raid Mode which also doesn't do much for me because the combat in general is just boring and these looter shooter RPG mechanics they implemented just overcomplicate things when these side modes were always about having simple fun. So I guess you can see why I also won't be spending any money on these lackluster DLCs they made for this game.

All in all, Resident Evil Revelations isn't a bad game but a very mediocre one. As I said it was probably more novel back in the day to just pick this up and play in short bursts on a 3DS and it's cool Capcom decided to do an HD remaster for the game so it can be ported to other systems. However, given all the RE games you can play on PC (Including the classic games on GoG) I just see no reason to ever pick this up unless you are a hardcore Resi fan who has to play every game in the series.

I modded it with a 4x texture resolution mod, a mod that makes Jill's wetsuit black, real weapon names, more weapon sounds, and a fix for an input device warning that appears. The last mod I'll mention is the best one: FOV mod. Widening the FOV makes this game a lot more fun and playable. Enemies can spawn out of nowhere in this game, and being able to see them on your left or right is much better than not seeing them due to the narrow default FOV.

This game manages to have an interesting, albeit detached plot from previous games in the series. The main thing to talk about is the gameplay, which is segmented into episodes. This is due to the game originally being on the 3DS, which has less memory than consoles at the time and even less than the average PC today. Because of this, the game had to be cut up into episodes, albeit this only really affects rankings, which are quite easy to reach. As long as you aim decently, and don't die, you'll get an S on episodes. You keep ammo, weapons and other supplies throughout episodes, although you jump in between characters and time frames often, which I think hurts the game overall. I would've greatly preferred if you were consistently playing several episodes back to back as a specific character, and then another several back to back as another character. Instead, the game has you jumping back and forth between Jill in the present, Parker in the past, Chris in the slight past and present, to a random soldier I forgot the name of, and back to Jill. Confusing for a narrative.

Enemy design has taken a hit compared to the games that came out before this one. The primary enemies are these tall gray monsters that come in a few variants. You also run into hunters which existed before this game, as well as wolves. What makes these enemies less fun to fight are the lack of reactions they have towards your bullets. In RE4, 5, and 6, enemies would react based on where you shot them, unless they were a particular kind of enemy like a boss or rare mob. Enemies in this game instead have a sort of hidden stagger meter, that fills up as you shoot them. Eventually, they'll flinch or go into a stunned state, where you can melee them like in RE4, 5 and 6. However, you can't just shoot an enemy in the head or legs and get a free melee hit on them. You can only get the melee hit if they become completely stunned, which requires a hard hit or a specific type of grenade. One fun thing you can do is charge up melee attacks, although this isn't as good as charging attacks in other kinds of games.

On the technical side, this game cooks your CPU more than it should. Whenever you go through loading zones on the ship, it demands a lot from your CPU. I don't get it. Open world games with much more loading at play don't go this crazy. I'm guessing it's something to do with it being an older game mixing with newer CPUs.

Would recommend this to any RE fan. Just don't expect it to be RE4 quality. It's a budget version of RE4-5 and that's okay. Nexus Mods has the FOV fix, which I highly recommend.

For players who have only played the newer Resident Evil games, I would highly recommend you pick this game up. Don't be turned away just because of its old release and outdated graphics otherwise you'll miss out on experiencing an amazing game. Either way, I genuinely hope that this game ends up getting its own remake in the near future because I see major potential for newer fans to fall in love with this entry in the series.

Ah, Resident Evil: I'm On A Boat. Revelations is a port of the surprisingly chunky 3DS title, able to stand shoulder to shoulder with the original trio and even sharing some DNA with 4, 5 and 6. Grab your thalassophobia(a word meaning "scared of the giant eel in Mario 64") and dive in, it's an enjoyable 4-6 hour ride you can knock out in a casual weekend with room for replays and the addictive mercenaries/raid mode. It's also frequently on sale for $10 or less.

Rev 1 stars series cuties Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield investigating an abandoned luxury cruise ship in a world where viral monster outbreaks are no longer a threat but a promise. The mystery ties back to the outbreak in the city of Terragrigia caused by terrorist organization and book club Veltro, eager to discuss Dante's Inferno. The game actually starts with Jill and hunky lunk Parker Luciani and his two last names and soon begins rapid fire point of view jumping with Chris and Jessica who completes the quartet by being horny enough for two. Although it's from the era and clearly looks like it Rev 1 does not support co-op for the single player campaign, though it does allow local and online matchmaking for raid mode. Partners mostly provide character-building snark with moral support damage but at least they don't have to be protected.

Despite all the inherent ridiculousness of a RE5-6 era RE plot... it's good? An enjoyable popcorn action movie with some moments of genuine tension, big set pieces and amusing twists. It's not going to win any arguments over the quality of video game writing but I found myself rooting for a few characters, laughing often and enjoying the slow build up to the obvious reveals that still make for better world-building than later games will manage. In a world where bio-weapons are routine they become part of a political power play conspiracy but don't worry you'll spend most of the time shooting fish-men.

Zombies are now oozes, freaky deep trench leech monsters. There's some modern ideas, like dodging attacks with a split-second input before impact and QTE wiggle motions to get out of grabs, but the game mostly plays like RE4 or 5 with slightly ponderous tank controls and stopping to aim and shoot. You can feel that it was made for the 3DS joystick but it's quite enjoyable and eventually you'll puzzle out the extras that can be missed in the early game such as charge-up melees. It took awhile to realize my options past the instinct of always taking the headshot with oozes having brittle bones and varying weakspots, though the head/mouth usually gives extra damage anyway. Rev 1 has pleasing combat, the most surprising thing being how tanky enemies can be or the sheer number of them you may face. The roster is robust too, though often that enemy variety is lopsided with Oops!! All Hunter! segments and some enemies only showing up near the end. Makes for good raid mode ingredients, at least!

There's plenty of resource management with gun juggling, a generous but not too set of grenades for crowd control and smart ammo tracking between the many different characters you'll bounce between, with Jill being the main PoV where you can actually customize guns. Maps are simple and replayed often but get a lot done with a little and even sneak in meaningful backtracking and extras for thorough exploration. All the classic itches of modern RE are scratched here. A new itchy, not so tasty is the scanning. You can build extra heals by scanning enemies with post-combat being safer but mid-combat building faster, as well as a limited number of extras like the handprint scavenger hunt, two brief puzzle rooms and seeing some hidden enemies(though usually not practically.) What it mostly does is pad out time spent exploring rooms to reveal resources, though mercifully you get a signal if anything is near you and the range is about as big as most rooms. A neat idea with a hit or miss execution, at least it's not too obnoxious.

A super hard mode greatly remixes the enemy numbers and spawn locations and finally we have beloved series staple raid mode, aka mercenaries, where character choice and preferred gun loadout are pitted against a further remixed sets of enemy spawns in time attack stages. Try to clear them quickly and cleanly as possible, watch out for some surprises like enemy variants(extra thicc, smol, tol, etc) and steadily build resources and level up stats to push further, clear harder difficulties, try to get that s rank with just... one... more... run! 

I first bounced off Rev 1 as it starts with quite a slow burn but giving it another try I was hooked by chapter 3 with the first standout boss fight and the pace picking up. The most Rev 1 suffers from is a fair bit of stage and asset reuse but it's certainly stronger than the sum of its parts. By comparison to modern wonders like the RE 2-4 remakes or RE 7/8, well, I'd honestly play through those first, but for the RE fan that has already done so and is intrigued by this unique little entry it's a great extra.

I played this when it came out, but my Steam copy has been gathering dust for years.

Whenever I see this thing, I wonder why I just don't think about it more often, since I don't recall having any particularly negative memories of the game.

Well, it became obvious pretty quickly why. It's a painfully unremarkable spin-off.

I guess the only interesting thing about it is that it was basically a Resident Evil made for a handheld, which, at the time, probably sounded like a lot more interesting than it does today.

And being a handheld game (from a time when those consoles didn't deliver anything of note), the game essentially plays like a canned version of a regular Resident Evil with shallow gimmicks.

It's somewhere between sticking with the more straightforward linearity of the more action-focused installments of the franchise and the slower-paced horror, claustrophobic level design, and sharp combat rules of the older games.

And I don't think the game manages to pull off either of those facets consistently.

It's a very unfocused game, organized into episodes optimized for short sessions rather than a continuous, unfolding experience. The traditional design formula of the series is left aside in favor of flashbacks, perspective jumps, and very uninspired exploration in bland environments, obtuse resource gathering, and boring combat sequences.

It's so monotonous and uncreative that it feels like the only idea they had was to add a gimmick of scanning the environment for extra ammo and healing items... You know, instead of you seeing them with your own eyes (Except sometimes you find items normally).

Combat is a mix of barely interactive damage sponges, excessive ammo, and weapons that sound and feel very weak. It's not a very well thought out combination and it's not particularly enjoyable.

And as expected, the production values ​​are pretty low, resulting in a presentation package with blurry assets, mediocre audio, low-res pre-rendered cutscenes, and very weak atmosphere.

Which doesn't help at all the rather stupid, lifeless and intrusive story they were trying to tell.

So yeah... It's a pretty average and forgettable game. However, it has enough polish in its execution to be at least passable. 

The pace is reasonably good, i guess? And the art direction is reasonable and has some positive points (Especially the enemy design).

The short mission structure with no significant continuity between them means it's quite easy to play just a few of them at a time and still make significant progress. It ends before it actually gets boring.

It's not a big game and they've done their best to not make it a complete waste of time.

The approach to higher difficulties, from what I remember, is quite interesting (although you definitely shouldn't play the game on Infernal difficulty from the scratch), with remixed enemy encounters and item positioning and an even greater emphasis on small mechanics, like dodge and melee.

And then there's the Raid mode, which can keep you entertained for much longer than the campaign.

So, all in all, it's a pretty average experience, but not bad enough to be offensive. 

It's worth it if you get a good discount, even if it's just to complete your collection.

Resident Evil: Revelations is one of the most underrated entries in the franchise, and honestly, one of my personal favorites. The story is gripping from start to finish, packed with classic RE twists, shady organizations, and just enough camp to keep it fun. What really sets this game apart is the way it shifts perspectives, you don’t just play as Jill Valentine, but switch between multiple characters, each with their own piece of the puzzle. It keeps the pacing fresh and the stakes high.

The setting is also a standout. Exploring the Queen Zenobia, an abandoned cruise ship lost at sea, gives the game a claustrophobic and eerie atmosphere that takes you right back to the survival horror roots of the series. The mix of tight corridors, creaking metal, and dark waters surrounding you creates a tension that few other RE games replicate.

And let’s talk about Raid Mode. Back when the game was in its prime and the community was active, Raid was incredible. It offered endless replayability with tons of weapons, enemies, and characters to unlock. Running missions, leveling up, grinding for rare gear, it scratched that itch between PvE and arcade fun in a way few other Resident Evil modes ever have.

That said, the game isn’t without flaws. The Genesis scanner, while a cool idea, gets repetitive pretty quickly. Scanning every enemy and hidden item slows the pacing more than it adds depth. Also, the controls haven’t aged particularly well, especially in 2025. They’re functional, but clunky by today’s standards.

Honestly, Revelations deserves a proper remaster. With modernized controls and improved visuals, this game could shine brighter than ever. It’s a unique blend of horror, action, and mystery that stands out within the Resident Evil franchise, and it deserves more love than it gets.

If you’ve never played it, give it a shot it might just surprise you !

When Resident Evil: Revelations first launched on 2012, it surprised fans and critics alike. It wasn’t just a portable spin-off—it was a carefully crafted, atmospheric survival horror game that brought the series closer to its roots than Resident Evil 5 or 6 ever did. Years later, it remains a strong entry in the franchise—especially for fans who miss the tension and slower pacing of classic Resident Evil.

Set between the events of Resident Evil 4 and 5, Revelations follows series mainstays Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield as they investigate a bioterrorist threat aboard a seemingly abandoned cruise ship—the Queen Zenobia. The ship is a brilliant setting: claustrophobic, eerie, and dripping with atmosphere. It recalls the Spencer Mansion or Raccoon City Police Department in the best way.

The gameplay strikes a satisfying balance between survival horror and action. Limited ammo, creepy corridors, and puzzle-solving are front and center. But make no mistake—this is still a modern RE title, and gunplay feels tight and responsive. The addition of the scanner tool, which encourages players to explore every inch of the environment for hidden items, adds a nice layer of engagement and resource management.

Revelations adopts an episodic structure, complete with "Previously on..." segments at the start of each chapter. It’s a clever format that suits portable play and helps pace the story well. The narrative jumps between different characters and locations, occasionally breaking away from the ship to follow Chris or other agents in more action-oriented sequences. These side missions vary in quality but serve to break up the pacing.

While originally built for a handheld, Revelations looks remarkably good, especially in its HD console ports. The lighting, in particular, plays a big role in the game’s tense atmosphere, casting flickering shadows down narrow hallways. The monster designs—oozing, mutated waterlogged horrors—are grotesque and fitting.

Some textures and animations show their age, but the art direction more than compensates. On Switch, the game runs smoothly both docked and handheld, making it an ideal platform for revisiting this compact horror adventure.

The soundtrack and sound design are effective in building dread. Creeping footsteps, ambient hums, and distant groans elevate the tension. Voice acting, however, is uneven. While Jill’s performance is solid, some supporting characters veer into camp or outright parody, which can clash with the game’s otherwise serious tone.

Aside from the main campaign, Revelations includes Raid Mode, a surprisingly addictive bonus mode that plays like an arcade-style shooter with RPG elements. You fight through levels filled with enemies, unlock new gear, and level up your characters. It's a great reason to keep playing after the story ends and offers a different flavor of fun for action-oriented players.

Resident Evil: Revelations succeeds where many spin-offs fail: it understands what fans love about the series. With strong pacing, classic horror vibes, and enough modern polish, it’s a return to form that helped re-center the franchise before Resident Evil 7 officially revived survival horror.

Recommended for: Fans of classic RE atmosphere, players craving portable horror, and those looking for a balanced blend of tension and action.
Not for: Players who dislike slower pacing, limited ammo, or backtracking.

Resident Evil Revelations 1 is a solid entry in the series, taking place between the events of the fourth and fifth main games. The story is structured well and keeps the player interested without becoming too complex. It gives a good balance of mystery and action, fitting in smoothly with the overall timeline of the series. The game builds tension effectively and keeps a steady pace from start to finish.

The graphics are quite good, especially considering the game was originally made for a handheld system. The environments are detailed and help create a dark and tense atmosphere. The gameplay system is well-designed, offering a mix of exploration, shooting, and limited resources. Raid Mode is a bonus mode available outside the main story, playable in both solo and co-op modes.

In conclusion, Resident Evil Revelations 1 is a good game with strong gameplay, well-made settings. 💬 Playtime: Enough to know the Queen Zenobia has trust issues.

This game is like that one cruise vacation that sounded great in the brochure — until you realized the Wi-Fi sucks and someone onboard is trying to infect you with a bioweapon.

✅ The Good:

Surprisingly solid atmosphere — the Queen Zenobia is creepy in all the right ways.

Puzzles that actually make you stop and think (but not in a "Google the solution" way).

Exploration is satisfying and well-paced.

A nice middle ground between old-school horror and action — even if it wobbles.

❌ The Bad:

Why is there no run button?! Jill feels like she’s walking through peanut butter.

The story is... well, bless its heart. Generic characters and awkward pacing.

Combat feels clunky at times, and enemy design leans more weird than scary.

It tries to be serious but ends up being melodrama with guns.

🎮 The controls and narrative might frustrate, but honestly? I still had a good time. It’s no RE4, but it’s miles better than Operation Raccoon City. A flawed but worthy entry for fans of the series — and an okay starting point for newcomers who want a taste of that RE tension without committing to a full outbreak.

Final Score? 6.5/10 — Would explore haunted luxury cruise again (with reservations).

Resident Evil: Revelations — Review

I spent over 130 hours with this game, and I still think it’s one of the most balanced entries in the series. It brings back the classic survival horror atmosphere but mixes it with enough modern action to feel fresh. The episodic structure works surprisingly well, keeping the suspense up and making the story flow like a TV show.

The gameplay feels tight once you get used to it. Managing limited ammo, exploring tight corridors, and dealing with grotesque enemies all capture that old-school Resident Evil tension. Raid Mode is the real highlight though — it’s fast, addictive, and easily adds dozens of hours of replay time.

The story is solid and fits nicely between Resident Evil 4 and 5. The setting on the Queen Zenobia ship is great — dark, claustrophobic, and full of atmosphere. It gives the whole game a unique identity that stands out even years later.

Not everything is perfect. Some sections drag on because of repetitive backtracking, and the controls can feel a bit stiff compared to newer titles. The pacing also dips here and there, but nothing major enough to ruin the experience.

Overall, Resident Evil: Revelations strikes a strong balance between horror and action. It’s atmospheric, replayable, and still fun to return to. For anyone who enjoys classic Resident Evil vibes with a bit of modern polish, it’s an easy recommendation.
