A middling entry in the RE franchise. I give it a Thumbs Up, but a small one. 

It exists in that weird period between RE5 and RE6 where Capcom was unsure on where to take the series. This game largely plays similarly to RE5, but more of an emphasis on classic RE: find keys to open doors and get from A to B. 

It unfortunately suffers from the bizarre choice to make the game episodic. Yeah... this has not aged well at all. If anything, this game would have greatly benefited from being just Jill on the ship. No Parker and no other scenarios. Just JIll exploring around on this large ship, because the design of the ship itself is quite Resident Evil-y.

In fact, there's a mission in the game's side mode, Raid Mode, that really should have been what the main campaign was: Ghost Ship has you trek through majority of the ship and fight increasingly difficult enemies as you progress. 

Instead, the main campaign will interrupt your current gameplay flow by throwing in different episodes with characters in different areas that you honestly don't give a crap about. It's kind of annoying. You'll be playing as Jill going through the ship and just having a good time exploring, but Oh No - we need to know the lore on Terragrigia and what happened to Parker and Jessica on the day it fell. We also apparently deeply needed to know the lore on what Chris and Jessica were up to during all this while exploring a bland snowy tundra. These side segments play just as well as I am describing them - it's easy to tell that they were developed after the ship was as they just feel so tacked on. 

When you do play as Jill, the game is mostly fun... as long as you aren't fighting a lot of enemies. This game's big bad BOW is the Oozes. Basically, imagine if you took the Regenerators from RE4 and made them more goofy. There's a wide variety of what these Oozes will come in: some just shamble at ya, some will shoot stuff at you, some have really long claws and will try to rip you up, some explode, some have a shield and sword and act like zombie knights. 
It's interesting to see what they did with the idea of the Oozes, but fighting them ranges from easy-peasy to extremely frustrating. 
Constantly, you'll be shot at by something off screen, and you'll be like "Where the hell did that come from??? Oh. That dude way over there." 
And the knight ones can be quite a threat when you destroy one of its parts. 
Destroy its torso and you got a walking electric tentacle spamming slaps at you. 
Destroy its legs and now you got this crawling lunging sword coming at you. 

Cool ideas, but boy does it get frustrating to deal with especially in Raid Mode where the enemies get different modifiers. Some get super speed. Some get a big buff to their physical attack power. Some get super tanky and take forever to kill. Etc. 

Raid Mode itself was a good idea, but Jesus is it grindy as hell. I don't think it's actually possible to complete Raid Mode without using co-op at some point. Maybe you can, but damn, you will be grinding a metric ass ton. Interestingly enough, completing the Ghost Ship level with a Trinity Bonus (no damage taken, all enemies killed, and be at the appropriate level) gives you some of the best weapon parts in the game - the problem is - you definitely need some of that gear to complete Ghost Ship. It's a weird circle of dependencies. I do not envy the person who completed Ghost Ship without any of that gear as that must have been one hell of a slog to play through. 

I actually prefer the 3DS version of this game's Raid Mode as it was way more straight-forward. I don't know why they felt the need to make it so MMO-y in this version. 

So, Revelations as a whole is decent, but it has its quirky rough spots. I very tacitly recommend it if you are just looking for something to scratch an RE itch or if you want to play a grindy loot based third-person-shooter in Raid Mode. It has its fun moments - especially when you get to explore the ship, but the lows are deep. If you can put up with, give it a play.

Resident Evil Revelations is an intriguing entry in the franchise, one that tries to balance classic survival horror elements with a more action-oriented modern approach. 
While it has its moments, the overall experience feels uneven, with flashes of brilliance overshadowed by some lackluster choices...
The game starts strong with its initial ship segment aboard the Queen Zenobia. 
This setting is easily the highlight of the experience, evoking a sense of claustrophobia and dread that harkens back to the series’ survival horror roots. 
Exploring the eerie, water-drenched corridors of the ship reminded me of "Cold Fear", a similarly atmospheric game that made excellent use of its isolated oceanic setting! 
For a while, the game captures the kind of creeping tension that fans of the franchise crave.
Unfortunately, this focus on suspense doesn’t last. 
As the story branches out to different characters and locations, the atmosphere gives way to action-heavy sequences that dilute the tension built in the opening hours. 
While the variety in environments and characters adds scope to the narrative, it comes at the cost of the intimate horror that made the ship so compelling.
Gameplay is a mixed bag. 
The return of limited ammo and resources adds a welcome layer of strategy, but the controls and combat mechanics can feel clunky at times, especially during more frantic encounters. 
The enemy design is also hit-or-miss, while some creatures are genuinely creepy, others come across as uninspired and repetitive.
The story, while serviceable, leans heavily into melodrama and convoluted conspiracies that are hard to take seriously. 
Jill Valentine is a welcome protagonist, but the supporting cast is less memorable, with some characters feeling more like caricatures than fully realized individuals.
On the technical side, the game looks great for its time, especially considering its origins on handheld platforms. 
The lighting and environmental details are standout features, but the game’s pacing issues and reliance on action undermine the strong first impression.
In the end, Resident Evil Revelations is a game of two halves. 
The initial ship sequence is fantastic, delivering a chilling and immersive experience that fans of classic survival horror will appreciate. 
But as the game progresses, it loses its way, becoming just another action-heavy entry in the series.
It’s worth playing for the Queen Zenobia sections alone, but don’t expect the rest of the game to maintain the same level of quality.

Surprisingly it all comes together fairly well! It's FAST, much more straightforward than other RE games, even WITH the backtracking. However things develop quickly and there are some unexpected twists and turns for good measure. The story is a 7/10 but interesting enough to keep things fresh. The episodic nature and disjointed perspective of the plot being told by different characters and flashbacks are a new take on the traditional linear RE plot. You to experience the story from the past, the present, and through the eyes of all your favorite characters! It's novel and it works pretty well. 

It's definitely worth a play if you're searching for a light experience. It's not a masterclass, but it's a fun time.

[b]TL; DR[/b] This is without a doubt my favourite [i]Resident Evil[/i] spinoff title, did my playtime give that away? It has everything I want, crazy conspiracies, fun encounters and enemies, heavy-handed literary references, and I, I can still fight.
I crave spinoff titles for my favourite IPs.

[b]Note[/b] this is about the rise of the BSAA, taking place just before the events of [i]Resident Evil 5: Lost in Nightmares[/i]

[h1] Story [/h1]
Jill, and Parker arrive at the Queen Zenobia, the derelict luxury cruiser, she disappeared a year ago, but now she has resurfaced, and along with her comes the resurgence of Il Veltro, the bioterrorists responsible for the Terragrigia Panic and the criminals who managed to kidnap Chris Redfield… 
Chris is somewhere on the Queen Zenobia, but as you track him down the BSAA discovers that not all things are as they seem, it is time to learn the truth.
So: Abandon hope all ye who enter here.

[i]Revelations[/i] is an episodic title, and it exploits that to frame the entire things as a TV series, it ends on cliffhangers, it recaps the previous instalment, and it wants to keep you guessing.
Sometimes they go a bit overboard with the twists and turns, but it is fun, it is enjoyable to see new revelations each episode that make you second guess the motives of your colleagues, and corporate rivals. What is the truth of Queen Zenobia? Is everything distraction and misdirection? You will have to play the next episode to find out!
This more focused and self-contained story makes the setting seem larger, that things are happening outside of the mainline games, and that the villains have had lasting effects on the world around them. It does not need to do more than a couple of references here and there to succeed in that because it introduces characters and groups to make the world feel more vibrant, and alive.

[i]Resident Evil[/i] is a series filled with groups with nonsensical ambitions, but Il Veltro is one of the more bizarre ones, they are led by a former university lecturer who opposed the construction of a floating city because it is powered by solar energy, and included cooperation between the EU and the US, or something, but despite that it comes across as intimidating, and its leadership comes across as almost charismatic. He is dangerous, and he has the means the cause terrible devastation if left alone. 
I also love much they quote Dante’s [i]Inferno[/i], it is so heavy handed and not at all subtle that it becomes amazing, especially how it relates to Veltro in particular, they are Italian ultranationalists, and they are led by someone who has read at least that one book, is he using [i]Inferno[/i] because he is Italian, and it has sick lines? Or because it is the only book he knows? Who can say!

[h1] Presentation [/h1]
The Queen Zenobia is a beautiful ship complete with an ornate dining hall, a casino, and sleeping quarters, it is also an abandoned seafaring vessel with dilapidated corridors, and spartan sections dedicated to the crew.
It is a great place to explore, there is a lot of things to see, and you never get bored with it. Not only is the Queen Zenobia a complete world onto itself but you get even more variety, as they let you explore the futuristic Terragrigia and freezing mountain paths during certain episodes.
Most of these areas are filled with Oozes, and other T-Abyss mutants, and as you can hear from the name, they ooze, they are slimy, disgustingly wet, and they have this mouth proboscis that is outright revolting. They also draw some inspiration from deep-sea creatures, who are generally strange enough as is, not only that but they stagger along in a very unsettling way, that makes fighting them very creepy.
In terms of [i]Resident Evil[/i] designs they are among the most inspired, and disconcerting.

The OST is mostly there to heighten this impression, complete with these creepy disharmonic loops, solemn pianos, and chilling violins, it makes normal exploration unsettling and serves well to increase the tension of combat.
There are a couple of standout tracks, [i]O vendetta di Dio[/i] is exceedingly memorable, it feels imperious, and epic, like you are an ant, and how dare an ant stand in their way?
Yet it is quite funny because the title track [i]Revelations[/i] is also hard to forget, not only because it is the recap song, and you hear it a dozen times, but because it is smooth, it immediately sets you in the mood of a thriller and the deep seas.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
As one might expect [i]Revelations[/i] plays a lot like the other 3rd person [i]Resident Evil[/i] titles. You have a gun, you have melee, you collect things and solve a couple of puzzles.
What sets [i]Revelations[/i] apart is the multitude of player characters, the scanner you will need to properly stock up on resources and the expansive world that was absent after [i]Resident Evil 4[/i].

Stalking the halls of the Queen Zenobia, dealing with problems as they arise, slowly uncovering the mystery, all while fighting off a swarm of Oozes is awesome. There are ambushes all over, encounters generally designed to catch you off-guard, and a couple of victory laps. Enemies are varied, mixed together to complement each other’s strengths, and cover their weaknesses, which ensures that the encounters are always different, and challenge you in different ways, meaning you will never get bored.
Add a couple of entirely optional areas with neat rewards, some great bosses (sometimes featuring adds to heighten to the stress), unique encounter designs for each of the four player characters which let the developers experiment without detracting from the main experience and you are left with a thrilling and amazing game.

Yet, what I find most satisfying about [i]Revelations[/i] is the follow-up attacks, which should be obvious for anyone who enjoys the 3rd person entries, since they have always felt impactful, but now they let you charge them up, letting you build anticipation and power before delivering a devastating strike, and knocking them down. It is hard to describe how thrilling it can be to deliver a fully charged attack on a boss, so it is something that is best experience for oneself.
They also gave us a dodge mechanic, and it feels [i]great[/i] to dodge a powerful attack, it is perfect to get out of tight spots, but it almost feels overpowered, once you get the hang of it. Of course, it is nearly mandatory on higher difficulties, cause if you run out of ammunition you are left with the knife, and trying to deal with a Scagdead, is um, not recommended without dodging.
You fall into a rhythm, tapping an enemy on their weak spots, weaving past other enemies to knock out a threat in one fell strike, as stated, it is satisfying, and these core mechanics are more than enough to carry the entire experience.

[h2]RAID MODE[/h2]
I love Raid mode, most of my playtime is in Raid mode, and it is not difficult to fathom why. 
It is an optional mode that builds on the combat, giving you increased customisability, and a whole host of levels of varying degrees of difficulty.
It utilizes the enemy roster in ways that were not reasonable in the campaign, adding challenges that were not narratively possibly during the story, and changing bosses up to make them even more imposing, Raid mode is great fun with a friend, but even solo is enjoyable.

The absolute peak of it, is the Ghost Ship, a veritable gauntlet of enemies, literally the entire Queen Zenobia at once, filled with every enemy and every boss you can think of. It is not only filled with difficult encounters, and exciting rewards, but it is also an endurance test, a drain on your resources, and the closest [i]Revelations[/i] ever comes to properly forcing you to manage your resources.
Play Ghost Ship, it is great, if you are prepared.

Resident Evil Revelations : By Triple F

"Resident Evil Revelations" is a notable entry in Capcom’s celebrated franchise, released initially for the Nintendo 3DS in 2012 before finding its way to other platforms. Positioned as a bridge between the more horror-focused earlier titles and the action-heavy sequels, the game successfully strikes a balance between survival horror and action, offering a refreshing return to the series’ roots while embracing modern gameplay elements. Set between the events of "Resident Evil 4" and "Resident Evil 5," "Resident Evil Revelations" features fan-favorites Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield on a suspenseful mission aboard a seemingly abandoned cruise ship, the Queen Zenobia, creating a creepy, claustrophobic setting that reintroduces classic Resident Evil tension.

The atmosphere in "Resident Evil Revelations" is one of its strongest aspects, with the Queen Zenobia standing as one of the most memorable and eerie locations in the series. Inspired by the classic mansion from the original "Resident Evil," the ship is filled with narrow hallways, dark corners, and winding passages, perfectly designed to induce dread and a sense of isolation. The confined spaces on the ship limit players’ mobility, intensifying encounters with enemies and adding to the feeling of being trapped. As players explore the ship, they uncover chilling environmental details and remnants of a disturbing history, keeping tension high throughout. This setting is complemented by the game’s moody lighting and sound design, which work together to craft an atmosphere that is both haunting and immersive.

The storyline follows Jill Valentine as she searches for her partner, Chris Redfield, who has reportedly gone missing on the Queen Zenobia. Jill teams up with a new partner, Parker Luciani, as they face a new threat from a bioterrorist group called Veltro, responsible for a virus outbreak that led to the city of Terragrigia's destruction. The narrative unfolds in episodic format, revealing different perspectives through playable flashbacks, shifting between multiple characters across various locations. This structure helps maintain momentum and breaks up the pace, allowing the game to weave together an intriguing mystery. The episodic design also lends itself well to tension-building cliffhangers, encouraging players to push forward and uncover the truth behind the events on the Queen Zenobia.

Gameplay in "Resident Evil Revelations" finds a satisfying balance between survival horror and action, embracing resource management, exploration, and combat. Ammo and healing items are limited, requiring players to strategize and conserve resources, a welcome return to the survival horror staples that were sidelined in more action-focused sequels. The game also introduces the Genesis scanner, a device used to scan enemies and locate hidden items, adding a unique investigative mechanic. Scanning enemies rewards players with health items when completed, adding a risk-reward element to combat. This tool not only encourages exploration but also serves as a tactical aid, giving players insight into enemy weaknesses and encouraging a more thoughtful approach to encounters.

The enemy design in "Resident Evil Revelations" also sets it apart, with a new type of threat called the Ooze, a slimy, grotesque creature that brings a different style of horror to the series. These enemies are disturbing in appearance and require players to adapt to their unique attack patterns. Some variations of the Ooze are fast and aggressive, while others, like the heavily armored Scagdead, require a different approach due to their resilience and strength. While these enemies aren’t as iconic as the zombies or Ganados from previous entries, they effectively create tension and force players to think strategically, especially in the game’s more confined environments.

"Resident Evil Revelations" also introduces Raid Mode, a multiplayer feature separate from the main campaign that allows players to tackle levels cooperatively while battling waves of enemies. Raid Mode is a highlight for many fans, offering a surprisingly deep and addictive experience. Players can level up their characters, earn currency to buy better weapons, and tackle increasingly challenging stages with friends or AI partners. This mode extends the game’s replay-ability significantly, providing additional content that is rewarding and skill-based, with the potential to unlock unique weapons and abilities as players progress.

Visually, "Resident Evil Revelations" impresses, particularly considering its 3DS origins. The upgraded HD versions on other platforms improve textures, lighting, and character models, making it feel polished and visually appealing even years after its initial release. The attention to detail in environmental design, from the rusting, waterlogged hallways of the Queen Zenobia to the ruined city of Terragrigia, enhances the game’s immersion and sense of horror. Capcom’s work in porting the game to larger platforms is commendable, retaining the eerie aesthetic and high-quality graphics that contribute to its unsettling atmosphere. Sound design, with ambient noises, creepy music, and ominous silences, enhances the game’s haunting tone, adding to the sense of foreboding that pervades every corner of the ship.

In closing, "Resident Evil Revelations" succeeds as a bridge between classic survival horror and action, delivering a satisfying, suspenseful experience that pays homage to the series’ origins while still embracing the changes brought by newer entries. With its strong atmosphere, engaging narrative structure, challenging gameplay, and the addition of Raid Mode, the game remains a fan favorite and a testament to Capcom’s ability to evolve the franchise while respecting its roots. Though it may not reinvent the series, "Resident Evil Revelations" stands as a refreshing return to form, proving that the series can still thrive in settings that prioritize horror, atmosphere, and strategic gameplay over sheer action.

TL;DR: A fun Resident Evil game.
Pros:
- Gameplay: Shooting feels great and ammo is scarce enough that you never feel too comfortable while exploring. The Scanner is also a fun edition that makes combat a bit more interesting (does one risk scanning a living enemy too try and get some desperately needed health or risk trying to take the enemy on with whatever health one has at that time). Puzzles are much easier then previous entries and seem to play a less prominent role this time round.
- Graphics: Surprisingly nice for a game originally released on the 3DS. The Aesthetic of the cruise ship we spend much the game on is great and suitably eerie. 
- Story: Cheesy but in a [mostly] good way. Very Resident Evil. If you've played a previous Resident Evil game you know what your getting and it doesn't deviate that much from that well trod path. The Dante theme is also hilariously hamfisted. 

Neutral:
- Characters: Legacy characters here are as fun as ever. But new characters are fairly flat and occasionally strange. Quint and Keith in particular highlight the latter issue. Both feel like they come from a different game and there humour is atrocious [and not in a fun way].
- Length: Took about 6 hours for me to beat the main campaign on Normal. 

Cons:
- Bosses/Enemy variety: Was not a fan of the 3 or 4 "big" bosses this game gives us. Some felt appropriately foreshadowed but mechanically there kinda boring, Enemy variety also wasn't 100% up to snuff.

Conclusion:
A fun Resident Evil game for the season but not one that redefines the series in any major way.

Resident Evil: Revelations follows primarily Jill and Parker, members of the anti-bioterror organization BSAA, as they explore a seemingly-abandoned ship that's rumored to have been re-purposed as headquarters for a major bioterrorist organization. Revelations' gameplay is most similar to Resident Evil 5, with less of a focus on limited inventory and puzzle-solving and more of a focus on frequent combat and gun-play. If I had to describe Resident Evil: Revelations with one word, I'd be stuck between "fine" and "weird". On the one hand, it's "fine"; not particularly good, not particularly bad, Revelations is a serviceable action-horror-zombie game with a cinematic story to keep you invested for at least a brief moment. On the other hand, it's "weird"; Revelations makes a lot of strange decisions in this entry in order to spice up the "traditional RE gameplay and story". Notably I think of the scanner tool, which you use to scan enemies and the environment in order to obtain healing items and secret stashes of ammo or trinkets, as these items are generally not as present in the environment. A strange tool that doesn't necessarily detract from the experience, but definitely doesn't add to it either. Additionally, the story is written and broken up into episodes, not just in the figurative sense but also in the literal sense, with writing like a telenovella and "Previously on Resident Evil: Revelations" recap segments before every new episode. I can't help but feel at times playing through this game that I'm actually just playing through some random late night TV show from the mid-2000s. In summary, Resident Evil: Revelations isn't necessarily a good or bad game, it's just kinda fine and just kinda weird. I wouldn't go out of my way to recommend it to somebody, but you probably won't hate it either, as you'll still get to experience some decent zombie-shooting action and an easy-to-digest popcorn flick of a story.

[h1] A Thrilling Revelation to Survival Horror [/h1]
[h2] Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5) [/h2]



"Resident Evil Revelations" is a captivating addition to the Resident Evil franchise that successfully combines classic survival horror elements with modern gameplay mechanics. Set between the events of "Resident Evil 5" and "Resident Evil 6," the storyline follows Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield as they investigate a mysterious ship filled with terrifying creatures and dark secrets.

Atmospheric Setting:
The game excels in creating a creepy, immersive environment aboard the Queen Zenobia. The foreboding atmosphere, combined with great sound design, keeps you on edge as you navigate through dark corridors and encounter grotesque enemies.

Engaging Gameplay:
The controls feel tight and responsive, allowing for a satisfying combat experience. The mix of exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat feels balanced, with plenty of room for strategic thinking regarding resource management. The introduction of new enemy types, like the terrifying Ooze and the versatile J'avo, adds variety and keeps the gameplay fresh.

Graphics and Visuals:
The visuals are impressive, especially for a game that originally launched on the Nintendo 3DS. The remastered version on Steam boasts enhanced graphics that showcase detailed character models and beautifully rendered environments.

Co-op Mode:
The inclusion of Raid Mode offers an enjoyable multiplayer experience where you can team up with friends or tackle challenges solo. This mode adds significant replayability, with various characters and upgrades to unlock.

Minor Flaws:
While the game shines in many areas, some players might find the story a bit convoluted at times, and the pacing can slow down during certain segments. However, these issues don't detract significantly from the overall experience.

In conclusion, "Resident Evil Revelations" is a must-play for fans of the franchise and newcomers alike. It masterfully blends horror elements with engaging gameplay, offering hours of suspenseful fun. If you're looking for a game that can both frighten and entertain, look no further!

Good ol' Resident Evil at its finest. If you want to experience RE on a boat/middle of the ocean, then you will enjoy this game! If you are a Resident Evil fan, you MUST play this game!

It isn't a return to form for the series, but it does take elements from new and old resident that makes for a fun game. Especially now that Resident evil is more of a horror series again, I think this game fits into a nice niche for fans of the action titles while also managing to have a creepy atmosphere that longtime fans would have been missing at the time of RE5. All of this is wrapped up in a story that I think is fun and is structured like a prestige television show. All that being said, it is important to note that this game originally came out on the 3DS which contributed to some of its best and worst elements.

In terms of mechanics, I especially like the new gun modification system.  exploration is now rewarded with gun parts which can be used to change the stats on your guns. They don't drastically change the behavior of weapons, they usually are just "20% more damage" "10% faster reload" "50% magazine size", but there are a couple standout ones like a gun part that reduces spread on a shotgun or a part that lets you charge a shot for more damage. overall I think these are a nice reward and by the end I was excited to test different combinations on my weapons. Infernal difficulty seems to expect you to have played normal and have gathered a good collection of parts so its worth going out of your way for them to take into new game+.

Combat in general is alright. This game features a dodge mechanic which was a lot simpler than I originally thought, but it does add some depth if you are concerned about ammo conservation. I don't think this game is very strict in resources, but they are limited. The pistol falls off by the half-way point in my opinion, and I spent my first playthrough hardly carrying it as opposed to the other weapons you get. Combat is a major focus in this game which is evident by the inclusion of raid mode, a PvE arcade mode similar to mercinaries from previous RE games. I didn't bother playing much of it, but if that is your thing it does give the game an extra dose of content. There are even some exclusive unlocks and costumes from playing the mode.

If you hated RE5 and RE6 to the point that you get sick at the thought of action in a RE game, then yeah pass this one. Otherwise I liked it enough to want to play it again after finishing the campaign. The only other deterrent I can think of is that the story and characters can be a bit cringeworthy, but I do think that it is a unique narrative in the RE universe and I'd be lying if I said that there weren't exciting moments that hooked me. I atleast think its worth getting on sale if you have any interest in it, but I also think it is worth the 20 dollars admission if you got the cash

RE: Revelations provides a really unique take on the Resident Evil franchise. of course, there's the standard virus-infected critters, the running around to solve puzzles and collect items, some form of gun management, and the likes. but there's also a few really interesting aspects. for one, i think using the genesis is a really cool idea. with the bonus of scanning enemies being herbs, there's some incentive to use it (unless youre a no dmg run pro). the genesis also detects different useful items and hand prints located around.

the monsters of RE: Revelations are also really interesting. the Farfarellos are modified versions of the Hunters, which are seen in several of the other RE titles. for me, it was nice to see the Hunter-type monsters again, as I've never played any of the games they were featured in (though ive watched playthrus). the Scarmiglione reminds me a bit of RE6's Rasklapanje, mostly due to the shared ability to split apart and survive/continue attacking. Of course, we also have Fenrir, which is just one of the many infected dogs in the RE franchise.

although the story told by RE: Revelations isn't necessary for fans or casual players to understand the main story line of RE 1-8, it definitely provides some fun gameplay and lore for those who want to dive a little deeper into the RE franchise.

revelations kinda drops the ball on the ammo management aspect of resident evil. in most of the games, you have to be careful about wasting ammo and youre more likely to dodge past enemies. by boss fights or by the end of the game, youre more likely to have enough ammo to waste some shots and kill enemies for convenience. in revelations, however, youve got a ridiculous amount of ammo. i constantly find myself having to leave ammo behind because i cant carry anymore. unless youre missing 90% of your shots, youll likely have to leave ammo behind too. its not a bad problem to have, but its very different coming from other resident evil games where ammo scarcity is a common problem leading to more cautious gameplay.

speaking of dodging, the dodging mechanic in revelations is got awful. you have to time your dodges just right by pressing w or space. it's so finicky though, as sometimes it works and other times it doesnt. other than watching the movements of the enemies, theres no visual indicators of when you can/should dodge. resident evil 4 (both the original and remake) do a nice job of this, as you can parry attacks with your knife pretty easily and there are visual indicators/QTEs for when you can dodge. revelations doesnt have that. dodging an attack may or may not work, and it gets pretty annoying during boss fights or evading insta-death attacks. as well, parrying can be kinda annoying too, as that has very strict timing.

other than those minor inconveniences or poor game mechanics, the only major issue i have with the game is that when i save and quit, the game physically cannot close all the way. in order to fully close the game, i actually have to shut down/restart my pc in order for everything to properly close. there are definitely greater issues that could have happened (like the game being entirely nonfunctional), but it's still an annoying problem to have. still, the game is tons of fun and a few inconveniences isnt the end of the world.

[h1]⚠︎☣︎ Action and Frustration ☣︎⚠︎[/h1]

[b]☣︎ Intro ☣︎[/b]
The mission: rescue Chris as Jill. As someone who knew Jill from RE3 remake (whichwas awful) and RE5 (where she was mostly brainwashed), this game finally made me understand why Jill is iconic!

[b]☣︎ Gameplay ☣︎[/b] 
The game is action-packed with barely any breathers, you're constantly dealing with enemies. While the enemy design starts off interesting, it quickly becomes repetitive, especially with the generous ammo supply. Enemies move at a slow pace to make aiming easier while moving, but this made the combat too easy for my taste.

[b]☣︎ Levels ☣︎[/b]
The level design is mostly great, but the backtracking was infuriating. Running back and forth for one item, through multiple aisles, elevators, and obstacles, was enormously annoying. Even Jill acknowledges it by saying, "[i]Running around in circles seems to be what this job is about,[/i]" and boy, is she right.

[b]☣︎ Playable Characters ☣︎[/b] 
Each chapter is divided into sections, so you play as Jill and Parker in one, Chris and Jessica in another, and occasionally Keith Lumley. The Keith sections felt like fillers and would have been better as cutscenes.

Jill and Chris are fantastic, but the rest are over-the-top cringe. Raymond looks like a ginger Jim Carrey from "The Mask," and Jessica is a stereotypical sexy spy with a Victoria’s Secret angel face. Even the designer seemed embarrassed by her design.

[b]☣︎ Story ☣︎[/b] 
The story is extremely cringe-worthy, made worse by the over-the-top new characters.

[b]☣︎ Location ☣︎[/b]
 The ship setting is interesting, but be ready for an eyesore when it starts sinking, and the camera sways everywhere. 

[b]☣︎ New Additions ☣︎[/b] 
The ability to swim and dive was so cool, especially the sections where you had to surface for air and hide from enemies without weapons. 

Another addition was the scanner that felt completely unnecessary and poorly designed, making it one of the most ridiculous features in the game. It's mostly giving herbs after scanning items or enemies. It had potential, like detecting invisible lasers, but it wasn’t explored enough.

[b]☣︎ Overall ☣︎[/b]
Not the best entry in the series, but worth the experience if you're a Resident Evil fan. I’ll definitely play again to unlock Jill's pirate outfit. However, if you're deciding between Revelations 1 and 2 - get 2.

[b]☣︎ Verdict ☣︎[/b] 
A mixed bag of action, frustration, and iconic moments. Play it for Jill, but brace yourself for the backtracking and cringe characters.

Resident Evil Revelations delivers a spine-tingling experience that harkens back to the series' roots in survival horror. Set aboard a seemingly abandoned cruise ship, the atmosphere is dripping with tension from the moment you step foot onboard.

The graphics are impressive, with detailed environments that perfectly capture the eerie ambiance of the ship's dark corridors and dimly lit rooms. From the creaking of the ship to the distant sounds of unknown horrors lurking nearby, every audio cue adds to the sense of unease.

Gameplay-wise, Revelations strikes a balance between action and horror, with limited resources forcing you to carefully manage your ammunition and supplies. The episodic structure keeps the pacing tight, constantly introducing new twists and turns to the narrative that kept me hooked until the very end.

One of the highlights for me was the Raid Mode, which offers hours of addictive replayability. Challenging missions and the ability to level up characters and weapons kept me coming back for more long after completing the main story.

That being said, the game isn't without its flaws. The story can feel convoluted at times, with multiple plot threads that may leave some players feeling confused. Additionally, while the AI companion is helpful in combat, there were moments where their actions felt more of a hindrance than a help.

Overall, Resident Evil Revelations is a must-play for fans of the series and survival horror enthusiasts alike. With its tense atmosphere, engaging gameplay, and satisfying progression systems, it's a worthy addition to the Resident Evil franchise.

Possibly the most difficult RE game after the tank era.  But for everyone who used to ask for another Jill-led game, this was it.  Plus for a good chunk of the game it's Jill and Chris.  And Parker is a forgotten fun character. The game returned to the atmospheric tight hallways that is the series signature. Ammo is scarce. [i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i] is best summed up as "Did you like [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]?  Here's that game again but it's a lot smaller in ambition, less famous and groundbreaking, and now it's on a ship."  I played it across the span of two cross-continent plane flights on a Steam Deck in offline/airplane mode, which I consider to be probably the best way to experience it.  [i]Revelations[/i] doesn't really stand on its own when placed against other survival horror titles of its era or even the [i]Resident Evil[/i] that preceded it, but it's optimized well for handhelds and the melodramatic storyline and clever monster designs are good for a few fun play sessions.

The hook this time around is that it's [i]Resident Evil[/i]-but-with-a-nautical-theme, and so you're exploring a moldering cruise ship instead of a moldering mansion, and the zombies feature creature features cribbed from pelagic and demersal marine life.  Beyond that, it's the standard formula for the [i]RE4[/i] era of titles and spin-offs: considerably more action-oriented than the original [i]Resident Evil[/i], with a tight third-person "corridor shooting" bent, but with very deadly enemies and strict rationing of ammunition and healing items to maintain horror tension compared to the even more actiony [i]RE5[/i] and [i]RE6[/I].  The storyline, per usual, is a nonsensical conspiracy parade of megacorps and bioterror organizations throwing zombies at each other while series standbys Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield struggle their way through the most stilted English dialogue this side of a 1970s Hong Kong kung-fu film.  All of this is on a rather restrained graphical and animation budget, which is a good expectations reminder that this is a handheld spinoff title, not a "full" [i]Resident Evil[/i].

To paraphrase a friend, if you wanted "more, slightly worse but still good [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]," this game is for you.  It's a good sequel and companion piece to that game, set in a novel new environment.

For a game built from the ground up for the 3DS, Resident Evil Revelations scales remarkably well to PC. It feels very much in the vein of Resident Evil 5, in its visual style and basic gameplay loop, though it does successfully capture a feeling of actual horror with its monster design and claustrophobic level layouts than 5 ever did. It's interesting how much it feels like a direct advancement of the late 2000s RE formula despite being a spin-off on a handheld platform - the ability to move while aiming and the vastly improved inventory system by themselves make the game significantly more playable than 5, and while the AI partner is still mostly an accessory that can't be relied on, the game is at least not built around an optional co-op mode, and therefore plays well as a solo experience.

The story is nothing special, mostly just standard, comparatively low-stakes RE fare, though the game's core twist at its midpoint actually ended up hitting pretty hard for me, though naturally they then went back to that well a second time and made it dumb. Structurally, it's broken up into chapters and sub-chapters like 5, which I imagine was meant to make the game playable in short bursts, appropriate for its handheld origins, though you can blast through it all pretty quickly in a marathon if you're so inclined.  Similarly, there isn't too much of a difficulty curve, remaining pretty approachable throughout, though the final boss is easily one of the worst bosses in the entire series, and I can't imagine how people dealt with it on the 3DS's tiny screen back then.

For a spin-off game, Revelations is a fun, easily-digestible entry in the series. If you really like Chris and/or Jill, it's absolutely worth playing. If you like the gameplay style of 5 (somehow), it's worth playing. Honestly, at its usual sale price, it's just worth playing in general if you enjoy the RE franchise.

For those not aware, this RE title was originally a Nintendo DS exclusive and was later ported and updated to PC (Steam). Strange aiming controls aside -- don't let it dissuade you, because this is actually an excellent game for what you get and in my opinion has aged well. 

The campaign is fleshed out and solid, with some character swapping pacing issues in the beginning, the locations as well are great - the enemy variety is just enough. The story itself is not spectacular but is very passable for any Resident Evil fan - the writing and spectacle is very much a post-RE4 and pre-RE5 "global saturation" affair, where the wrongdoings of Umbrella Corporation become a global bio-terrorist conundrum - where you play mainly as Jill Valentine and her partner Parker, while occasionally swapping to Chris Redfield and his partner, in their earlier years being part of the BSAA.
 
There is also an excellent 'Raid' mode that even most mainline Resident Evil games could have learned from even years later.

I would recommend this as long as you are comfortable with playing a lower budget and slightly finicky once-handheld title. It is surprisingly not as casual as you might expect and for an RE entry of its caliber, it can still give you the old survival horror business.

I already played Revelations 2 before playing this and I think this game still has some aspects I like more than the 2nd one. Comparing the 2:
Rev 1:
  +Graphics hold up exceptionally well considering its release date
  +Environments are much more pleasing to the eye than I would have imagined for being mostly located on a ship(s)

  +Enemies are much more unique compared to typical resident evil zombie games (their weak points are not on the head and you must shoot these weak points to stagger them so you can do a charged melee attack)
  +Raid mode retains the horror tension and feels much less arcade-like and linear compared to Rev 2

[h1]Resident Evil Part Review: An Okay Experience with Notable Issues[/h1]

[h3]Experience:[/h3]

This Resident Evil entry offers an intriguing experience but doesn’t stand out as the best in the series. The gameplay includes some enjoyable elements, such as the “Quick Turn” function, which I personally appreciate. The game length matches my preference, and the graphics are decent for a title released in 2012. However, the overall enjoyment is dampened by several significant issues.

[h3]Cons:[/h3] 

[list]
    [*][b]AI Character Support:[/b] Except for Jessica, the AI characters are notably unhelpful when you’re grabbed by an enemy. Unlike Sheva in Resident Evil 5, who quickly assists by kicking off enemies, the AI here is passive and doesn’t intervene during these critical moments.
    [*][b]Inventory System:[/b] The inventory system is a departure from previous Resident Evil games, but its major flaw is the limited storage capacity for ammo and herbs, which can be quite frustrating.
    [*][b]Map Design:[/b] The map design is poorly executed, making navigation overly complicated and challenging.
[/list]

[b]Controls:[/b]
 [list]
    [*]The healing button is now “TAB” on PC, which may be inconvenient for some players.
    [*]Movement feels sluggish; holding “W” to run combined with strafing slows down the character significantly.
    [*]Precise aiming issues, similar to GTA4, make it difficult to target distant enemies due to unresponsive mouse movements.
    [*]The zoom function for sniper rifles requires pressing the mouse wheel instead of scrolling, which feels unintuitive.
    [*]Inventory and grenade buttons have an awkward layout that detracts from the overall experience.
[/list] 

[b]Gameplay Pacing:[/b]
[list]
    [*]The game often overwhelms players with too many simultaneous events, making it chaotic and difficult to manage.
[/list] 

[b]Boss Encounters:[/b]
[list]
    [*]The first boss, “Scagdead,” is frustratingly difficult, with excessive ammo requirements and continuous enemy spawns making the fight unnecessarily stressful.
    [*]The final boss, “Norman Mutant,” is also excessively challenging. Despite using fully upgraded weapons and dealing significant damage, the fight felt overly drawn out.
[/list] 

[h3]Overall Rating:[/h3] 
While I found some aspects of the game enjoyable, the persistent issues significantly impact the experience.

[b]Fun Fact:[/b]
I unlocked the achievement “[b]Surviving Deep Darkness[/b],” which claims no deaths during the playthrough. In reality, I died over 25 times but restarted from checkpoints to avoid counting them as deaths.

From the looks of recent reviews, it seems that the publisher's new DRM can cause performance issues. I'd recommend RE Revelations if it were on sale - though you might need a refund for it. I myself experienced new screen tearing issues after taking a break from  the game for a couple of years. However, I cannot say whether the cause was my computer, my graphics card driver, or the game itself. Turning v sync on took care of the screen tearing, despite v sync not working for me in the past 15 years. I guess it does now?

The game otherwise performed well for an 11-year old game. My only gripes were with the camera and the dodge button. The camera felt rigid and snappy, making it more difficult to respond to enemies in tight spaces. At least it wasn't tank-style control of the character like with RE 4. To dodge with full i-frames, you have to input forward into the enemy at the right time. This was not intuitive for me. I would often dodge by accident, simply because I was holding forward to keep moving while the enemy attacked. Quick turn could also be used to dodge, so I rebound it to spacebar and became more successful with dodging incoming attacks. The downside was turning 180 degrees, thus missing out on the opportunity to punish enemy whiffs because I was busy reorienting myself for a second. 

I got a little burnt out from having to remember all of the unexplored rooms/chests/safes, which is why I took a break from the game after 7 episodes/11.5 hours. Sadly, I accidentally deleted my notes where I wrote down what I was missing. I just pulled up a walkthrough to make sure I didn't miss any goodies for the remaining 5 episodes. 

Storywise, RE Revelations takes place after RE 4 and essentially goes over some beef between the Federal Bioterrorism Commission and the BSAA with our heroes Jill and Chris getting caught up in the mix. Conspiracy and mutants were expected, but this title also gave me Dead Space vibes! You were mostly stuck on a ship trying to get off while having to explore every part of it, fix broken stuff, and survive. The atmosphere got spooky at times, especially with so many corridors and small rooms to fight in. I enjoyed the action of RE Revelations, though I might have enjoyed Revelations 2 better. The latter was set in a different environment with a more involved partner system. In Revelations 2, I remembered using commands on my partner NPCs much more, whereas in this game I never touched them. Revelations 2 also made you switch between partners within each pair in addition to the POV switches between pairs. Your civilian partners were generally less combat-oriented, which not only made sense from a logical standpoint, but also highlighted the survival horror style of gameplay.

That is not to say that Revelations 1 lacked survival horror elements. Even on Normal difficulty, I felt the squeeze of ammo scarcity. I felt safer when I had my partner NPC with me and less assured whenever we split up. By the final chapter, I had a powerful stash of weapon customization kits, but the end boss was tough. It depleted my ammo and heals and killed me repeatedly before I figured out the approach that worked for me.

As much as I hate all this DRM nonsense, it still doesn't change the fact that this game is good, DRM will forever be bad, but the quality of the game itself FOR ME anyway stays the same, which is good.

Overall, I won't say it's outright bad, but there are better games to spend your time on.

DRM is not always a bad thing, if used correctly, it protects initial sales. Then good publishers will remove it later on allowing for better experiences. Recently, denuvo was removed from RE8, which is good. But, when it was first added the game suffered many problems which modders had to remedy until its removal. Enigma seems to be capcom’s replacement for denuvo.

Earlier this month, RE Rev was updated and performance was harmed. Shortly after, capcom reversed the update. This update to add DRM to an old game is incredibly fishy, especially with how it came with no announcement from the publishers themselves. Almost as if somebody was trying to hide it.
Denuvo a very good DRM, since there’s few who know how to crack it, even then it’s tough. Denuvo itself costs ~$5,000 per month for the license, ~$60,000 a year. A game’s sales can’t keep up with the fee forever, and the DRM has to be removed/replaced to salvage income. 

Enigma is $59,920 cheaper. It costs about $400 for initial purchase, and $80 annually for upkeep. Enigma was checked with a virus scanner, and got 34 positive flags, ~%50 of what Virus Total checks for. Scanners can have false positives. The REV .exe will show 1 positive flag (at least for me). This one is easily written off as a false positive. Generally low single digits are fine. When you are getting into double digits, there’s problem. The dev for Enigma has been purported to have a fake address in the US, and the domain name’s been alleged to be bought through a Moscow front (fact check me). I want to help the people with AMD cards to enjoy this game so I will write everything I did to avoid it to crash:

First of all, with your game open go into the Windows Task Manager, find the game process, right click on it, compatibility tab and check the "Disable fullscreen optimization".

Second go to Windows settings, go into the "Games" section and disable "Game Mode".

These first two passages almost guarantee you to avoid like 80% of the crashes.

Now, I encountered mainly two types of crash in this game: the game closes without any warning and the ERR08: Memory Overrun

For the first one you simply have to play the game with the Anti-Aliasing turned off even tho sometimes you have to turn the graphics all the way down (just reach a savepoint and turn it back to the highest settings), I know it may suck but it works.

For the ERR08: Memory Overrun crash, simply open your Adrenalin Software, go to Gaming, Graphics and clear the Shader Cache, I suggest you do this everytime before opening up the game so you can avoid this problem completely.

I hope you fellow AMD users found these infos useful and I really hope that you can enjoy this game.

[h1] Resident Evil Revelations: Action Packed Minisodes With A Pinch Of Horror [/h1]

Remember when we were first welcomed into the "world of survival horror"? Those were the days. But recent Resident Evil games have wavered in delivering both survival and horror. Resident Evil 4, however, was a brilliant mix of grotesque and action. Resident Evil 5, though, seemed to lose its way and played it safe. So, what does the 3DS exclusive, Resident Evil: Revelations, bring to the table?

Well, it's both more and less than you'd expect. Revelations harks back to the series' horror roots. It brings some significant changes to the recent Resident Evil formula, especially in its combat system. Resident Evil 4's combat system was excellent but not exactly conducive to horror. Skilled players became nearly invincible. To amp up the horror, Revelations ditches the ability to stun enemies with headshots and introduces the "oozes."

These oozes are a departure from the usual Resident Evil fare. They look like waterlogged corpses, and you mainly encounter them on a massive cruise ship where the game unfolds. Sadly, they're one of the biggest missteps in Revelations. The combat feels odd, almost like an RPG. Instead of reacting to individual shots, oozes only get "stunned" when a damage threshold is reached. It's like you're shooting into a pile of goo – not very satisfying.

This enemy design issue seems to permeate the game. The oozes, the returning Hunters, and even the dogs feel unoriginal. You'd expect spin-off titles to experiment, right? Later in the game, you face more intriguing ooze mutations, but it feels too little, too late. There's even an attempt at invisible enemies. Yes, invisible. However, they're more of a joke than a challenge. They show up as outlines every few seconds, negating any subtlety in the environment and making these encounters more like a shooting gallery.

The campaign, set in various environments within the cruise ship, evokes classic Resident Evil moments. Dark, gloomy rooms, secret offices, and labyrinthine hallways all make a return. The new characters, though, are a mixed bag. The script occasionally veers into cringe-worthy territory, where moments meant to be tense are undercut by oddball humor.

However, the ship itself is the savior of the campaign. It oozes atmosphere (pun intended), with striking 3D visuals, ambient lighting, and particle effects that set a new standard for the 3DS. One of the most pleasant surprises in Revelations is how it keeps you on your toes. Doors slam, noises scuttle in the dark, but you see nothing until just the right moment. The bosses are also notably freaky and nightmarish, especially a particular chattering hag who stalks you through the ventilation system.

However, there are exceptions. Some boss fights against massive monsters are fought from mounted guns, which feel cliché and unexciting. The underwater sections, where you'd expect scares, are disappointingly bland. It's a missed opportunity, especially considering Resident Evil's knack for delivering horror in unexpected places.

The campaign itself is more than eight hours long, and it's backed up by the crown jewel of Revelations – Raid mode. Raid mode is a departure from the usual Mercenaries mode, offering a series of assault courses inspired by campaign environments. You have to clear out enemies while moving from point A to B, either solo or with a local or online partner.

Raid mode is a fantastic concept and it's executed with flair. It combines online co-op with a leveling and loot system. After each run, you get graded and rewarded with loot and in-game currency. The gear you earn can be used instantly, and you can spend the cash in the shop for even more items. There are loads of locked characters and gear to unlock, making it highly replayable.

Raid mode is the standout feature of Revelations. It's a bold score-attack mode that deviates from the usual Resident Evil style. It's challenging, persistent, and offers loads of customization. Buffing your guns to ridiculous levels tempts you back for more.

Revelations' campaign sometimes feels like a rollercoaster, alternating between exciting sequences and missteps. Yet, in the end, you'll find yourself running through its corridors with a decked-out shotgun and a smile on your face.

In conclusion, Resident Evil: Revelations may not be the perfect survival horror comeback, but it delivers where it counts. The campaign is a mix of hits and misses, but Raid mode stands out as a brilliant addition. The horror comes and goes, and the enemy design could be more imaginative, but overall, Revelations is worth diving into for a solid dose of classic Resident Evil.

Perfect Game #19, Resident Evil Revelations.  I love this game.  It was the first Resident Evil game I've ever played, and it was just as fun and exciting on my recent replay. RE Revelations is an extremely fun game. Anyone who's enjoyed Resident Evil 5 or Dead Space 2 will be right at home here. I love reading anthologies. I love how I can read each story at my own pace. It feels new and engaging every time I pick up where I left off with an anthology. And knowing there's an interconnected web of themes and ideas between all the stories helps me keep track of the bigger picture while still appreciating the particular. Maybe that's a big a reason for why I liked [u]Resident Evil: Revelations[/u]. I thought the episodic nature lent itself to an enjoyable and casual experience. My biggest gripe is probably that Jill should have been the only main character.

The game is horror in name, mostly, but it makes use of the aesthetic well. The ship Jill boards is a traditional ghost ship. It's filled with bloated creatures infested with the t-Abyss virus and deformed by sea moss...It's creepy in concept, but its firmly action in execution. The level design of the ship was remarkable - Queen Zenobia is a dangerous enemy in of itself, with treacherous and narrow hallways reminiscent of Racoon City Police Department. 

I never thought I'd enjoy a game originally intended for the 3DS but [u]Revelations[/u] proved to be an exception. The game persistently refers to Dante Aligheri's Divine Comedy, so I decided to explore that, among other comparisons, in an essay in a different post. If that sounds interesting to you, please go read it and leave a comment.

Pretty good game when you consider that it was originally made for the 3DS.

Controls and gameplay mechanics are pretty solid and the game does feel more in line with older titles compared to 4, 5 or 6. It's a pretty good combination of tank controls mixed with some of RE6's full 3D movement. You can move whilst aiming and you can move in any direction but you can only run forward. Plus the camera is locked to your back so it's not as easy to bail out of situations or move around enemies as much as you can in RE6.

However, I wish the game featured an actual inventory with resource management since that's one of the defining factors of old school Resident Evil. There are item crates but these only allow you to store, switch or upgrade weapons. Not items. This hurts the backtracking of the game, since you'll never be in a situation where you'll need to go back to get an item. Ammo? You'll acquire more just by continuing the game. Herbs? You'll acquire more just by continuing the game. It's not even worth doing it for weapons since if you drop one weapon to pick up another, the dropped weapon is automatically transferred to the weapon box. So despite being a interconnected ship, most of the time you'll just be going to the next objective instead of exploring. 

My only other complaints are that I think the game goes on for one chapter longer than needed, there's no puzzles (another old school Resident Evil factor), and the balancing for Infernal difficulty is ABSURD (in the early game, you'll run out of ammo before killing an enemy).

One thing that does bother me is the lesser amount of replayability and extra content compared to the main games, but considering it was a spin off for a handheld console I can forgive that. It's more consistent in quality and it doesn't stray too far from the franchise's roots unlike 5 or 6.

Otherwise, solid game. Worth playing if you a fan of the series and if you want to see more of Jill & Chris working together.

A  game that started life on the 3DS, and just like when I first got to play it on the PS3 I once again find it staggering with the amount of content they fit into that cartridge. 

Story: The game is set before Resi 5 but after 4 so you see some of what Chris and Jill were getting up to. Overall as far as Resi stories go this one starts of interesting but gets straight up bonkers mid way XD. When all of the balls get to rolling I had no idea what was going to happen by the end.  I don't want to spoil anything if you want to see what I'm talking about, but just take it as an endorsement.

Gameplay: It's a scaled down version of the Resi 5 combat style of 3rd person shooting with semi tank controls. It adds a much needed dodge to avoid some of the most nonsense attacks. This will be near mandatory to learn on the highest difficulty. You don't have an inventory system to manage but you do have 4 weapon slots and 6 weapon types. You will be swapping as you run out of a certain type of ammo but I strongly recommend you always keep a shotty and a sniper. For whatever reason outside of handgun ammo on my first run I almost always kept getting maxed on those two so I was walking by so much ammo that never got used. This barely changed by the hardest difficulty but things did get tight near the end. PRO TIP: Save the first rocket launcher you get for your second playthrough on the hardest difficulty against the final boss. This saves an ungodly amount of headache for then.

Replayability: Outside of 2 playthroughs on the main game you have arguably the best time killer in any Resi game (outside of Revelations 2 version of this) RAID MODE! It's a level based objective mode to get through as quickly as possible while killing enough targets to activate the clear condition. I do not know how but on the PS3 in both Revelations 1 and 2 I have probably lost well over 300+ hours on that. That's really the best indicator that I can give this game. 

Summery: For what's here I would definitely say that it is worth the $30 asking price but it goes on sale often for far less. DO NOT PASS THIS GAME IF YOU LOVE RESIDENT EVIL!

Revelations was a 3DS exclusive game and it's noticeable: despite being on PCs and home consoles, the texture quality is questionable, animations are stiff, and models are rather low poly for that generation. It's also divided into episodes, though the episodic format makes sense when considering it was on a mobile device.
On the gameplay side it's RE5 with the ability of moving while shooting. However, it's much slower than RE4, 5, or 6, and more atmospheric and creepy. Back in the day it was considered a large step in the right direction after the mentioned action fests, though it was not until RE7 did the series truly return to its roots.

Storywise it's a conspiracy, within a conspiracy, with a conspiracy topping, but it's better than most games in the franchise. I like the implication that Chris wants to continue the Redfield bloodline with Jill. Unfortunately, it can be really corny due to Keith's and Quentin's behavior and design, Raymond's goofy anime hairstyle, and Jessica's ridiculous costumes.

Other notes:[list]
[*]The final boss is one of the best in the series. Difficult, but not overwhelming. Deals heavy damage, but has no instant kill abilities. Requires precision and reflexes, as well as patience and perception, all the while being fairly easy to understand.
[*]There are multiple swimming sections, but due to the smooth controls they're significantly better than RE6.
[*]Surprisingly good music, especially the final boss track.[/list]

The bad:[list]
[*]Partner AI is the worst in the series, but it cannot die and you don't have to worry about its ammo supply. [*]Not that it is useful in combat in any way.
[*]A bit too many one hit kill enemies.
[*]So. Many. Hunters. Especially in the flashbacks.
[*]Nobody knows how dodging actually works, even after all these years.[/list]

[h1] Review[/h1] 
Initially a 3DS game I absolutely didn’t expect anything from it. Whether or not you like the course Resident Evil went with RE4,5 and 6 this one tries to play more like the original except being a third person shooter. Tries is a good word as it doesn’t, yet considering it was a mobile game it’s pretty neat.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
At its core the main goal of the game is figuring out why you’re trapped on a ship full of monsters and how to get off of it. Those monsters are a one-off version of the original zombie virus, making monsters mostly into snail looking humanoids, fitting the situation being on the ship. Those come in different forms, there are also older ones, but not a single regular classical T-Virus zombie to be seen.

You explore the ship and find various keys or items to proceed further, while sometimes backtracking. Although no inventory management, but you do have an item box that is used to modify or swap out weapons. The game starts more or less horror focused with low amounts of ammo which in the later stages of the game changes to more something you see in RE5, explosions and combat everywhere.

Its more linear but you also have to backtrack sometimes because the mission says so or can go back to get a new item. It holds your hand way much more than RE1-3, mostly because people probably played this on the go, making the mission objective always clear is a good design choice in that case.
Its relatively clear where to go most of the time, the ships’ structure is not in any way resembling the design of the first two originals, although it does have a few keys here and there and some interconnectivity later on.

In order to pad the gametime, you also play different characters set in the present or the past that correlate to the story more or less. In those scenes the horror atmosphere is more or less completely dropped.
Combat is pretty okay, having also the rare melee attack and a few grenade types. Biggest difference is the ability to scan enemies, which only purpose is to dispense healing items. Movement doesn’t have anymore tank controls but rather more to what we seen in RE6 or Raccoon City.

There are weapon mods to find, although when playing the main characters at some point you can carry up to three weapons, meaning you drop the pistol relatively quickly.

I enjoyed my playthrough, it’s a very simple horror game in the resident evil universe, more memorable would have been that the AI you are constantly with, could also be played by another player. Game has aside raid no coop.

Raid mode is pretty fun for a while, being a grindy coop shooter where you level up buy and upgrade new weapons, although the amount of loot can at some point be overwhelming, the grind too.

[u]Story[/u]
Not really sure what is ment with revelations, but it more or less serves as a tie in towards resident evil 5. Not really that memorable but better than nothing.

[u]Sound[/u]
I really liked the ost. Not only does it create a lot of suspense and dread but also fits towards the nautical setting a lot. For such a game the length and variety of the ost is absolutely bonkers. 

Also fully voiced in a couple of languages, making second playthroughs always more interesting to switch things up a bit.

[u]Graphics[/u]
Its clear that it looks like a mobile game. Due to the HD port on the pc everything looks pretty but the textures and colours itself aren’t that great. On the other hand I’m absolutely impressed what they put onto the 3DS.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
This is definitely not a must have game. While it does offer some horror atmosphere its more for people who wanted to see how the 3DS port turned out and for completionists. Its not a bad game and especially the raid mode is rather interesting. Its just a bit mediocre compared to the other games out there. What sets it apart is the still neat atmosphere, especially due to the soundtrack and interconnected design that requires backtracking of the ship´s structure. Probably a way much more impressive game on the 3D, solely an interestening one on the PC

After playing Resident Evil 4 Remake & filling out my library with all the Resident Evil games during the Capcom Gold Week sale I have been on a RE kick. During this time I decided to go ahead and play all of the RE games. This time I decided to take the plunge and play one title that slipped underneath my radar: Revelations. I have played and beat the game and can now give my thoughts on the game and whether it was worth the purchase or not. Let us dive in.

Loading the game up and going through the graphic settings I found that the menus felt fairly nice and not too clunky. I initially attempted to play the game in 21:9, however, it did not function properly. I found some fixes online but they required more effort than I was willing to put in. So for this playthrough, I played on my secondary 16:9 -- 1440p monitor. Once in the game world, I was actually blown away. Despite the game being 10 years old it still maintains an impressive graphic fidelity and overall smoothness. -Most- textures throughout the game still hold up today and the few "bad" textures are simply due to the fact they were reused assets from RE4 & RE5. Another point I enjoyed was the cod-style minimap that persisted throughout the game. I found it easier to use than the main map found in the game. 

Moving on, the combat feels great and after playing RE4R it feels like an early version of that game. Oddly enough, this game performs and plays better than RE6 which came out many years later. Throughout the game, the player will find numerous firearms -- in addition, I had purchased the game during a sale so I got all of the pre-order + DLC guns so that was a fun bonus. All of the weapons felt great, except, the pistols. They honestly felt like peashooters and had no "weight" to them. Another thing I noticed is the game reusing animations and sound files from OG RE4 which came out 7 years prior. While I admit they are great and still sound incredible I do wish Capcom wouldn't have been so lazy. 

Continuing on with combat let's discuss the creatures found within the game. Some of the creatures were nicely designed, however, most of them were honestly lackluster. I do appreciate the aquatic theme and was a nice addition that hasn't been explored really in the RE series. The amount of copying and pasting of mobs is apparent though. Something I do not appreciate is that some of the creatures within the game can chain-stun lock the player causing unavoidable + frustrating deaths. One example of this is the hunters. If you get backed into a corner or unfortunately caught between two of them they will spam the same attacks over and over and the player will be unable to break out of the cycle before being killed. This happened numerous times during my Normal playthrough. I cannot imagine how much more frustrating this could be on Infernal or Professional. In terms of boss fights none of them were really "mind-blowing" the turtle boss fight was sort of fun but the final boss and the next-to-last boss were more tedious than exceptional. 

The setting of the game is truthfully one of the coolest ideas in the RE universe. I love the thought of being on a cruise ship. In the opening sequence of the game, I was getting major "Ghost Ship" horror movie vibes. The game features a nice mix of beautiful scenes and creepy + eerie locations. Multiple times throughout the game, especially, within the cabin sequences I felt a sense of claustrophobia while playing as Jill and being separated from Parker. In sections such as the upper cabins, main lobby, and the cafeteria I could tell the developers were going for a design language found within the original games mansion. In these locations, I believed they absolutely nailed the atmosphere. Meanwhile, in other sections of the game it was either decayed and rotted or heavily industrialized (think RE4 island). The music throughout the game was either mediocre or good. Not the best found in the series but far from the worst. One thing that kind of killed the immersion was the obvious loading screen sections (the parts where you would go through the turning wheel doors). Typically these do not bother me (looking at you Fallout 4 elevators) but the game would experience abrupt soundtrack skips + FPS dips into micro stuttering. I truly wish the game would've blended the previous area's music into the new area but I digress. Overall I was extremely pleased with each area the player was able to explore.

After playing RE6 and playing this game while my buddy was offline -- one thing I appreciate is rewarding the player for exploration and having a unique + fun customization concept. Throughout the game, the player will discover "custom parts", "illegal custom parts", and a variety of weapons. Most of these can be discovered by doing puzzles, backtracking after receiving key items, or during extremely tight time sections. Once parts are acquired the player can then equip them with any weapon they wish. "Custom Parts" are generic modifiers such as: +Damage, +Fire Rate, +Ammo Cap, etc. Meanwhile, "Illegal Custom Parts" are unique weapon mods that feel game-changing. One incredible addition is the fact you can freely swap these modifications across any gun you own. While I prefer the merchant + treasure & currency system this is an awesome way to do an RE game without a merchant in my opinion. 

While the game does some things extremely well, it falls flat on its face in other sections. The story is all over the place and the ending is quite possibly one of the worst endings I can think of in recent memory. Another thing that is rather hit or miss is the voice acting. In some sections it sounds great and believable in other moments it sounds like a "B-series" movie. Some notable characters that I thought were obnoxious were Parker, Jessica, Raymond, and especially Grinder + Quint. Sadly it seems all of the original characters were just too over the top and more annoying than memorable. Something that I felt did not contribute to the game was switching from Jill + Parker to other characters in the series, especially, the Grinder + Quint sections. It really took me out of the game and killed all of the immersion that had built up while playing as Jill. The game is also obsessed with swimming sections. Thankfully it does not bother me as much as it should, however, it becomes tedious after the third or fourth time. I am just grateful swimming in this game is much more polished and easier than in RE6. 

To conclude, I am shocked that this game flew under my radar. While not impressive in any particular category it does a lot of things well. The game features a unique and well-designed setting, combat + movement that still holds up even by today's standards, nice weapon selection with a unique weapon customization system despite no merchant being present, and finally, it rewards the player for exploring and taking their time. The game has a weak plot, repetitive and unimaginative creatures, a mediocre soundtrack, and annoying "new" characters". The game took a lot of risks and overall I believe it did a good job. I beat the game on Normal and took my time and finished it around 11 hours. I still want to grab most if not all of the achievements and I think most players could squeeze over 30 hours out of their purchase easily. While I cannot recommend the game for its original price I wouldn't hesitate to pick the game up during a Steam / Capcom sale.

EDIT: Capcom better be grateful I posted my review earlier in my play session. Infernal is an absolute cesspool even on NG+ with every mod. Just room after room filled with CTRL+C / CTRL+V enemies that litter each section of the game. Certain sections are brutal due to how many enemies are within a hallway or tight room with minimal ammo / healing items. Enemies are either a joke or absolute bullet sponges. I am glad I got the achievements, however, I cannot see myself ever touching the campaign again.

I really wish there was an option for a neutral review.  I neither enjoyed or disliked Revelations.  I first played this version back in 2016 after it had been sitting in my library for awhile.  I decided to revisit it after playing the RE4 Remake because this game has always just sitting there and I was down for more Resident Evil.

In terms of gameplay, this game is the sequel to Resident Evil 5 and is the first RE game to feature moving while aiming.  And that was definitely an impressive thing on the 3DS back in 2012.  If you're someone who loves playing RE5, this game will be an absolute blast for you.  Personally, I've played enough RE5 on the PS3, after having that [i]revelation[/i], I played Chapter 1-3 and thought to myself, "Yeah, I get it." and turned it off.  I have no nostalgia for RE5, but if I ever have the urge to replay it or something similar: Revelations is there waiting for me.

Lastly, I never expected the plot's of Resident Evil games to be all that compelling after RE4-6, but Revelations is a special kind of cheesy.  The new partner's that tag along with Chris & Jill are Jessica & Parker and their backstory is nothing short of hilarious.  I don't want to spoil it for you, but expect to be rolling your eyes at it.  Additionally, how the game references and is tied to the first game adds nothing to the experience.  At every opportunity it feels like this game is trying to say:  "Hey remember this big moment in Resident Evil [x]? Here's a callback to that!".  Its all too self-indulgent for me.  

TL:DR a more appropriate title for the game is Resident Evil 5 2.0 [i](though I remember that was the Lost in Nightmares DLC update for RE5 back on the PS3, but you get what I'm saying...)[/i]
