While replaying through Revelations I could not help but be reminded of Resident Evil: Infinite Darkness, a TV show that was not supposed to be a TV show, it was easy to see that in its original form it was a movie, cut to pieces for market reasons, and by trying to be something it wasn't it failed completely in delivering just that. Resident Evil: Revelations mostly does the same, with its presentation trying very hard to be like a TV show for no discernible reason. From the cliffhangers (that are useless because they will be answered 5 seconds from now) to the coming and going of characters, settings and subplots (that don't change the pacing and gameplay enough to justify themselves but end up changing just enough to be an annoyance), to all the flashbacks (that serve zero purpose to the narrative outside of one throwaway scene), they try too hard in some places just to end up almost never doing anything right in terms of what they're trying to accomplish, and the dialogue is nothing to write home about, but then again, it's Resident Evil, good dialogue seems to be almost a betrayal of what it stands for. Not to say that gameplay-wise things are perfect either, the game has a few gimmicks that get old a bit too fast for their own good and there's always the ultimate realization that the game only has three real settings that you will play in so much that you'll sometimes feel like you're stuck in a loop, but despite all that, Revelations is genuinely not a bad game. When you keep in mind that this was originally a 3DS game, what they ultimately achieved here is nothing short of impressive. It has everything that forms a good Action RE game, and the exploration doesn't feel too linear, so it still maintains some of the old RE charm. The Raid Mode is also a great addition to the series, that is fun to the point of easily deserving its own standalone game. Ultimately, this is a fine game that's just a bit misguided when it comes to its presentation, Resident Evil as a series, be it in any media, should not pretend to be something that it isn't, because every time they try it, they just fail.

Resident Evil Revelations is a very good survival/horror and action game, whose story is situated between Resident evil 4 and 5. The game puts us once again in the shoes of Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield and we learn more about the "past" and the functioning of the BSAA.

This game is more story oriented than the other opus, with a lot of cinematic and a more advanced scenario. The game is divided like a series, with episodes (chapters) and recaps at the end of each of them. You will regularly switch from one character to another in different places in order to advance the story in a rather original way.

As for the gameplay, the gameplay is very good and has not aged badly, the game mechanics are quite simple, mixing elements of all resident evil, action and survival horror. There are several weapons to unlock as well as improvements for each of them. There are some nice action phases in the Resident Evil 5 style, which are well placed in the game, so the gameplay is renewed quite well throughout the game.

In conclusion I recommend the game to any fan of the license. I think that if you are a beginner in resident evil games, you should start with the main games but if you just want a good survival horror with a pretty good atmosphere this one is also very good.

Played this one straight after Resident Evil 4 and it pretty much stood up the expectations. The campaign contains 12 chapters which are all split up through a maximum of 3 missions. Normal mode got me through the story in a decent 10 hours but the game mode that will hook you is the Raid Mode. This mode let's you revisit certain missions from the campaign but with more monsters and new enemy locations but you can level up, loot weapons or upgraded versions. TL;DR: gameplay's fine; story's bad, especially for being called Revelations; idk how other people call this gamespooky survival horror when it's mostly RE5 crammed into a Nintendo DS This is the first Resident Evil game I have played that I would say is actually bad. There are plenty of entries that I know I would not enjoy not because they are bad, but because the gameplay isn't suited for me. For context: I am someone who prefers the more action-y entries over the more classic survival horror, that's just my personal preference. I genuinely enjoy RE5 and 6, and believe that many people claim these games are significantly worse than they are because said people just don't care for the gameplay. That being said, I distinctly did not enjoy this game, and it's mostly not because of the gameplay, though there are problems there.Everyone else here seems to praise this game for being a return to spooky survival horror. I couldn't disagree more.Despite my previously stated preference, I have thoroughly played and enjoyed Resident Evil 2 Remake, which I don't thinkI need to explain that that's an absolute stand out for survival horror. There are definitely moments where Revelations is genuinely unsettling and creepy, but those are few and far between. Maybe I should have turned the brightness down (I was on the default setting), but it was almost never dark enough for me to wonder what's around the corner. Granted, I only played on the easiest difficulty, so I almost never had problems having enough ammo to kill anything in my way.However, this game plays very much like 5, so it did not seem like not having enough ammo would increase the tension and horror, but would simply increase the frustration in the unreliable dodge mechanic and limited mobility. I'm not denegrating the movement, as this was originally a handheld console game, my point is just limiting ammo doesn't make a game scary. For comparison: RE2R is designed for you to not have enough ammo to shoot everything, even though you pretty much can on easy difficulty. You've got just enough room to move around zombies often enough, and can stagger them with much less ammo than it takes to kill them. Most of the game is dark, and the ambient noises even when you aren't being hunted by Mr X really crank up the feeling of impending doom. Revelations does none of this.Now I said I prefer the gameplay of the less scary RE games, and this is definitely one of them. The gameply is mostly fine for what it is. I do like the color of the crosshair telling you when an enemy is definitely dead. I do like that they did at least use the survival horror element of going back and forth through the same areas unlocking new things along the way. While I do like that your AI partner is invincible, as far as I can tell I never witnessed mine actually do lethal damage to an enemy, so that's a thing. Idk if it's a difficulty thing, but it seemed like Jill couldn't drown during swimming sections, so that's nice. I do find it slightly compelling to have to use your screen to tell your health. My main problem with the gameplay is that a number of sequences go on for way too long, like every stop and defend section and the turret sections. Also a lot of bosses feel excessively tanky. Ok, now for my primary complaint: the story. It's so bad. It would be significantly less bad if the RE game with a completely insulated plot taking place entirely in new locations that are completely unconnected from the overall plot with almost entirely new characters wasn't subtitled ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ REVELATIONS. Not a single piece of new groundbreaking information regarding existing characters, locations, or events is shown. The "revelations" inside the plot itself can bespotted a mile away (wow, the obvious bad guys are the bad guys? amazing). If Capcom wanted to make an unconnected story with a grand total of two existing characters and one existing organization for a handheld title, then subtitle it literally anything else. While it's neat to see Chris and Jill together again, breifly, the story is boring and uninspired. And don't get me started on the two dorks who would never have passed field agent training that we're forced to play as for three chapters.

Graphically and mechanically a very functional and fun game to this day. But the writing is among some of the most blatently sexist I have ever seen in any video game, every single woman is dumbed down to the max. Don't recommend for just that reason, the story isn't very important or original anyways.

Set after 4 and before 5, Revelations mainly follows Jill Valentine navigate through a spooky ship looking for Chris Redfield's signal who was looking for a terrorist group who sent monsters on a city in the middle of the ocean a year prior. Things go sideways and Jill and her partner Parker must survive on the ship that's now full of monsters. Sometimes you cut away to the past controlling other characters or other characters in the current time doing other stuff, to some success. One section was walking in a building for 5 minutes before going back to the action (usually Jill's POV) so it kind of undercuts tension sometimes.

The game is episodic but since it came packaged all together originally, it falls a bit flat when after each episode there is a 'Previously on...' of what you literally just did since the bits in the episode range so far from either 30~minutes to 5 minutes in length so it feels like you're stuck in some time loop reliving what you just did. I know they did episodes in the sequel but at least that one the episodes were released every few months so a catch up on what happened makes sense.

Gameplay wise it's fairly fun, I like scanning around rooms looking for loot and collectables and the combat is fine as well and translated well from its 3DS roots to get onto the PC. The one gripe of moment to moment combat is the dodge is real finicky when it works as you either do it by hitting w or space bar before an enemy attacks. I did it accidentally with w many a time and doing it with space is a bit more reliable but still not fully right as you'll think you did it but still get it. I'll try to sum up gameplay changes so you know what you're getting into before you buy.

Gameplay:

This time around you will almost always have a partner with you, like in RE5, but the partner has infinite health and ammo which can make them a highly effective meat shield if you can position enemies (and even BOSSES) to attack them instead of you. You cannot affect your partner's inventory and they generally do pitiful damage on their own. There is no currency in this game, new weapons must be found, and upgrading weapons is only done through what I call weapon upgrade "chips". Every weapon only has so many slots for the chips, but you find plenty of them in varying strengths and they can be freely unequipped and swapped around so no big deal. You can only carry 3 primary weapons at any time, REGARDLESS of size, but the weapon caches around the levels are all synchronized with each other and you can swap/customize weapons relatively often. The knife and all types of grenades are now subweapons, mapped to a different button and they don't take up any kind of inventory space so you CAN hold a maxed stack of every kind of grenade at once, if you stockpile them.

Herbs only come in green and will always fully heal you when used, but knowing when to use them can be tricky since THERE IS NO HEALTH BAR, and you judge how close to death you are by how bloody and desaturated the screen gets. There are no typewriters or manual saving of any kind, the only saves occur at predetermined checkpoints and chapter ends. 

The game features both shallow water and full underwater sections, with many enemies that are significantly more dangerous in water and the water-only "Sea Creeper" enemy which is a master of stealth. The returning Shock Grenades are now more useful because they now do bonus damage to aquatic foes, but less to land base enemies like hunters. When swimming underwater you can't kill anything, but can use Pulse Grenades to momentarily stun enemies and escape... or you can just pro dodge them all but Sea Creepers are fast and swim silently.

One touted new feature is the "Genesis" which is a Scanner. You need to use it to find many items invisible to the human eye, and it makes fighting cloaking or underwater enemies easier by letting you (temporarily) detect them. It's also necessary to scan various enemies before they die, and hand prints hidden around the game, to get every achievement. When you scan enough things you get a free herb, which can be a godsend if you are running low. You can't use the Genesis in Raid Mode, which can make fighting Sea Creepers a lot harder.

Side missions with other characters are almost always action packed and loaded with ammo, not to mention you have a different non-customizable inventory compared to when you play the main missions as Jill. Side missions will take you to other locales such as a beach, snowy mountains, and old Terragrigia, not to mention showing you some new enemies. The side missions are less serious, and will please the Action Gamer in you not the Survival Horror gamer in you, but I still enjoyed them. This game doesn't have as many boss fights as I would have expected, but every boss is memorable... especially the final boss who will give you a fight that you probably won't have anything to compare it with in all Resident Evil history.

Raid Mode is the new side mode. It makes a number of advances with some RPG elements and full control over weapons and their customization compared to the strict limitations of past iterations. It also takes some steps backwards, with only one melee move per character and no rewards for combos of any kind. One of the best new features are VISIBLE HEALTH BARS AND DAMAGE NUMBERS for enemies in this mode, which also displays the enemy level and any "buffs" they may have, such as frightening double speed enemies which also have a smaller model and are thus much harder to hit. The objective of the mode is now just to get to the end and hit the goal, which usually involves a lot of room clearing kill fests to get keys to continue. Score is based on four things: time taken, damage taken, enemies defeated, and hit accuracy. There are special bonuses for 100% accuracy, ALL enemies defeated, and NO damage taken, while managing to get all 3 of those bonuses will also net you a "Trinity Bonus" and tons of points, but oddly there is no special bonus for clear times. The points double as both the currency of the mode and experience to level up. The game keeps one inventory for all characters you can play as, but you can upgrade weapon/ammo/grenade/herb storage capacity as well as buying new weapons/chips and refilling ammo/grenades/herbs for pretty cheap prices. You also find weapons/chips in the stages themselves, with better performance netting better items. Raid mode can be played Solo or with local/online Co-Op modes, if you play Co-Op both players reap the rewards evenly, which can net you very powerful items at a low level but you cannot equip a weapon with a higher level than your level, keeping things balanced. Raid Mode also has higher difficulties which adds replay value, and you can manually lower your character level and purposefully equip lower level weapons to make the game much harder (everyone likes a challenge.)



Control:

No real complaints, things are very similar to how they have been except grenades are now on the same key as the knife, meaning they can both be used with any primary weapon but it's more awkward to use both the knife and pulse grenades (the new flash grenades) together.  Globsters instakill you underwater, even on Normal difficulty. 



Graphics:

Astonishing, some really high detail texture enemies are in this game. There are a few brutal scenes that I won't spoil, and the actual cutscenes in the game are amazing. When the game is saving/loading data you will notice some framerate drops, but this generally only happens when stationary in a chamber or elevator while you load a new area. For the astute gamer a short frame skip in Raid Mode is very useful, as it almost always signifies an enemy just spawned nearby and the game was loading it. You may not notice these at first since they last only a few frames (5 or 6) but they can be very useful when you are confused where to go in Raid Mode, it's usually an enemy you missed.



Sound:

Volume up of course, this is a game where hearing is useful to alert you of enemies nearby. There are some great creepy sound FX with Rachel having some of the best lines, and various firearms still sound epic. The game has some excellent ambient tunes, as well as a few good heart-pounders, but the best place to hear the music is in Raid Mode where you can pick a level with the song you want to heard. There's no Sound Test in the game, which is still something I think all games should have, but you can get by with Raid Mode.




Survival Horror vs Action Run-n-Gun:

The side missions are generally not that scary, and very combat oriented. The main game has a section where you lose your equipment and the underwater sections which are both focused on avoiding and evading rather than actual combat. The game runs the full gambit, which is clearly Capcom trying to please everyone. It's still going to be argued about and bashed for not being scary enough for some people, but I jumped a few times and I still dread fighting more than one Sea Creeper at once. I personally never ran out of ammo for any weapon, but that was on Normal difficulty. Try to play through the campaign on Hell difficulty before commenting on how scary the game is... tons more enemies and way fewer ammo pickups.




Score:
Resident Evil: Revelations 9/10

[h1]A Chilling Echo: Resident Evil: Revelations Review by Kiba Snowpaw[/h1]

[h2]Introduction[/h2]
Greetings, fellow gamers and furries! I’m Kiba Snowpaw, the alpha male from the icy world of HowlStrom. Today, we’re delving into the eerie corridors of Resident Evil: Revelations. As someone who grew up with the original Resident Evil on the PS1 at the tender age of 13, I have fond memories of the chills and thrills this franchise once delivered. But has Revelations recaptured that magic, or is it another cold echo of its former glory? Let's break the ice and find out.

[h2]Basic Plot Summary[/h2]
Set shortly after Resident Evil 4, Revelations follows the adventures of counter-terrorism agents Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield. Their mission? Uncover the truth behind a bioterrorist organization threatening to infect the world’s oceans with a deadly virus. The narrative unfolds through a series of episodes, blending puzzle-solving, exploration, and combat.

[h2]Originality[/h2]
Resident Evil: Revelations attempts to marry the survival horror roots of the series with modern gameplay elements. The episodic structure is a nod to TV dramas, providing bite-sized chunks of horror and action. The setting aboard the ghostly Queen Zenobia cruise ship is a unique twist, adding claustrophobic tension. However, it sometimes feels like the game is treading on familiar ground without introducing much innovation.

[h2]The Studio[/h2]
Capcom, the masterminds behind the Resident Evil series, have a storied history of horror games. Known for their attention to detail and ability to create atmospheric settings, Capcom aimed to bring back the essence of survival horror with Revelations. Despite their efforts, the game occasionally struggles to break free from the shadows of its predecessors.

[h2]Analysis/Evaluation[/h2]
[i]Mechanics[/i]
Revelations emphasizes survival, evasion, and exploration over fast-paced combat. Limited ammunition and health resources force players to strategize. The Genesis scanner, a device for finding hidden items, adds a layer of depth to the exploration. The controls, especially with the Circle Pad Pro on the 3DS, allow for smoother movement and aiming, though they can feel clunky on other platforms.

[h2]Character Development[/h2]
[i]Main Characters[/i]
Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield return as the main protagonists. Jill, the seasoned veteran, is as resourceful as ever, while Chris provides the muscle. Their partnership, though familiar, lacks the depth and development seen in earlier titles.

[i]Supporting Characters[/i]
Parker Luciani and Jessica Sherawat join the fray, each bringing their quirks to the table. Parker's loyalty and Jessica's mysterious motives add intrigue, though they often feel underutilized. The villain, FBC director Morgan Lansdale, is a classic caricature of corruption and evil.

[i]Character Arcs and Relatability[/i]
While the main characters are iconic, their arcs in Revelations are relatively static. Jill and Chris remain largely unchanged, with minimal personal growth. The supporting cast, though interesting, doesn't receive enough screen time to develop fully.

[h2]Structure[/h2]
The episodic structure breaks the game into manageable segments, ideal for handheld play. However, the frequent shifts between characters and settings can disrupt the narrative flow. The pacing varies, with some episodes feeling drawn out while others rush through critical plot points.

[h2]Impact[/h2]
Revelations aimed to revive the survival horror genre within the Resident Evil series. Its atmospheric setting and emphasis on resource management are commendable, but the execution falls short of the mark set by earlier entries. The impact is a mixed bag, with moments of genuine tension overshadowed by uneven storytelling.

[h2]Hook and Thesis[/h2]
Resident Evil: Revelations tries to hook players with its blend of old-school horror and modern mechanics. While it succeeds in creating a spooky atmosphere, it struggles to maintain a consistent tone. The thesis of returning to survival horror roots is clear, but the game doesn't fully commit to it.

[h2]Praise and Critique[/h2]
[i]Praise[/i]
Revelations excels in creating a chilling atmosphere. The Queen Zenobia is a fantastic setting, rife with claustrophobic corridors and eerie silence. The sound design, especially with headphones, heightens the sense of dread. The game’s graphics, particularly on the 3DS, are impressive, showcasing Capcom’s technical prowess.

[i]Critique[/i]
However, the game falters in its execution. The enemy variety is limited, and the AI of companions leaves much to be desired. The controls can be frustrating on non-3DS platforms, detracting from the experience. The episodic structure, while innovative, disrupts the narrative flow and fails to deliver a cohesive story.

[h2]Personal Opinion[/h2]
[i]Enjoyment[/i]
As a longtime fan of the series, I found moments of enjoyment in Revelations. The return to a slower, more methodical pace was refreshing, and the atmosphere often hit the right notes. However, the game’s inconsistencies and lack of innovation left me yearning for the glory days of Resident Evil.

[i]Highlights and Drawbacks[/i]
The highlights include the immersive setting of the Queen Zenobia and the tense sound design. Drawbacks are the limited enemy variety, clunky controls on some platforms, and a fragmented story that fails to engage fully.

[i]Evaluation[/i]
Revelations is a game of highs and lows. It captures the essence of survival horror but struggles with execution. The episodic structure, while suitable for handheld play, detracts from the overall narrative. It’s a decent entry in the series but falls short of greatness.

[h2]Comparison[/h2]
[i]Similar Games[/i]
Compared to other survival horror games, such as Dead Space or The Evil Within, Revelations lacks the polish and depth. It shares similarities with earlier Resident Evil titles but doesn't quite reach the same level of impact.

[h2]Overall Conclusion[/h2]
Resident Evil: Revelations is a nostalgic journey back to the series’ roots, wrapped in a modern package. It offers moments of genuine horror and atmosphere but is marred by inconsistencies and a disjointed narrative. For fans of the series, it’s worth a playthrough, but don’t expect it to reignite the same passion as the original games. As an alpha male Ice Wolf with a lifetime of gaming, I can appreciate its efforts but can't ignore its flaws. Until next time, stay frosty, my friends.

Resident Evil Revelations is an off-shoot of the main Resident Evil Series, originally designed and released for the Nintendo DS, and now on Steam with an HD update. As a game outside of the normal numbered series, Revelations is more free to change certain aspects of the Resident Evil Formula. It uses many of the Third Person action elements of RE4 and RE5, but changes up much of the pacing by using an episodic story and level structure. These changes, along with a host of new characters, provide a distinctly different experience as compared to previous titles, mostly in the way of pacing and progression. To be truthful, I did not enjoy Revelations as much as I have other titles in the series, but its unique story structure did allow it to pull off some interesting tricks within its self-contained narrative, even if its gameplay remains fairly similar to the last two main series titles.

You'll switch frequently between characters, starting with the STARS of the first game, the increasingly macho yet redoubtable Chris Redfield and the Kind and Capable Jill Valentine. Now members of the BSAA, Bioterrorism Security Assessment Alliance, Chris and Jill investigate BOW outbreaks and the terrorist groups which orcehstrate them. Joining them is one of the broadest casts of supporting characters introduced in a Resident Evil game to date. Jill is partnered with Parker Luciani, whose quiet charm and cool professionalism often give way to sincere care and compassion. Chris, in contrast, is partnered with the flirtatious Jessica Sherawat, a more hot-headed and upfront personality in contrast to Chris's venerable stoicism.

These four will make up the main cast, while the more comedic duo Quint and Keith also have a few levels to themselves, mostly to set-up key information in twisting plot of the game. This wide cast of playable characters is, perhaps, the first major divergence from the main series, and in some ways tips the games hand. If you read the above, and consider in addition to these characters we also have the supporting cast and villains, you might reasonably conclude that Revelations' plot is rather busy.

Indeed, Revelations is something of a hotbed of ideas, for gameplay, story, and characters. Structured as a series of Episodes, players jump between characters engaing in a brief portion of one story, before switching to the next. As the game progresses, these stories start to converge as the games mystery is revealed. This switching allows the game to try out a variety enclosed gameplay and story styles, and taken individually, these can be quite well executed. The larger problem, however, is that the brevity of the game and frequency of the switching prevents Revelations from building a consistent tone.

To illustrate, Jill's opening segments are quiet, with a focus on exploration, investigation, and puzzle solving. She even has a unique sequence where she does not have her weapons, during which the game's dodge mechanic is introduced. In contrast, after Jill's initial stage we jump to Chris, whose segment is strongly action focussed, with large numbers of enemies. While such contrast can be used to deepen the player's experience and appreciation of both kinds, the harsh transitions make this difficult.

It is worth noting that the core gameplay is familiar in all these cases, however. Like RE4 and 5, players have third person, over-the-shoulder view. This time, however, players can move (albeit somewhat slowly) while aiming. This allows players to check corners and fire while repositioning. This is also requirement, as the sensitivity for aiming leaves much to be desired. I found the regular fine movements I have used in previous games did not impart the same level of accuracy as I would have wanted. The laser sight has also been replaced with a crosshair, which lacks some of the specificity of the red dot.

In addition to the change to aiming, players can now dodge, though I found this was also spotty. It is worth it to note that both these changes are also found in later releases, in particular the RE3 remake, a coincidence which suggests, again, that Revelations was used to test the development of mechanics for use in the main series. A part of me wonders if the difference in quality is the result of the steam version being an HD port instead.

Along with this, Jill gets access to an item box, allowing her to custom tool weapons and swap them out. Rather than a true inventory, each ammo type now has a set capcity, upgrades for which can be found. The custom tooling is an interesting mechanic, as you must choose which guns get which buffs, spuring on decisions and helping the player to develope their own loadout. Because customizations can be swapped in and out, players are more free to experiment, unlike the harsher buy-upgrade. This mechanic is unique to Jill, but she is the most frequent character played.

Speaking of, there are 12 episodes in total, most with 2-3 sub-stages. While players can jump between characters and locations during an episode, most episodes have you playing as Jill, and the game is better for it. While the other segments are fine, Chris running to the rescue, Parker's Flashbacks to the game's inciting events, and the odd-ball duo's investigation are all less engaging than Jill and Parker's investigation of the game's main location, a delapidated cruise ship, now home to all manner of mysteries and monsters.

The Queen Zebobia, is a luxury cruise liner which eagle eyed note readers will discover was designed in part by George Trevor, the original designer of the mansion from the first game. Once an austentatious ship, the Zenobia has become a dripping nightmare whose pelagic denizens infest every deck and hall. This marks a return to some the quiet and haunting moments that typified the survival horror experiences of the series. The game also reinforces the player's exploration by using a new scanning mechanic. Player's can scan various the environment to find hidden supplies. This encourages players to observe each room they are in. They can also scan enemies, eventually acquiring healing items as a reward. This return to the pensive style of the early games was greatly appreciated.

Story of Revelations is not incredible, but serves to clarify a great deal about the changes in the world following the events of Raccoon City and the formation of the BSAA. It also underscores the series underlying messages about the terrors of corporate interests and the how greed and desire for power drive the world to horror and ruin.

Revelations features some great monster design, eschewing regular Zombies in favor of increasingly aquatic horrors. The most standard enemies are the 'Oozes' whose slimely cartilagenous forms resemble the Regenerators from RE4, though not quite as terrifying. These along with numerous aquamarine mutants fill out an impressive gallery of enemies, despite the limited run time of the game. Graphically, the characters are the most detailed, while the upscaled textures do an admirable job. Still, the game would benefit from better lighting, as currently things can feel somewhat flat. Taken overall, however, it is impressive given its hand held origins.

In the end, Revelations is not, in my mind, the greatest of Resident Evil titles. Its tries too many things in too short a time span, while its story and characters can become confused as the story jumps around. That said, for a port of a handheld game it is impressive, and it can be fun to play. I consider it worthy of playing, though I doubt I will be returning to Revelations the next time I want to revist Resident Evil or the survival horror genre.

So an already lackluster experience is being bogged down by numerous frustrations. 

Oh, and the game insists you non-stop use a detection device (and a cumbersomely handled gun-replacement-equipment styled one, unlike an easy to toggle Arkham's detective mode or similar). So expect more annoyances and even less atmosphere/immersion as a result of that terrible, terrible design decision.


Again, the Raid Mode's a decent experience, wherein you can steadily gain currency and account levels, the combination of which allow the unlocking of better gear. It's simple, but that makes for a nicely casual co-op experience when you're not up for much else.

Moreover, co-op play does a good job of compensating for the outdated gameplay, so the whole experience is a lot better (the campaign actually has you paired up throughout it, but your AI co-op partners in the campaign are all too often ineffective and confused, or even legitimately abandon you without any clear narrative explanation as to why they're doing so).

Unfortunately, the only two ways of unlocking Raid mode are to play through the campaign or to use someone else's save file. If you do choose to find a save file to download, even that hard-won convenience may backfire compared to you choosing to alternate between campaign and Raid play yourself, given the large amount of Raid currency one can earn from Campaign play, even without having touched Raid. 

Which is to say, a fully completed Campaign file would still give you a pretty strong early advantage in Raid play, which may diminish the appeal of the experience for you and/or your co-op partner. I mean, I still absolutely encourage you to go for a save file over trying to balance the two experiences (or, really, playing Campaign at all), but it's a further example of how badly designed the game experience is.


Finally, the game itself just.. hasn't dated well. Rather, none of the games from the RE:4 era or before really have, given the cumbersome nature of tank controls, the limitations of early 3D graphics, and the simple, often overly clunky nature of early RE games. However, with this being a budget-y feeling release, and not feeling comparable to the main releases in terms of quality, the whole experience actually presents itself even more disfavorably than that of the other games.

Honestly, this is a game I'd only recommend after a full remake (as is the current RE trend). Unfortunately (or perhaps, maybe, actually fortunately?) this game doesn't seem like it'd encourage a re-release from its publisher.

If you're hard-up for a co-op experience and don't mind first playing through a game based more in Gamecube/PS2 era gameplay and graphics than its release date would lead you to expect, that's troubled by various frustrations, or are willing (and able) to find and use an external save file simply to be able to play the only part of the game that was given some proper handling..

Then sure, I could recommend this. Similarly, for those that enjoy playing the original RE3~4 generation of games even to this day, and favor underdeveloped, buggy gameplay over the similarly substantial flaws of the other games (ie, Ashley) then there'd likely also probably be some appeal.

Otherwise... well, with recent RE releases having diverted so much from series roots, my best recommendation for those wanting a solid RE experience would be the remakes of the early games. Especially for those wanting a similar but better experience to this game, the RE4 remake seems like a good recommendation for those who didn't burn out on the game the first time around.

 For those looking for a co-op alternative... well, honestly, I've got nothing that's really in the same vein of 3D Raid Mode FPS/TPS play to recommend. :S But at the same time, this one doesn't offer a compelling enough experience on that front to really recommend it for genre alone, what with so many better co-op experiences existing out there. 


 So yeah- while you save up for the new Saints Row or Goat Simulator or whatever other multiplayer experience is notable at the time you read this, maybe see if you can catch this game in a Tier 1 bundle purchase. Definitely don't spend meaningful money on this, because this is a game that arguably wasn't worth a purchase (due to lack of polish, depth, and user convenience) even when its gameplay and graphics and interface weren't as outdated as they now are.

If you are anything like me and are often curious about strange and obscure spin-off media for big franchises and are in any way interested in resident evil as a brand, then I would gently recommend revelations especially if you are fond of the over-the-shoulder combat systems present in resident evil 4-6. Revelations is by no means a masterpiece, hell it's not even a very good game but considering the context of resident evil in 2012 and its origins as a game released a decade ago for the Nintendo 3ds it has become a very interesting piece in resident evils long and convoluted history, between the awkward transition of the absurdity and artificially amplified stakes of the series sixth entry to the traditional horror of the seventh.

The story in revelations is well awkward, to say the least, it even goes so far to implement “previously on” recaps, desperately trying to emulate the feeling of an American action drama to an embarrassing degree, I have to admit witnessing capcom's attempts to desperately cling on to trends from the early 2010s is adorable and if you are a fan of resident evils trademark cheesiness you will no doubt be enamored by these. I understand the recaps were implemented due to the game's originally portable nature, however, in the modern high-definition versions these only serve to interrupt the pacing even while desperately trying to skip them and save the game.

The story here is the bog-standard affair when it comes to resident evil with a layer of a counter-bioterrorism organization plot strewn together over the top of a very simple premise with returning character Jill Valentine and newcomer Parker investigating the bio-organic weapon-infested Queen Zenobia one of three sister ships in the middle of the Mediterranean. Revelations also transitions to different perspectives and flashback sequences which are more action-oriented with returning blackhole of personality Chris Redfield.

Characters in revelations fall into two categories that is either a plank of wood devoid of any notable personality or charisma like Jill and Chris, or they fill the role of an obnoxious and cringeworthy side character the infamous example being Jessica with her trademark one-legged wetsuit, the other primary examples being the duo of Quint and Keith who appear in some action levels in a snowy environment they play to their stereotypes to an infuriating degree and as a result aren’t funny in the slightest. The narrative lacks self-awareness and takes itself completely seriously. As a result of a combination of the characters, a b-story plot and uninteresting melodrama between the antagonist Morgan Lansdale and Colonel Roy Campbell stand in Clive Obrien I ultimately fail to care about what is going on.

The gameplay is very average with weapons that leave little punch or semblance of impact that is only highlighted when the game transitions into the more action-oriented flashback sequences which I must add are just outright awful to play. The gameplay's highlight is, funnily enough, it's raid mode which is a stand-in for the mercenaries from previous entries, I imagine that it benefits from a second player however as my runs were completely solo. The game also sometimes transitions in bland turret segments, but I must admit the final one did have a fascinating monster design. To further expand on the game’s presentation the enemy design while not scary is outstanding and the atmosphere for the ship setting itself is stellar, especially in the earlier bedroom segments and a beautifully realized main hall that the player backtracks through on multiple occasions, the music is also surprisingly decent.

I would only recommend this game to those who have played the other higher-budget entries and are curious about the series' other endeavors.

I had a really good time with Resident Evil Revelations. It feels like a mix between the action style of Resident Evil 5 and the more classic survival horror elements the series is known for.

The gameplay is mostly fun. One of the biggest improvements is that you can move while aiming, which already makes the combat feel better compared to some older entries. The enemies are also more manageable and don’t swarm you constantly like they do in Resident Evil 5, so fighting them is actually enjoyable instead of frustrating.

The game is structured like a TV show with episodes, each one having a “Previously On” recap and an ending scene, which is a really cool way to present the story.

Speaking of the story, it’s good overall but not perfect. The return of Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield is great, and their interactions are easily the best part of the narrative. However, many of the new characters are forgettable and the villains aren’t very interesting.

The graphics still look pretty good for their time, especially the environments on the cruise ship. The sound design is also excellent, with great enemy sounds, solid voice acting, and music that helps build tension during the horror moments.

My biggest issue is probably the map, which can be confusing when you need to travel to areas that are far away. Sometimes it’s hard to figure out where exactly the game wants you to go.

Replayability is also a bit limited unless you really enjoy Raid Mode or want to replay the campaign on higher difficulties.

Overall, Resident Evil Revelations isn’t perfect, but it’s still a very enjoyable Resident Evil game with fun gameplay and a good survival horror atmosphere.

As someone who doesn't like almost any of the mainline Resident Evil games, I still fondly remember playing RE Revelations 2's first episode with my cousin in co-op when it came out. This is the main reason I even gave the first game of the spin-off series even a try and I must admit, even if I had some fun with it, Revelations is an incredibly dull and predictable game.

Me having fun with the game can largely be attributed to wanting to play something that doesn't require me to use my brain after having played loads of rather immersive and long games. If it wasn't for that, I would have probably quit halfway through because there really isn't anything unique or well-done about it. The story is insanely cheesy in all the wrong ways, all the twists are either stupidly predictable or they don't even make any sense, and the voice acting and the dialogue is painfully bad, but combined with the typical japenese body language animations, it feels like a damn fever dream.

Of course, that's just the story mode of the game (which is arguably the main selling point of RE games), but considering the gameplay aspect is rather mediocre, I can't really find a reason for me to bother playing the Raid Mode and fight off waves of monsters and such. It's a step up from Resident Evil 4 sure, but it's nowhere near the level of Dead Space which came out 4 years earlier (!!!). And while we are at Dead Space, that game isn't perfect either, but is pretty weird how that game happens to outclass Revelations graphically as well, although, originally being a 3DS game, I'm willing to let that slide.

To conclude this review, I would not recommend anyone buying this game for the full price, but if you happen to be the biggest RE5 fan to ever live, I guess it's worth to grab during a sale.

OBS: Antes de começar a citar os negativos eu gostaria de dizer que esse jogo me deixou uma impressão de que na verdade existiam 3 times de desenvolvedores trabalhando nesse jogo, um deles realmente tinha muita coisa interessante e funcional em mãos e os demais trouxeram mais do que nós já vimos em titulos anteriores apenas para segurar os fãs antigos da franquia.

This just isn't a very fun game.

Yes, it's a mobile port, and if you want to use that as an excuse to forgive its shortcomings, then good on you! But I am judging it based on how fun it is to play.... and it isn't.

The controls aren't nearly as precise as any of the mainline Resident Evil entries, including even RE4, released nearly a decade earlier.

The graphics are "enhanced" from the 3DS version, but still wildly subpar. (Take a look out any window and notice a gigantic vertical seam in the basic skybox, because it's actually a *box*.)

The classic RE navigation is mostly intact, but feels streamlined and linear, cut up into bite-sized mobile chunks that ruin exploration and any sense of real place. You'll pass locked doors, but you won't access them until a later chapter forces you to go back, so there's no requirement to learn your environment. Which is a good thing, because the map is utterly, completely, shamefully uninformative.

Combat is fine.... just fine. If you don't disable mouse acceleration, aiming is quite literally broken, with small hand movements remaining undetected in a wildly large dead zone. But once you do, you'll get some squishy, crunchy headshots when you get used to the bizarre way the creatures move. It still feels janky compared to the mainline entries, but it's much better than what you would expect a 3DS game to feel like.

There's a scanning mechanic, which is cool, but it's also how you find invisible hidden items. In practice, Revelations encourages you to take your scanner out every 20 feet of movement to see what's hidden around you. This hurts the game's pace and atmosphere.

The game's writing, from cutscene dialogue to item descriptions, was clearly not handled by a native English speaker, or an intelligent person for that matter. Hey writers - a manifest isn't a flight plan. It's a list of passengers, and you can't navigate with it. Or how about this item description:

"The bright green herb not only heals fatigue, but it also helps to strengthen the natural healing process so that wounds heal faster."

If that sentence doesn't trigger you, maybe you'll raise an eyebrow when your female companion shouts, "Me and my sweet ass are on the way!"

The story isn't any good either, and since it probably has more cutscenes than any other RE game I can remember, there is lots of sitting through awful exposition waiting for something to happen. And for you Resident Evil lore nerds, you should know that this game doesn't add anything interesting to the canon despite featuring both Chris and Jill.

The sub-par, boring, piecemeal campaign is supplemented with a Raid Mode, which turns Revelations into a gear game. You have to level up and collect weapons and mods to tackle each level's increasing challenge. Enemies now show up with health bars and damage numbers, which is weird for Resident Evil, and they feature more variety in terms of size and ways to kill you. This makes the combat more interesting as you continuously improve your loadout to contend with the game's various modified challenges.

There's a lot to this mode, and it's much more substantial than most of the tacked on score attack side games Resident Evil titles have featured over the years. Most importantly - this is the closest I felt to the game being fun! The added depth of the leveling and gear mechanics make this a better offering than the sparse, dull campaign.

Unfortunately, Raid Mode is very, very long - I would estimate upwards of 20-30 hours to complete the whole thing. And since it recycles the campaign's small set of maps over and over again, it quickly begins to feel like a grind that the game's limited amount of content just isn't designed to support. If it were to have been expanded into its own thing with a larger variety of maps and enemies, Raid Mode could have been worth your time. But as it stands, especially now that co-op partners are hard to find, I'd say most players won't want to pump in 20+ lonely hours.

Unless you're a diehard Resident Evil completionist, this is an easy game to skip. Watch a story summary if you want to know its minimal implications to the silly-as-bananas Resident Evil lore, but otherwise you can find much, much better survival horror shooters to play out there.

So many issues with a small portion of fun 
The story follows Jill Valentine and the BSAA on their mission to take down the terrorist group known as Veltro, however there's more going on behind the scenes that Jill will soon discover. The characters in this game are really unforgettable. There are those who have already been developed such as Jill and Chris Redfield, but even in this game they feel really bland and don't have that much personality to them and i haven't really mentioned any of the new characters cause they are completely forgettable. Not to mention that some of their character models are pretty hideous and the voice acting is so dry. The story itself is not the greatest thing about this game. While it may give you a simple premise at the start of the game, it tries to make it this crazy story full of twists and turns, but the execution was really poor with the twists being really obvious to the player. There's even one instance where a character is going to betray the team and the game devs really weren't subtle about it which is unfortunate cause an unexpected twist in the story could have benefited the game. 
The main setting of the Queen Zenobia takes Resident Evil yet again to a completely different location and I must say that having the majority of the game on a big ship was really creative with the way that it was executed. The other locations on the other hand such as the snowy mountains and Terragrigia really aren't that fleshed out and can be quite boring to traverse around. Thankfully the main focus is on the ship and I must say that there is a great amount of detail and variety in this place, such as the living quarters of the main hall with its grand presentation. 
Visually, it could have been a bit better. Graphically, this game has aged poorly even when all settings were put on max. The art direction isn't that great either and cause of this there really isn't anything to comment on how the game looks. The most i can say is that its serviceable but not the most pleasing thing to look at. 
Sound and audio are fine with the soundtrack being full of generic action and horror pieces (mainly action) and is completely forget able. The Audio for this game is also serviceable with guns sounding like something ripped off of youtube or a sound board and enemies being the standard growl noise. It works for the game but it isn't anything to write home about. 
In terms of gameplay, this (in my opinion) is somewhat the saving grace that this game has. The movement and shooting controls felt really smooth and satisfying to play with. One thing i really like is the way you can change stats on your weapons with the parts that you find throughout the levels, giving the player variety with what they can enhance their weapon with. Something that was upsetting to me was the way inventory was treated as it doesn't have the usual management that RE games are known for as these would be like a mini puzzle game where what you choose would determine whether you survive or not. It does make it easier for the player to grab items and go into combat immediately, however i do prefer having that aspect in the game for more of a challenge. There are many enemy types in the game which does keep combat fresh and challenging. There are the odd puzzles here and there that a decent enough to do, but aren't like a major game mechanic or anything. The boss fights that you get to play out are pretty decent even if they aren't that grand. 
Finally I would like to highlight how poorly this game runs. This game has a high tendency of crashing and dropping frame rates especially when it comes to elevators. There is also a section of the game where you have to change the resolution in order to progress in the game which i have to say being the second RE game that has had issues running on PC, Capcom should at the very least make sure that these games are even playable to be on steam. 
Overall, while there are a handful of things that make the game enjoyable, Resident Evil Revelations is overshadowed with problems. The only people i really see playing this are fans of the series like myself, but even I don't i have any intentions of ever revisiting this title.

I picked this up eons ago. Idk how much I paid for it unfortunately. I dropped it way back because the story bored me and managing ammo was something I seriously did not care to do. I'm glad I gave it another shot. Though Raid Mode almost made me forget how the Campaign worked, and I readied myself to equip a Magnum and waste all the ammo before remembering. Oof.

The only thing I remember about the story is how annoyed I got because nobody can interact with things while they're chatting on comms. So when people decide to spark up a conversation when you're standing in front of a weapon chest, extra excited about what you found, you have to wait for the jabber jaws to get tired before you can enjoy yourself. 

What really floored me in the best way, is Raid Mode. Raid mode is basically Arcade Mode of the Campaign. No talking, cuscenes, drama, nothing. as far as I know, every character you have seen in the game can be unlocked, and used here, most are unique, and sport perks that will assist whatever silly tasks you wish to do, as well as negate issues weapons have for you, like slow firing speed, reload. They come in three difficulties: Chasm, Trench, and Abyss. And each after Chasm really turns the experience into something you'll either scream at, or enjoy, probably both, as leveling up to, or over the enemies level will invalidate a lot of the difficulty they posed to you. 

The simplest way I can describe the feel of Raid mode is, if Phantasy Star Portable was made by Capcom. There are a lot of pop in enemies who attack at or before the time they're vulnerable, and enemy spawns are basically Megaman tier, where there's a very strict amount of push pull you need to do to not be hit by things. Something could literally be spawning in that great hiding spot you found, so much so that if your guns are in order, it is safer to move in the direction you're shooting and turn around every few seconds to make sure the spawns aren't going to ruin your bonus. It's definitely borderline unfair, but it's fun, trust me.

You can also get skills to equip to weapons to customize them the way you want, some really good skills have serious drawbacks, so if you plan to run one weapon, don't use them, getting a -30% damage buff will be noticeable. Weapons are somewhat diverse, though I feel a few have way better options than others. I'm not level 50 yet, so I can't really give you a better answer at what's on the top, but if the game is allowing being higher leveled to be broken, I'd imagine the skills get stupid good. 

I almost forgot something HUGE... I got the complete edition back when it was available, so a lot of my skills have green icons instead of white. I think green means DLC. Probably 95 percent of the skills I equip nonstop are green. So my experience, and yours may sharply differ. Though, I've also been playing this by myself, and if you had a partner I don't think some of the difficulty I've had would phase you at all, as several of the problem monsters have incredible weaknesses on their back, in the same way the Omega Metroids did. I'm seriously fearing my Revelations 2 experience will suffer greatly from not having the DLC there, but I guess I'll see after I get fed up with this one, or hit a wall where I tell myself that having a friend would make this infinitely easier, and not require me to do cheesy things like throw grenades at myself to be invincible to attacks I'm not ready to avoid. 

I could probably go on and on about why I like Raid mode and how something this simple could carry my enjoyment of a game, but if you ever wanted to play a resident evil game with a bunch of different playstyles to try, a handful of guns, boatload of skills and outrageous amounts of replay value, this is the game. I haven't tried Revelations 2 though. If you have a Co-Op buddy, this is a definite grab, try to find a deal on the DLC if you're going in alone, or consider using characters that have buffs for your favorite weapon. Watching Jill reload handguns faster than I can snap my fingers is always going to be a sight to see.

Resident Evil is a franchise that hits a lot of bullet points for what I consider to be fun gaming. It's horror themed, which I love. It's campy horror that doesn't take itself too seriously which adds to the fun factor. The atmosphere, zombie/monster-killing gameplay and item management aspects are consistently engaging. And I just really like the whole concept of a malevolent biotech company conducting fringe genetic research and experiments, opening the way for all those wonderfully twisted monstrosities. It's a backdrop that is rife with possibility, and apparently Capcom agrees, judging by the number of installments in this long-running series. I had let Resident Evil Revelations slip through the cracks for a long time, and decided to finally remedy that in 2019. 

In the first place, I was impressed by the visual fidelity for this game that had its roots on the 3DS. I tend to be pretty forgiving on the technical front, and it's not a stunning achievement by any means, but I wasn't expecting things to look as nice as they did, given the origins. And the primary setting of being on an ocean liner makes for an interesting environment for the bio-terrorism eradication. Granted, it's really just a mansion on the sea in most practical regards, but the overall atmosphere was a bit different, and I enjoyed that. This installment plays out in episodic fashion, where we jump between characters and locales in the intertwining narrative. And while that was a fresh approach, I actually prefer the singular protagonist viewpoint through a campaign. But the narrative itself was suitably epic and befitting a tale in this wild universe. In terms of item acquisition, we are the beneficiaries of a new gadget called the Genesis that lets us scan environments and enemies for items in addition to finding things laying around as we normally would in the series. It had the effect of slowing exploration down, although I didn't mind that. There were a nice variety of bosses, and they could be pretty significant difficulty spikes, which isn't uncommon for the series. In the case of the first boss - the communications officer - if you forgot to pick up the shotgun, which I overlooked, it's quite the hurdle. And all of the bosses, for that matter, take tons of damage and do a good job depleting your ammo reserves which ups the tension and sense of accomplishment quite nicely. We're granted a new dodge move in Revelations that is timing-based relative to enemy attack animations, and utilizing that can serve to make the boss fights much more manageable. It also works effectively against the regular mutants, and allows you to get out of some precarious situations. 

There are some sore spots worth mentioning. I did miss the inventory tetris. I know it's an annoyance to some, but I like the item juggling/management. I also wasn't a huge fan of the bite-sized design. I understand the choice based on the original hardware being a handheld, but the relatively short, albeit interconnected, missions made it feel less like a big traditional Resident Evil adventure for me. I like the long, seamless feeling adventure more than the disconnected but related episodic content. Another point of note I'd like to mention is the camp. It seems the cheese is more self-aware here, like it's intentionally placed rather than having that naivety and innocence of the earlier entries. It just felt more forced rather than genuine with  a bit of self-parody sensation.. And I didn't think this entry had the charm of the mainline entries. It felt, in many ways, like a spin-off, although a very good one. I can't say that this is my favorite Resident Evil. I've played 1 through 5, REmake and Code Veronica X, and it probably would rank on the lower end of the franchise from what I've experienced, but that certainly isn't an insult to the game. As stated, I really love this fictional universe, and Revelations is another fun trip into survival horror. And there’s plenty of incentive to stay with Raid mode too. Despite some unfavorable comparisons to other series entries, I still had a blast here. If you’re a fan of the series, pick it up. 5/5

Resident evil revelations (or Biohazard revelations, as its original japanese name is a more accurate description of the game) is an action game, where the tension comes mostly from the scarcity of ammo, and to a lesser extent from longish reload animations. Most enemies will be slow moving bullet sponges, and early on the only sane solution is to jogg around some of the more resilient enemies. It mostly works because the enemies cannot travel through doors, once you travel to a new room you are safe from whatever was in the previous one. However you will have to deal with them again if you return to the room. Which you will do several times, because on the ship you will have to re-visit the same locations. 

The main part of the game will happen on a ship, but there will be external acts at other locations too. Some are flashbacks, some happen parallel to the main events. That means that you will play with a varied cast, always working in pairs. One such pair is mostly for a comedic relief - a nice change of pace. In the ship duo you control Jil, and Parker is her support buddy. In other sections you control a male protagonist, and an eye candy female will be your support, in revealing and fairly impractical outfits. Also the game will shamelessly reuse a lot of environments. While it could be defended in the case of the ship, where some backtracking makes sense, it will happen with other places too.

Early on a scanner will be unlocked. It can be used to scan enemies, which will progress to bonus healing items. But enemies are not the only things to be scanned for. Hidden stashes can be found through scanning along. Once I realized the scarcity of ammo, I always scanned around new locations, hoping to discover new ammo. A few times even healing items are revealed. Another use of the scan is to collect fingerprints. Through normal gameplay I managed to unlock the 15 fingerprints required for the mid tier achievement.

The healing in the game is done through green leafs, represented by a flower in a pot. As you take damage the screen gets bloody, with heavy heartbeat. Consuming a green leaf removes all injuries. Not the most immersive way, but perhaps the intention was not using healing at all. Still I had to use healing a lot of times, especially during boss fights.

There are a few boss fights, I could only finish the final one on the first try. I played the game on normal difficulty, suggested as the intended experience for the game on start. Once started, the difficulty cannot be changed. Ironically, the difficulty of the bosses was mostly in their encounter order, with the very first boss being the most hard for me. That Mayday boss fight was very difficult, mostly due to the infinitely respawning enemies. I tried that a lot, till I eventually passed. Comparatively, the second boss fight was much easier. As an alternative to boss fights there will be sometimes horde fights, when a large number of enemies will be thrown on you. I’m not sure whether those end after a given amount of enemies are killed, or when a timer finishes. A few times there will be on the rail shooter segments. That made sense during a boss fight, but the other one felt more like a tacked on arcady thing. I had to use a lot of healing items while making through it.

The inventory and weapon upgrade system is very barebone. The map system just shows a generic approximation of your location, and was fairly hard to navigate. Still, it proved helpful to guide you towards the highlighted target. There will be a minimap in the corner of the screen, whose most useful function is probably to show the yet un-openable doors. If there is a red door, than you have to go to somewhere else, or have to find an unlock mechanism first. It also can be hided for more immersion.

Weapons can be found while progressing through the story, and a character can carry 3 weapons at most. With 3 weapons already equipped, the currently selected will be swapped for the found one. I had to read a walkthrough to find the rifle (i.e. the sniper weapon). If you didn’t find it naturally, by the time you encounter the Mayday boss it should be already obtained. It requires a side exploring, as it will be in an entirely optional part of the map, which I left for later while I was following the storyline. Once unlocked, a weapon can be freely swapped back at a weapon upgrade terminal. Also, near boss fights there is generally a weapon upgrade terminal, allowing to switch to / tune the weapons to the nature of the encounter.

The game can be played with keyboard and mouse, or with a controller. Normally I would played with a controller, but this was the first game to play on my new computer, and the PS4 controller wasn’t yet configured in Steam, and as such was unusable. So I started with keyboard and mouse, and stuck to those. The aiming was somewhat problematic, made worse by a small field of view. During combat I had no awareness of the nearby monsters on the side. Also the enemies swayed a lot, making headshots that much more difficult. I still got the achievement for killing enough enemies with a headshot. You can dodge, but I forgot how to do that after the tutorial, and in the keyboard mapping there wasn’t a description for that, so I couldn’t rely on dodging. There will be a fair number of enemy types, with different attack patterns and sponginess. Most of them will be slow. Still, in cramped locations they will eventually reach to you.

The graphics of the game is mostly dated, with some clutter having clearly very low resolution, even for a 2012 game. In contrast the protagonists will have reasonably detailed graphics, and the animation of the enemies will be good too. It can be called a HD remake only when compared to the initial version of the game.

During gameplay there are only predetermined save points, which trigger automatically. The user cannot save manually during a chapter, but there is a chance for it on some summary screens between acts. Not that it would really matter, as there is anyway an autosave at the same point too. It was especially annoying when the save point was before a series of actions to be executed, after which a small cinematic event plays, after which I died repeatedly. So I had to redo the exact same actions, watch the cinematic, and proceed to another try. Putting the save after the cinematic would made that experience much less grating.

I played the game with the japanese voice acting. Generally I say that the japanese voice acting is good, but strangely in this game it was fairly bad, on par with a generic run of the mill english voice acting – which I seldom encounter in japanese voice acting. Especially Parker’s voice actor gave a very bored performance, but even Jil wasn’t much more enthusiastic. At least some of the supporting cast (over)acted a bit better. The music was subdued, the accent was on the creepy sound effects. Also the japanese recapitulation narrations on loading a scene will consistently use the term “Biohazard revelations” when referring to the game.

There is a raid mode, which can be played cooperatively or in single player mode. I only tried the first raid, it was a stroll through some rooms in the ship, with a few enemy encounters. These raids are unlocked by finishing portions of the main game, completing the main storyline I think should unlock all of them. You gain some BP points during the campaign, they can be spent in a shop to unlock better equipment or consumables for your raid characters. Those BP points can be obtained during raids too, but the first, and only one that I finished gave a very small amount. There are several difficulty levels for raids, but I obviously only tried the easiest one. Also there will be health bars for the enemies, and you will see the numeric damage done, a feature that is not present in the story mode.

The main storyline took me around 11 hours. The game was stable for me, it didn’t crash at all.

I feel that this game is highly underrated. It has a good mix of horror and action. I found the characters to be good overall having Jill as the main and Chris playable as well made the game much more interesting however I found the side cast like Parker, Jessica, O'Brian, Raymond, Jack and Morgan as interesting characters and liked the dynamics. Clint and Keith less so however I found the statements about how bad they were to be highly overstated. Quint has bad social skills yet is a genius and this contrasts well with Keith who is more straight laced in missions. The game even has it's own pursuer like the Tyrant pursuers in Rachel and I found her to be a great character as well. Storyline is all over the place as it has a mystery behind it yet plot twists galore, this may sound bad but this makes the story something that needs to be able to evolve as it does while playing as it unravels. Gameplay is very good and I find it much more to my liking than games like Re4 or Re5. Re4 and 5 often have this over the shoulder and side gun aspect with them (particularly with Sheva in Re5) that I wasn't fond of while this one was more of a behind the back one instead of merely over the shoulder I preferred. Also 4 and 5 felt stiffer in movements while this game was more fluid. Moreover it has a dodge system similar to Re3R (remake) though one complaint is having the aim button the same as the dodge button however this was similar to the og Re3. A plethora of weapons and varieties abound, however I wish there were not these levels to them based on your character level as you may need to purchase another of the same but of a higher level. I like the fact that you can use parts for upgrades of weapons like more ammo capacity or damage and unlockable outfits. Raid Mode to me here is far superior to Mercenaries Mode in Re4 or 5 which I didn't like as Raid has you exploring and doing missions in an entire level whereas in Mercenaries I felt limited in area and constantly did the same looping circles. Also in Raid you can dodge enemies it is often not about killing all but clearing an objective, these things gave me more of an Re feel where I can judge when to run or gun and to think fast to solve puzzles. One criticism is I wish there were more places however it did such a great job that I never felt bored in going back to a place I been before or even on a similar mission as story mode as I often forgot these by then, are often in a different context here and great practice for the story mode and remembering certain events and mastering them. There are no item boxes here in story mode or elsewhere and unlimited space so no need for item management but the game doesn't need it and works well in the storied puzzle/action pace it has instead there are item upgrade boxes to upgrade weapons (in story mode there aren't levels for the weapon only in raid and you can find weapons in game). The areas were really well done with an aquatic/marine feel to them and though not to many varieties in enemies the one's here are very good so make up for that downside too. The BSAA and Terragrigia stuff are such events that can be expanded on and have ripples affects even in games now and the characters were intriguing to the point I want to see them again. Would be nice to see Parker save Jill or more on Jessica and Raymond's mysteries or O'Brian on the BSAA (who had a cameo reference in Re7). Also it would have been nice to see Keith in the events of Re5 (maybe in a Remake). Anyway i think I spoke enough on why I think you should buy this game and why it has been highly underrated.

I never thought that Resident Evil spin-off games would be so fun and enjoyable. Resident Evil: Revelations has great story-line on campaign mode. The idea to start the game on a ship with all new type infected form is also outstanding, and also make the game has special story with different stages (we know that Resident Evil 0,1,2,3,4 and 5 all started on the land). This spin-off version also has different bonus mode than other series, it's called Raid Mode. It doesn't look like Mercenaries, there's no time limit to clear a stage and no combo bonus. You can clear the stage with just killing a few enemies, since there's no locked door all you need is just go through finish line by punching/kicking a golden coin. But the game also give special bonuses if you clear a stage on raid mode by killing all enemies, getting no hits/damages, high accuracy rate, and finish the stage with short times. 

Based on my experience on this game, here advantages and weakness that I could give:

🌟Advantages:
1. It has special dodge move, that mean you can avoid enemies when they try to hurt you. A little bit improvement from RE4 and RE5 which there's no ability to dodge attack from opponents.
2. You can shoot enemies or reload with still moving/walking (RE4 or RE5 only allow us to shoot enemies but need to stand still on your spot).
3. We play with AI, but no need to worry about their health or ammunition (it's all like RE6).
4. This is the first series of RE that allow us to customize parts of weapon, so we won't get weapons only here, but also their parts to make weapons more stronger.
5. No need to buy weapons on campaign mode, all will be given to you. Just seek it from everyplace or complete some campaign achievement and it will be rewarded to you.

❌Weakness:
1. There's no chances anymore to play multiplayer on campaign mode (only possible on Raid Mode).
2. On campaign mode, only Jill who can use item storage to change weapons and its part instead Parker and Chris.
3. Jill's Samurai Edge DLC won't appear in game for some players and it hasn't being fixed.
4. The AI won't help you a lot since their all weapon's specification are lower than yours.
5. The controller settings for pad are similar like RE 4. There's only 2 choice, Advanced type and Shooter type that cannot be set manually by players.
6. On Raid Mode, enemies spot aren't detected on the map. So even you try to memorize all enemies spot by learning from some walkthrough, there's no guarantee you will get easily trinity bonus because enemies spawn on random spots sometimes. Enemies should be readable on the map (example: by giving red spot or something) so players can defend their selves from enemies that spawn behind them.

My Rating for Campaign mode: 8.5/10
My Rating for Raid Mode: 7.5/10

Footnotes: If you wanna be a true special-skills player on Resident Evil, I think this spin-off version is the most precise for you. Raid Mode is not easy mode to play, so you need to learn to dodge, try to use Shooter controller types to shot enemies and still moving around, also memorize every enemies spawn place to avoid them attacking you. Once you got it all, you can try to get trinity bonus on all stages and it proves that your skill on dodging and shooting are 'fully-madness'. The community of this game is still active until  now even it's categorized as an old game. Many pro player will help you a lot to guide you on Raid Mode, and also some of them will teach you how to be a pro on shooting game.

Despite REV being a (decent) port of the 3DS title, and definitely not quite like the obviously superior original old school entries in the series, there is a lot to love here.

Let's get the bad out of the way first. Among REV's worst aspects are the uninspired enemy design (the majority of which are a bunch of unscary bullet-sponges), the facepalm-inducing story that is being conveyed using cringeworthy voice acting from forgettable characters who more often than not contribute nothing of importance to the RE universe.
Whilst REV is episodic in structure, there is no way to select individual chapters. There's nothing wrong with a healthy slow build-up but REV sure takes its sweet time get to the good stuff. Plus there is quite a bit of a grind to endure for weapons to feel effective and powerful, though they are fun to use once all upgraded with custom parts.

Soundtrack-wise, except for composer Takeshi Miura's contributions (RE: Code Veronica), it's just generic and awfully dull. Good grief.

So what's there to love? Well, REV admirably manages to maintain a quite atmospheric & claustrophobic tone throughout its fairly lengthy and varied single player campaign. It offers somewhat satisfying gunplay, and the replay value extends far beyond the campaign into the fun and addicting Raid Mode.

REV's original release wasn't all that long after RE5's, yet it feels quite a bit closer to the classic RE that I know and love. Far closer than RE5 could ever be. Plus, it's a fun game that's well worth a purchase at a discounted price.

3/5 stars. This is a decent little RE game. Gameplay's a bit simplistic by PC standards (no inventory, green herbs only), the plot's as terrible as you'd expect, the characters are irritating, and the dated graphics make a lot of the enemies look a bit goofy. But it (mostly) delivers the satisfying 3rd person shooting of RE4 & 5 with the tension of older RE games.

My biggest complaint is the episodic structure, complete with cliffhangers, flashbacks and completely unnecessary TV-style plot recaps. It really undercuts the sense of isolation and claustrophobia, and forces the terrible plot (and its terrible characters) centre stage. RE is at its best when you can ignore terrible plot and get immersed in the moment-to-moment experience. Revelations nails the atmosphere and the tension, but then they go out of their way to screw it up with the episodic structure.
