[h1]Disclaimer[/h1]
I’ve finished the game on hardest available difficulty once and played a bit of raid mode before reviewing.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
This game is more expensive than the incredible Resident Evil 1 remake, while delivering a much lower quality entertainment.

This is a shooter with even less strategy required than in Resident Evil 4, which at least encouraged movement and controlling groups of enemies.

It can be fun, but it’s overall pretty underwhelming as a whole.

Recommended only to the fans of the series, who want to play all the games.

[h1]Description[/h1]
Resident Evil Revelations tells a separate story from the main series. It focuses on Jill and her partner investigating a suspicious ship in the middle of the ocean. This ship is, of course, overrun with bio weapons. There are no zombies in this game.

The ship itself is not linear, but also isn’t open for you to explore. Instead, you will open up new sections and side areas as you complete objectives.

This game is a shooter through and through. You will acquire new weapons and modular upgrades that increase their stats.

There is also a new mechanic – scanning – which lets you analyze rooms for hidden items. You can also scan living or dead enemies, which will build up a meter and when it’s full – you get a healing plant. There are no other rewards for scanning enemies.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[b]+ Jill’s model[/b]
She looks real nice, which is good since you’ll be looking at her from behind for 90% of the game.

And yeah, that’s all the good I have to say about this game.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[b]- Shooting passable at most[/b]
There is no real depth to combat. In theory you can stun and melee enemies, but since ammo is plentiful – that’s rarely a necessity.

Combat bogs down to – point at enemy and shoot. Preferably aim for the head, since that deals more damage. Then you run away if enemies get too close. That’s it.

[b]- Uninteresting story[/b]
Boring. It has only loose connections to the main games. Once again – no zombies. You know, that thing the game was popular for in the first place?

[b]- Tedious scanning[/b]
Having to scan every room for items is not fun.

[b]- Overall forgettable[/b]
If not for a Resident Evil title – this game would be forgotten already. Hell, even with the title I think it’s mostly forgotten.

[h1]Lowdown[/h1]
This is not really a “bad” game. You can have some fun with it but it is forgettable and uninteresting. What is bad is the price – this game is more expensive than the incredible Resident Evil 1 remake.

As such I cannot recommend it with a clear conscience.

I'm going to be honest, this game is a long way from Resident Evil's best. It scratches the RE itch though and its harmless enough that I think it is worth playing. Just as long as you come at it with tempered expectations.

Let's start with my favorite part of the game, the plot. The plot of this games is completely bonkers. It makes very little sense and I enjoyed the hell out of it. The best way I can explain this game is playing three player Uno when the other two players have nothing but Reverse cards and for some reason you have a hand from a poker deck. In the game you mostly follow Jill while she tries to make sense of this mess meanwhile the two boss players keep double crossing each other over and over again. Everything that happens is really through those two boss characters and you just get left stumbling through it. It's the kind of plot that shouldn't work, but this game is so ridiculous that some how it just does. 

The game play is fine. By default aim assist is enabled, so if you play with keyboard and mouse make sure to disable it. Aiming in the game is okay but for some reason the characters don't seem to like aiming up or down. They'll do it, but it doesn't feel right. The dodge sounds nice too, but I had a hell of a time getting it to work on purpose. I kept doing it by accident. I understand how it works, but it just kind of doesn't really. The puzzles in this game are kind of not great too. In the long run this game ends up feeling a little bit like diet RE 4. It's by no means bad, it just doesn't feel great.

The biggest issue with the game is the exact same thing that happened in RE 6. There are three or four separate character pairings and plot going on at pretty much the same time. It's a lot more tolerable in this one since it doesn't hop around nearly as much. It definitely chops up the game a lot though, and it also does the annoying thing where each character has their own gear sets that don't transfer to other characters so you can suddenly be way under powered compared to how you were before. Along with that there is really only one character that you do any exploring with, so most of the other character chapters end up feeling more flat by comparison. I don't hate how this story is told, but I can't help feeling it would be better if it just stuck to following Jill around. 

I had a good time with this game. I would recommend buying this on sale rather than full price. It's a fun game to just chill with. I don't plan on ever trying to speed run this or anything like I might with some of the others. I could see myself kicking back and playing this again on a snow day though. Just for the laughs on a bonkers plot.

I do understand that this is the remastered version of the game that was released alongside PS4 and Xbox versions, however the game still has the feel of Resident Evil. The segments where you play as Jill feel like classic Resident Evil where you have to conserve ammo and healing items, and the other segments where you play as a variety of different characters feels more like the action side of RE found in games like RE4 and RE5. 

While remastered there are moments where the graphics do look like a 3DS game and that is quite jarring. It is also noticeable that this game reuses the same 3 locations for multiple missions, this is likely because of the hardware it was made for. The game also for some reason has quite a few 'on rails' moments which are incredibly easy.

The game does a good job of creating a solid narrative that kept me guessing and thinking about what was happening even when i wasn't playing it, however it does wrap up quite abruptly and does end with additional text on the screen explaining what happened to the rest of these characters.

Overall this game was a short but enjoyable experience that is let down by some lazy dialogue and a quick ending, however it does strike a balance between both styles of RE that have been present throughout the franchise so far and with its watered down mechanics i would recommend this game to anyone who wants to try the RE franchise out as this game does feel like a good jumping off point.

Revelations is, hands down, the best Resident Evil spin-off. Or at least, my personal favourite. 
Basically, Revelations was made during the dark age of Capcom, where corpo-rat Keiji Inafune successfully convinced the studio to pander to a wider western audience at the cost of the identities of their franchises. One of the factors for this was the massive success of Resident Evil 5, a shooter which served as the 7th main entry of the franchise and most successful game in Capcom's library up to that point, and fittingly, higher-ups decided that the series would continue in the actionised direction and go even further with it, with the end results being the REALLY love-it-or-hate-it Resident Evil 6 (I wrote a really negative review of it, ICYW). However, Masachika Kawata, a producer of several RE titles, whilst convinced that the franchise was too big for traditional survival horror at that time, still felt that people who felt like the series was going too far with the action deserved a dedicated spin-off for that niche, and thus, Revelations was born. And thank god for it!

This game suffers from similarly botched writing as RE6, but thankfully not to the extent of that game, as it still carries likable characters, good ideas, and some solid albeit flawed explorations into the Resident Evil universe explaining how the world considered Bioterrorism a major threat. However, the atmosphere, scares and gameplay are what carry Revelations and make it so good. The Queen Zenobia is one of the best settings ever featured in RE history: Sure, the franchise has explored abandoned cruise ships before, notably in the 2003 game Dead Aim, but the Queen Zenobia sets the benchmark for creepy cruise ships in this series. Every area, nook, cranny and vent has been created with the intent of unnerving the player and laying down the tension thick, and it succeeds immeasurably. Also, the enemies you encounter are really unique: Instead of Zombies or Ganados, we get The Ooze, Zombie/Sea Creature hybrids that come in various shapes and sizes and are utterly sickening to look at. Despite lacking extreme gore (it was originally made for the 3DS), Revelations nails the iconic RE horror and monsters whilst taking it in a new direction.

And the gameplay is brilliant. Playing out like a prototype of what would become Resident Evil VII: Biohazard, Revelations manages to prove that the OTS perspective could still be used for an effective survival horror experience, as the gunplay and controls are substantially improved from Resident Evil 6's and the level design, puzzles, and signature RE death traps are all present and accounted for. Action-freaks need not worry though: Interspersed with the main exploration are segments where you leave Jill Valentine's perspective and play as various other members of the BSAA, and these serve as perfect breather levels as you take down various BOWs and explore varied locales. And unlike RE6, the default FOV is also really good and doesn't make me want to claw my eyes out (though I am playing with an FOV mod).

Overall, Revelations is a brilliant game. It lays the foundation for what the main series would eventually become whilst also delivering a solid survival horror adventure that leaves its own stamp on the RE universe. Of the many RE spin-offs, this one is what I would recommend the most, and it is a must buy.

Resident Evil: Revelations is a RE game originally made for 3DS, and the version here is the PC port. Don't be surprised if the graphics look simpler and outdated compared to the back then recently released RE6 since this game is a port. However, compared to RE6, RE:R feels more closer to earlier RE games, where the map is not really linear, bigger emphasis on exploration-survival rather than action, and of course being more horror-like. Timeline-wise, RE:R is a prequel to RE5, since the epilogue shows Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine going to the mansion in Lost in Nightmares, a flashback DLC in RE5.

Gameplay-wise, RE:R seems like a good blend of RE4/5's simpler combat, while having RE6's ability to move while aiming and a bit smoother combat movement. However, the gameplay kinda presents a problem to me as it feels kinda slow and difficult. Like you cannot sprint, and to dodge enemy attacks you have to read their body language since there is no prompt. Aiming also feels a bit clunkier, but it's not really a big deal. There is no inventory management, you can pick up everything you see until the allowed quantity. The only thing you have to manage is which 3 weapons you want to equip at one time. Enemies are also harder to stun and finish off with a melee kill.

In this game you can play as 4 characters, but most of the time you'll play as Jill who is the main character of this game. This game has an episodic format, and in some chapters you play as the 3 other characters. But the sections where you play as them are usually quite short. Most of the game is set on the Queen Zenobia, a large, quite maze-like cruise ship. Many parts of the ship are free to roam after you collect the required items, allowing you to backtrack to get previously inaccessible/missed items or collectibles. Sadly, there is no option to replay a chapter unless you load a saved game, with the equipment you have from back then.

There is also another game mode called Raid Mode, a more action-oriented game where you fight enemies and follow a pretty linear path to the stage end. It uses levels that are similar, yet modified from the main game. Raid uses universal level and inventory, you can try multiple characters with each their own unique skills to help you through the stages. It is unlike Mercenaries mode where you chain kills for a high score and set in a small area, here you aim to get 3 medals (same or lower level, take no damage, kill all enemies).

I think Resident Evil: Revelations is a pretty good, albeit kinda simplistic RE game. It has the scary atmosphere of the older games, and quite often you are separated from your partner. Despite not being a numbered, main title game from the franchise, I think Revelations is worth a play. Even more if Jill and Chris happens to be your favorite characters in the franchise.

Before anything else, at the time of writing I was heavily binging Resident Evil post completing RE Village so might have slight bias but... wow what a game. 

Despite it being an older title, I actually thought it was one of the spookier RE games, something about the setting made the atmosphere in this game very strong while you were aboard the Zenobia. The visuals also look a little dated - I heavily modified the game with ReShade and got it looking close to RE6 in visuals, which made me quite happy. 

Gameplay wise, it's about on par with Resident Evil 6, allowing you to strafe whilst aiming. Constantly using your tools to scan the environment for ammo and other goodies actually made it more fun, likewise, necessary for ammo conservation as the enemies in this game don't drop ammo, so you can VERY quickly run out if you're not checking the environment thoroughly. The guns available in the game aren't super varied, but feel very responsive and are very useful for taking down the game's baddies. There are a few boss fights sprinkled across the game as well that were tense mainly because most bosses can one or two shot you even on Normal difficulty. The game took me around 6 hours or so to complete according to the game's timer, but there are a total of 12 Episodes.

Two glaringly negative things that stood out to me, however: First off, the game has some pacing issues at times due to the fact that you're not JUST controlling Jill aboard the Zenobia. The game has a few flashback and "Meanwhile" sessions where you're controlling other characters with their own preset weapons and ammo count. The gameplay style doesn't change, you're still required to scan the environment to find more ammo, but I didn't really struggle to maintain ammo count in these sections compared to Jill herself. Secondly, there is a pretty big lack of enemy variety which kinda soured me a little bit as these enemy types in particular, I feel could have taken a lot more forms than just the hulking dummy zombies. There were a grand total of 3 ooze types, a big tentacle ooze monster that you fight maybe twice in the entire game, big blobs with teeth that you fight literally one time in the game (not counting RAID mode) and the ever annoying Hunters that, to me, felt extremely out of place in the game. I guess a small negative I could add is how wonky the dodge mechanic is but it's not really mandatory in the game's standard difficulty.

The rest of the game however, was really good. Story is serviceable, gameplay is great and for me the biggest plus was being able to hang out with Jill again. You can get this game on the cheap often if you scour for Capcom deals and it's worth the playthrough if you're an RE fan!

The idea was in place for a really solid setting with a lot of exploration and route planning, but I never bothered learning the map layout because there will always be objective markers to where you need to go. As far as controls, it plays fine, I'm just used to playing the 2 and 3 remakes, so it felt a little off. The enemy designs were honestly really bad, and probably the worst in the whole series, almost all being lumpy white anthropomorphisms with sharp bloody teeth. At first they are horrifying and disgusting, creating genuine fear just by looking at them, but the effect wears off after an hour or two, and it just comes off as lazy. The other enemy I should spotlight are the hunters, which are sent in swarms and are relatively easy to take down with just a pistol, a far cry from their original presence as the most threatening enemy you could possibly come across that required your strongest weapons to kill. Overall, what I'm trying to say is that this game was advertised as "the great return to survival horror" for the Resident Evil franchise, but it really is just another Resident Evil 4. NOW, I cannot stress enough that IF YOU LIKE RE4 and the later games, THIS GAME IS REALLY FUN and I definitely recommend it, I just prefer the 0-3 style of Resident Evil so it doesn't really appeal to me as much.

Full review: 
When playing through the campaign I was sure I would give the game a positive review. 
It's quite classic RE gameplay with just a few things mixed up. The story is cheesy and not really good but is still entertaining just like every other RE game. The campaign consists of multiple episodes, each one ending on a cliffhanger. That way it keeps you interested. 

Probably the biggest feature this game added is scanning: you have a tool which you can use to scan your surroundings to find hidden ammo or other items or scan enemies to get a health item if you do that often enough. I mean at some point you get used to that, but it can also be annoying. Like at some point you pretty much have to scan your surroundings otherwise you will barely find any ammo. Pretty much the same thing with scanning enemies and getting health items.

Besides that there is not really any inventory management in the game: you can pretty much pick up every item you find, except the different ammo types and health items. For all these you have a max value you can carry which you can simply increase by finding bags for them. This is pretty much like in a lot of generic action games, but not like survival horror. And then you can only carry up to 3 weapons, which in my opinion just sucks. 
I think it would have been way better if the inventory system was like in RE4, so I could carry more weapons if I want (and if I have the space for it) and have to worry about other items too.

Besides that I dont have much more to say about the campaign, wait, maybe just a quick word: that you definitly see that this game is "just a hd version of a mobile game". It doesn't look that well, especially for a game from 2013. 
But that's not a big deal for me.
I know, I didn't sound that positive about it, but trust me, I still had my fun with it.
I played through the campaign three times (once normal, then another run for achievement clean-up and a third one for highest difficulty). This took me overall like 25 hours.


Now let's talk about the reason why I write a negative review for this game: raid mode.
This simply turns the survival horror like gameplay from the campaign into a loot shooter.
Now before proceeding I have to say I absolutly hate loot shooters. But besides that a loot shooter mode does not belong in a RE game imho. And this one is grindy af.

So basically raid mode consists of 3 tiers of stages, each tier having 20 stages plus one end game stage. But those 20 stages are the same one in every tier, only the enemy placements, the types of enemies and the levels of the enemies change. Everything in raid mode has a level: your character, enemies and weapons. Over every enemy you see his huge health bar. After every 1 or 2 stages the recommend level increases, same as the level of the enemies in that stage. The problem is you often have to grind, i.e. replay levels over and over to keep up with the level and to get better weapons. I mean it's mostly fine in the first two tiers. In those you will still succeed a stage if your level is like 1 or 2 below the recommended one (usually). But the third tier is just ridiculous.
If your level and the one of your weapons is not at least the recommend one you will die. And even if it's equal, those stages are way too hard. Which means you have to grind way more for those.
This raid mode was pretty much the reason I stopped gaming for a certain time, because this mode is so grindy, boring and even unfair at the later stages. Because of that I cheesed my way through it: I found a guy who carried me through raid mode, i.e. most stages in tier 3 and then farmed Ghost Ship with me (the late game level) for xp and weapons.
Even with that huge help (shout-out to Diamond Girls) I needed like 45 hours for raid mode. That's way too much for my taste. But without that help I would have needed so much more time.

Honestly raid mode would be way better just with the first tier. And I would even say the game would be better without raid mode.

I know it's maybe a bit unfair to rate this game negative just because of one mode while the campaign is not that bad, but because you will spend so much more time in raid mode than in the campaign it feels like raid mode is the main mode of the game. And that is something I can't approve.

As much as I love the Resident Evil series, I cannot recommend this game at all unless you’re suffering from insomnia and need your entertainment to act as sleep aids. 

The game already wasn’t winning favor with me by having one of the mainstays of the series (Jill Valentine) look and act like an utter bimbo for the first act of the game, appearing more as a pornstar than an experienced anti-terrorism specialist; spouting out trite and redundant dialogue that serves no purpose. Then when playing the chapter with Chris Redfield, it reinforced the fact that your companion in any chapter is just there for set dressing. They are literally useless in combat, and my most prominent example is that I decided not to shoot the most basic fish zombie in the game and let my partner kill it. As Jill, with an un-modded pistol, it would take less than a clip to take one down. My partner used five whole clips and the monster wasn’t bothered at all. 

Outside of that, the design overall is just a mashup of ideas that don’t live up to their potential. The large and intricate level design of the early games is here, but the environment is often mundane and linear. The Resident Evil 4 gameplay is present but the punch is missing as well as proper action move sets, with the camera often being too close and the dodge function being a poorly explained, frustratingly implemented mechanic. Backtracking is endemic but is done in the most blatantly padded manner. Example being that when I beat the first boss, I got the key that could open up an area that was closed off, so I moved all around the ship to get back to that point (which I already had to do to find the main path), only for the door to give me the Dark Souls treatment and say “Does not open from this side.” despite the fact I was on a side with a keyhole. Blatant padding or design oversight? Who knows!

Resident Evil is not just a horror action game or a puzzle driven exploration simulator, it’s all of that and more. So when bosses are nothing more than bullet sponges with two attacks and re-spawning lessers, it's a slog. When puzzles are nothing more than match the dots or another fetch quest for specific keys, it's a slog. 

Every RE game has its annoying quirks and bizarre design choices, but Revelations 1 is just the sum of conflicting ideas and acts as the Greatest Hits compilation of all the stupid and boring parts of the series.

I know my playtime is low, but if you can’t engage me by Chapter 5 on anything but waning morbid curiosity, I’m not forcing myself through the boring corridors, boring enemies and boring story. 

Can you tell I’m bored? Straight into the depths of bore.

Despite this particular port having some frustrating issues, I mostly enjoyed my time with the game. It’s at its best when bought on discount.
[h1] Overview [/h1]
This port and the game overall are a mixed bag. The most potent version is still the 3DS original which fully takes advantage of the exclusive handheld mechanics, while other ports of this game feel restrained by lacking at least more simple puzzles to make it retain the feel of the original RE trilogy. It really depends if you’ll care playing the game after completing the main story or not, and on your willingness to put up with major flaws plaguing PC and last-gen console ports. If completing both main Campaign and dumping some/lots of hours into Raid Mode alone and/or in coop sounds like your thing, it’s a solid game, even if you are just looking for another RE game starring your fav characters.

However, if you own PS4, Xbox One or Switch, I recommend skipping this port and getting the updated Unveiled Edition on one of these systems instead.

[h1] Story [/h1]
Story takes inspiration from the ambient original RE trilogy, overall pretty refreshing. Game setting circling around exploring a spacious, complex sections of a cruise ship and being on water are definite highlights of the game and a reason why you'll get it in the first place. Some simpler side-story sections were nice.
Events take place between RE4 and RE5. A year before Rev 1 story, there was a city on water – Terragrigia, where a T-Virus outbreak occurs. The game later reveals there was an outbreak on a ship, but you’ll soon discover there are more malicious plans for using the virus and more behind-the-scenes drama going on, mixed with personal business. That’s the base of the story. It’s pretty solid as the first “back to horror roots” game. Not the best, but done mostly well + great OST. Story here doesn't have much impact on the canon aside from sharing details of BSAA's early days.

Rejected early story concept was quite interesting and it's a shame this wasn't used and executed somehow differently in the final game: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Es0xReoS2nA

Also don’t expect a survival horror title, this game encourages plenty of action shooting sequences in Campaign. There's a new mechanic that slows down level progression by having you scan surroundings for more ammo, herbs, grenades and custom parts, so you are less likely to run out of ammo if you take time to scan bits of all locations.
[h1] Story / the bad [/h1]
My biggest issue with Campaign - story presentation and characters.
The game switches between character perspectives and time frames after first few chapters frequently ; unnecessary “Previously” summary clips are still present from the 3DS port. All of this makes piecing together the story rather difficult on 1st playthrough. You may want to check RE wikis or such if you are interested in fully understanding small details of the plot and questions the game may leave you with because of occasionally bad story presentation.

Most new characters are bland and forgettable. There’s no/barely any character development that’d make you attached or like them (Keith and Quint being the worst). They are around for one game so you won't see them in newer games at all. The game also suffers from RE5 appeal syndrome by having Jessica and Rachael dress revealingly, which takes all seriousness out of the game’s original “back to horror roots” plot feel. Here you'll once again get female characters having distinct curvy+revealing features and designs clearly highlighting them for the audience.
Series veterans (Chris, Jill) are sadly a weak part of the game as well, but can’t exactly fit “there” because of said vet status and these two just not having too much personality to being with, aside from set ones established in previous games.

[h1] Controls [/h1]
Both Mouse&Keyboard and Controller options work the same as in RE5, but you can finally move while aiming. I’d recommend M&K at least for Raid Mode, you’d need quick reaction times if you want to get all bonuses needed for 100%ing this mode, manual mouse turning for this is extremely responsive (don’t confuse with the existing in-game button for turning around).
The dodge mechanic isn’t well implemented and took a while to get used to. Please save yourself trouble : wait until you are about to get hit, then press Up and keep holding it for a second. With some practice, you’ll get timings for almost all enemies and dodge consistently (insta-kill bigger enemies are still hard to predict). You can also dodge by pressing Space, but it’s way too risky and unreliable.

[h1] Replay value, Raid Mode [/h1]
My first Campaign run lasted less than 10 hours, it sadly doesn’t hold much replay value, unless you wanna experience the story and nice environments again. But, Raid Mode does. This mode offers custom enemy placements for all 3 difficulties.
It becomes easier and fun with a coop partner, the community is active and very kind, so go ahead and have fun looting or planning out strategies for all Raid bonuses!
Costumes, reskins, various lighting mods/fixes from fans for the game are also quite nice to spice up the experience.
[h1] Raid Mode / the bad [/h1]
As you progress from Chasm/Easy to later Trench/Medium and Abyss/Hard stages, this is where bs enemy spawns come to ruin the fun. Even when I took the time to note most conditions (entering new area, or killing a particular enemy) for new enemy spawns, I still gave up and looked up vids for more strategic approaches to some Trench and most Abyss stages from other players. I simply had no idea how to deal with tons of enemies spawning in a restricted/open space where they can hit you from behind, or fast enemies in restricted space.
Game forces you to grind a lot for better weapons, weapon drops for much rarer, powerful weapons are dangerously low (unless you are lucky with rewards from RE net’s events). Please search for Better Weapon Drops mod on RE modding threads, this replaces bad drops with updated better ones from PS4/Xbox One/Switch ports.
A lot of good Raid-exclusive weapon parts require you to get all Raid bonuses (including No Hit bonus) in frustrating or very few ridiculously long stages. Thankfully strategic approaches to stages and having coop partners help out a lot after some trial and error.
Coop netcode here is a trainwreck. I've played with people from various regions, frequently had times when the game wouldn't load position or actions of partners correctly, not registering hits and kills, or heck, even SOFTLOCKED me once when trying to open a safe (which for some reason require instantly-responsive connection from both players at that exact moment). Me or my partners had very few extremely frustrating moments when the game lags after I aim the weapon and closes itself.
From lots of sessions, it seems connection to RE net causes these issues. When RE net is turned off, coop sessions tend to be more stable.

This game got updated for PS4, Xbox One and Switch. Reasons why you might wanna avoid the PC port and get Unveiled Edition: hints on loading screens actually having images of enemies (better introduction to enemies), better weapon drops (existing PC mod does help a lot, but the fact this PC port got abandoned right after release is still really bad), new+better weapon parts, higher quality of character models and environments. PC port lacks all of it, honestly could've used a next-gen upgrade like this too.

All in all, it's a filler game which for most people will get forgotten in their game library (either after Campaign, or after pouring lots of hours into Raid Mode) for the lack of impactful survival horror tension and better interactive puzzle elements, ending up being an awkward RE4+5 hybrid suffering from appeal syndrome, but a solid one if you are looking to discover another RE story chapter with a simple story, great atmosphere+OST and progressively greater struggles in Raid Mode.

This feels like the moment Capcom remembered what Resident Evil was supposed to be. It blends that classic slow-burn tension, limited resources, and claustrophobic level design with more modern controls, which makes it a surprisingly smooth experience even today.

The ship setting is easily the game’s standout element. The Queen Zenobia becomes a character by itself — dark corridors, locked rooms, eerie echoes, and that constant feeling that something is watching you. It captures the survival horror tone far better than a lot of the mainline releases from that era.

Story-wise, it’s a mix of serious bioterror mystery and over-the-top RE cheese — in the best possible way. The constant switches between locations and characters keep things interesting, although not every section is equally strong. Some of the action-focused segments feel slightly out of place compared to the tense exploration on the ship.

Combat is solid and enjoyable: enough ammo to defend yourself, but never enough to feel safe. The scanning mechanic for resources is a clever touch, encouraging careful exploration instead of rushing through rooms.

It’s not flawless — enemy variety could be better, and a few segments disrupt the pacing — but overall, this game delivers what many fans had been missing for years: true survival horror with just the right amount of modern gameplay polish.

If you're a Resident Evil fan, especially of the older style, Revelations is absolutely worth playing — and still holds up remarkably well.

[h1] Gameplay / Story [/h1]

The gameplay of Revelations is based on the survival horror-influenced earlier games in the series with recurring elements such as a limited supply of ammunition and a greater focus on discovery and solving puzzles. The in-game camera maintains a view over the character's shoulder. In contrast to previous Resident Evil games, the player can now move the figure while aiming with a weapon and has the option to switch between a third-person and a first-person perspective. A new game concept, the Genesis scanner, can be used throughout the course of the game to find hidden objects in the area.

Resident Evil Revelations is set in 2005, between Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5. It describes the events shortly after the establishment of the Bioterrorism Security Assessment Alliance (BSAA), a group to fight terrorism that was introduced in Resident Evil 5. The plot revolves around the co-founders of the BSAA, Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield, the protagonists from some parts of the series.

In 2005, the head of the BSAA, Clive R. O'Brian, sent Jill Valentine and their new partner Parker Luciani to look for Chris Redfield and his new partner Jessica Sherawat. During their mission to investigate the possible reappearance of Il Veltro, they lost contact with headquarters and disappeared. Jill and Parker are sent to their last known whereabouts, the cruise ship SS Queen Zenobia. Shortly after their arrival, they see a video message from a masked man who claims to be Il Veltro and threatens to take about a fifth of the world's oceans with the T-Abyss in retaliation for the FBC's involvement in the wiping out of the Veltro members in Terragrigia Virus, a marine virus derived from the deadly T-virus. During their search for Chris and Jessica, they encounter numerous bio-organic weapons in the ship that are infected with the T-Abyss virus. So the events take their course ...

Das Spielprinzip von Revelations orientiert sich an den durch Survival Horror geprägten früheren Spielen der Reihe mit wiederkehrenden Elementen wie begrenzter Versorgung mit Munition und einem größeren Schwerpunkt auf Entdeckungen und dem Lösen von Rätseln Die Kamera im Spiel behält eine Ansicht über die Schulter der Spielfigur bei. Der Spieler kann die Figur im Gegensatz zu früheren Resident-Evil-Spielen nun auch bewegen, während er mit einer Waffe zielt und hat die Möglichkeit zwischen einer Dritt-Personen- und einer Egoperspektive zu wechseln. Ein neues Spielkonzept, der Genesis-Scanner, kann während des gesamten Spielverlaufs zum Auffinden versteckter Gegenstände in der Umgebung verwendet werden. 

Resident Evil Revelations spielt im Jahr 2005, zwischen Resident Evil 4 und Resident Evil 5. Es beschreibt die Ereignisse kurz nach der Gründung der Bioterrorism Security Assessment Alliance (BSAA), einer Gruppe zur Terrorismusbekämpfung, die in Resident Evil 5 eingeführt wurde. Die Handlung dreht sich um die Mitgründer der BSAA, Jill Valentine und Chris Redfield, den Protagonisten aus einigen Teilen der Serie. 

2005 sendet der Chef der BSAA, Clive R. O'Brian, Jill Valentine und ihren neuen Partner Parker Luciani aus, um nach Chris Redfield und dessen neuer Partnerin Jessica Sherawat zu suchen. Diese verloren während ihrer Mission, ein mögliches Wiederauftauchen von Il Veltro zu untersuchen, den Kontakt zum Hauptquartier und verschwanden. Jill und Parker werden zu ihrem letzten bekannten Aufenthaltsort, dem Kreuzfahrtschiff SS Queen Zenobia geschickt. Kurz nach ihrer Ankunft sehen sie eine Videobotschaft eines maskierten Mannes, der behauptet, Il Veltro zu sein und damit droht, als Vergeltung für die Beteiligung der FBC an der Auslöschung der Veltro-Mitglieder in Terragrigia etwa ein Fünftel der Weltmeere mit dem T-Abyss-Virus, einem maritimen Virus, das aus dem tödlichen T-Virus gewonnen wurde, zu infizieren. Während ihrer Suche nach Chris und Jessica treffen sie im Schiff auf zahlreiche bioorganische Waffen, die mit dem T-Abyss-Virus infiziert sind. So mit nehmen die Geschehnisse ihren lauf...

[h1] Atmosphäre [/h1]

Permanent hat man dieses gewisse unwohle Gefühl wenn man sich umdrehen muss. Andauernd hat man das große Bedürfnis die Tür hinter sich zu schliesen. Ich bin ein großer Horrorfan von allen möglichen Arten des Horrors, aber selten hat ein Spiel es geschafft mich in innerhalb von 45 Minuten komplett in den Bann zu ziehen.

[h1] Grafik/Sound [/h1]

Man merkt der Grafik an, dass diese portiert wurde. Bei der sehr düsteren Soundkulisse fühlt man sich wie im Geschehen. Alles ist einfach stimmig aufeinander angepasst.

[h1] Kampfsystem [/h1]

Es gibt verschiedene Waffenarten wie z.B. Messer,  Pistolen, Gewehre, Flinten, Granatwerfer und Flammenwerfer. Manche findet man so im Spielverlauf und für andere benötigt man Schlüssel oder muss Rätsel lösen. Es gibt für jeden Gegnertyp die richtige Waffe. Munition ist eher Mangelware, allerdings kommt es ganz auf den Schwierigkeitsgrad an, da dies variiert. Man wird später über jeden zur Verfügung stehenden Schuss in der Tasche froh sein.

This is one of my least and most favorite games, but is still totally worth playing!

To start with the good, the game feels fantastic to play! The gunplay is strong, feels like RE4 but with movement while aiming, and weapons feel great to use. You can find custom gun parts to modify weapons and there's a ton of them to collect so your weapons always feels personalized specifically for you. The enemies are really weird in a great way! I love the nautical theme and the ooze (or infected) are horrifying and fit really well with the setting. Revelations finds the perfect balance of action, horror, and just enough corniness to be a true Resident Evil game. There were many times where I was fighting for my life as enemies continuously spawn while trying to kill a boss, genuinely on the edge of my seat. While other times I was blowing through the game with a modded shotgun, feeling like a king, until you turn a corner too fast and an ooze moans at you and tackles you as the door behind you slams. Scared the **** out of me and turned the whole vibe around within a matter of seconds, and it works wonders!

Now for the negatives... The story is borderline useless and has no bearing on the main plot of the series and has very little connections whatsoever other than having a reference or two. Jill sounds and acts nothing like herself and Chris is even more boring than usual. Some of the few interesting characters such as Parker and Raymond are great but some of the decisions they make in cutscenes are just outright dumb. Without spoiling anything, a major enemy reaches for a gun on the table in front of them, and you and your special agent partner with decades of experience have handguns pointed at the enemy who is an active threat for over a minuet now and don't fire (even though it is obvious that your enemy is going to go for the gun to attempt to kill you). This is ridiculous and I understand that Resident Evil games are not meant to be taken entirely seriously. They are deliberately corny and it gives them a lot of charm, but it gets to a point where you're borderline yelling at your screen because the characters can be so brain dead half of the time.

Another thing, this IS a mobile game. It has lower quality graphics and was generally made for the 3DS. It does not look amazing, and the map and menu looks like it was made in 2003. So don't go into this game looking for gorgeous looks, as it looks slightly better than the RE4 remaster. The good thing about this is that you can run it on a potato, though. And it doesn't necessarily look bad, but not gorgeous by any means.



Overall, Revelations is a great Resident Evil game, even though it has some major drawbacks. Wait for the next sale and absolutely pick it up!

(I actually closed this window while I was writing a long-winded review so I gotta do it again).

So... I know my current timer says I played this game 21 hours, but that doesn't reflect the amount of time or how many times I actually bought this game. In 4 different platforms and 5 times total.

I played the original 3DS release and even played Raid mode up until level 50 with randoms during that time (when it was my only 3DS game while I waited for MH3U to release). Then PS3 (gifted it to a friend later), PS4 digital (played up to level 20 in Raid with another friend) and now I bought it on PC for me and a friend too.

I will now proceed to comment about what I like and dislike in detail about the campaign (i have not dipped my toes too much back into Raid mode so I won't talk about it too much.). I'll try to keep it as spoiler-free as possible, but read it at your own discretion.

Like:
-The setting: I really enjoy the idea of exploring a ghost ship infested with "zombies". This game is not a straight-line stage, but rather incites exploration in between the different sections of the Zenobia, as you slowly unravel the secrets and story around the Terrorist organization Veltro, the Terragrigia Panic and the ghost vessel known as the Queen Zenobia, set adrift on the Mediterranean sea.
-The weapon modding system: Unlike the simple yet effective "upgrade weapon" from other games, the weapon system this game offers allows for a somewhat deep level of customization. Do you want a charged-shot OHK M40A1? you can do that. Do you want a P90 that spews bullets faster than Eminem spits rhymes? Granted. Do you want a burst fire M3 shotgun? Just add the burst mode to it. However... There is an underlying problem with this, and it is some weapon balancing. I will cover this on the dislikes section and I'll go into detail about it too down below.
-Gun Variety: Again, it is nice to have so many guns at your disposal, but this also has the underside about balance I mentioned prior.
-Jill's butt: Self-explanatory, and you'll be seeing it a lot due to the camera angle. Jill is still best RE girl and has not made an appearance since 5 story-wise. Thanks, Crapcom (also ♥♥♥♥ you for changing her looks on RE3R, she looked beautiful here and you had to go and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mess with it. Now you make Chris a baddie in RE8? Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ you if you don't come up with a very good explanation for that AND we get to save him).

Dislikes:
-Campaign length: At my current 21 hours on PC I played normal first (seeing all cutscenes), Infernal mode, some stages on Raid mode and started Casual mode (no-healing challenge, currently on chapter 3). As you may guess, the length is rather... short. The story feels slightly rushed IMO.
-No co-op option on Campaign: This would have made some of the story stages way more bearable. I know some characters are doing "certain actions" and that going in with someone kills the "horror factor" from a jumpscare, but it also takes out some replayability it could possibly have.
-All stages you don't play as Jill (Terragrigia/Valkoinen Mökki): This has to do in part with the fact that you CANNOT customize/change your weapons as anyone else but Jill (and your ammo reserves are fixed in those stages too). I understand why, but I swear to whatever is up there, I DREAD playing ANY Terragrigia stage. I hated them in every single iteration and I still do.
-Weapon Balancing (slots): So, this is one of the things that have annoyed me recently the most, so sit tight, because this is going to be a long one. Some weapons are clearly vastly inferior compared to their counterparts, and this is painfully obvious to me when I look at 2 weapon classes specifically: The Magnums and the Rifles (shotguns and handguns are more or less balanced off, and "Machine Guns" have some outliers like the G36, but yeah, it is not as bad as with those 2). I will continue the rant down below.

Rifles: M40A1 and PSG-1:
The M40A1 is the first rifle you find (if you search well enough), and has both higher damage, 1 extra slot AND bigger capacity than the PSG-1, which you unlock by finding 15 handprints by scanning around. The only real advantage the PSG-1 has is the ability to fire semi-automatically, which, taking into account how powerful you can make the M40A1 it is not even fair. For this, what I would do is either double mag capacity for the PSG-1 or add 1 (or 2 better) extra slots.

Magnums: The (Colt) Python and L. Hawk (Desert Eagle):
This one is even worse, and it is due to the weapon class they belong to. The Python should be (technically) the first of the 2 you find, having a somewhat bad RoF, 6 in the chamber and the slowest reload, but has very high damage (1500 base) and 3 slots for mods. It is a very powerful weapon, but you need to use it sparingly due to how scarce Magnum ammunition is. 
Then comes the L. Hawk: 1200 base damage, faster RoF (but still has brutal recoil), faster reload speed (magazine vs drum) and capacity (8 vs 6), but only 2 slots. You see the problem, right? Right out the gate, you have LESS damage and LESS slots to compensate that. Despite having 3 advantatges over the Python, the only reason you could use it over the Python is for *damage burst* a boss since Magnum ammo is EXTREMELY scarce, and a well-modded Python would dust the L.. Hawk any day (Damage + Charge shot + Burst and you're set for ridiculous burst damage, or reload speed + damage + ammo capacity/RoF if you wanna overshadow the L.Hawk in almost everything), when the Hawk could only equip 2 of those. This shows the integral unbalance of these  weapons, and how an "upgrade system" could have helped mend it (as in, i.e. when you upgrade it you gain more damage and an extra slot, two in some cases like, say, the L. Hawk or the PSG-1 to have an actual fighting chance against their counterparts).

With that said, I still overall enjoy this game and I recommend it. You'd probably guess going by how many times I bought it.

Edit: Forgot to give it a score. Despite the problems I have stated, I still thoroughly enjoy exploring the halls and rooms of the Queen Zenobia. I give it an 8.6/10.

Resident Evil Revelations
════════════════════════════════════════════
This game consists of a story mode (Solo) and a raid mode (Solo/Coop).
In short this game is like half of a good meal imo. It's a good experience. However it feels like it could or should have had more content.
Spoiler Warning! (Scroll down for the TL;DR version)

[b]The Story[/b]
The story of the game is divided in 12 episodes with different settings where you follow up to 3 different character duos with a review after each episode. The reason behind this is probably to make it easier for the players to follow each storyline. However this feature feels quite unnecessary as the campaign isn't that long. It shouldn't take longer than 7-10 hours, depending on your speed, the difficulty and if you go for achievements.
In general the story of the game isn't that impressive.This is probably due to the game's rushed production, since the developers originally intended a different story. The outcome is a story with a very good setting in terms of horror (At least the ghost ship, the other settings and storylines aren't really necessary and should have been maybe an unlockable bonus campaign), but with a story telling that lacks behind that setting. Fortunately the soundtrack, the action and the occasional jumpscare lift this story up; so depending on your expectations you can have a very enjoyable experience.

Another thing worth mentioning would be that this game features a lot of characters. Through the campaign you follow 3 characters and their partners: Jill(and Parker), Chris(and Jessica) and Keith(and Quint)
Besides these there are a bunch of characters which also play a role in the game like Morgan Landsdale or Raymond and his partner Rachael.
As expected due to the duration of the campaign this leads to a lot of characters being not much developed throughout the game. Even the main characters can seem dull because of this.

When Capcom reworks this game as well at some point in the future, hopefully they redesign the layout of the ship and rewrite and expand some story parts to fix some plotholes f.e. since Raymond is the mole in the FBC, why is he sending Jill and Parker on a dangerous scavenger hunt instead of helping them directly or indirectly to find out what's going on onboard the Queen Zenobia, which he btw. later does which makes his actions in the beginning more than pointless. He also infects a bunch of researchers of the ship and is probably responsible for the death of his partner Rachael, since he left her in the dark and alone. All of this makes him a pretty weird character. He wants to be a good guy, but he does so many questionable things, which is just confusing.
Most of the character in this game have these sort of problems. Why did they end up here, what is there motivation, why are they doing this or in Rachael's case who is she exactly? Capcom bothered enough to make them to characters but they couldn't be bothered to really develop them. Which is a shame and probably the biggest weakness of the campaign.
They should also allow to play the campaign with a friend since you always have a partner in the campaign, however this partner is always controlled by an AI that is close to useless.

[b]The Raid Mode[/b]
The biggest selling point of this game is definetely the raid mode. It offers quite the action and has enough levels to keep you entertained for a lot of hours. It has 3 difficulties, a lot of stages and a ton of weapons and customization gears. You can also unlock and play every character of the campaign with each of them having their own specializations. Additionally some paid DLC's have bonus characters. All in all the Raid Mode is extremely good, especially with a friend. The only drawbacks I see to this are the fact that have to play the campaign first before you get access to the raide mode and that the raid mode can be asynchronous in Duos. The latter one being not that bad since this mostly affects the enemies position and how they are displayed on each screen, but it doesn't affect that they still receive the damage as usual even when your partner shoots in a completely different direction.

My hope here would be that a future iteration of this game has even more variety considering the amount of levels, weapons, customization, type of enemies and their boss versions as well as the character being even more specialized to raise the skill ceiling and replayability.

[u][b]TL;DR:[/b][/u] This game offers a lot (especially the Raid Mode) and the only downside is that it doesn't offer more content which it could have if the developers invested more time. This game is also at least 50% off in sales so waiting for a cheaper price will also save you a good amount of theyour money if you're willing to wait. 
A new version should also add more content and expand the story.
Also please give us the option to save Rachael in the story, when we're fast enough. It's sad that this character is simply thrown away even though the design team liked her so much that they made her into a character to begin with instead of just a anonymous dead body with a key.

Resident Evil Revelations is a game that tries to blend the classic survival horror of the franchise with more modern, action-oriented gameplay, but it doesn’t fully succeed in either area. While it has its moments, the overall experience feels inconsistent and underwhelming.

The story is serviceable but forgettable, with convoluted twists and cheesy dialogue that don’t do much to keep you invested. The episodic format feels disjointed, breaking the pacing and making it hard to stay engaged with the characters or plot. The attempt to weave together multiple storylines is ambitious but ends up feeling more confusing than compelling.

The gameplay is where the game struggles the most. While it does attempt to bring back elements of classic survival horror, such as limited ammo and creepy atmospheres, it’s undercut by repetitive combat and uninspired enemy design. The "Ooze" enemies lack variety and personality, making encounters feel tedious rather than tense. The environments, though occasionally atmospheric, are often bland and recycled, especially on the ship where much of the game takes place.

Combat mechanics are functional but clunky, with stiff movement and awkward aiming that make it hard to feel fully in control. The game introduces a scanning mechanic to find items and secrets, but it feels more like a gimmick than an engaging feature, adding unnecessary downtime to the flow of the game.

The Raid Mode is a highlight, offering a fun and replayable side experience that focuses on action and co-op. However, it’s not enough to save the main game from its shortcomings.

Resident Evil Revelations isn’t a terrible game, but it’s far from the series’ best. It feels like a missed opportunity that doesn’t live up to its potential. If you’re a die-hard Resident Evil fan, it might be worth a playthrough, but for most, it’s skippable.

[h1] “He’s turning [i]GUPPIES[/i] into [b][i]JAWS![/i][/b] Shhhh, quiet!” [/h1]

This is a bizarre ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. This [i]IS NOT[/i] a normal Resident Evil game. This is a 3DS Resident Evil game. Yes, 3DS, the handheld Nintendo System. This game originally launched in 2012 for a handheld console. This steam version is an HD upgrade of that game released a year after It’s original [i]HANDHELD[/i] launch. Other reviews I have read talk about the weird controls. Yeah, that’s because you originally had to use touch inputs, dual screens, a D-pad and a stylus to control this game. I understand I seem to be emphasizing the fact that this was a handheld game, but it’s for good reason. This is a seriously lower budget game than [i]Most[/i] other Resident Evil games because of that one simple fact. The game was presented in an episodic format, like a television series or the Telltale games, because they thought “short chapters made it more suitable for playing on a portable console”. I mean, the game originally launched with a spelling error on the damn box for 3ds. Not even kidding. 90,000 copies of this game were sold as Resident Evil: Revelaitons. 

Now, with that said. That doesn’t mean this is a bad game. Like I started saying…

[b] This is a [i]Bizarre[/i] ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game... [/b]

[h1] Story/Characters [/h1]

I remember reading about this game briefly when it launched and at the time didn’t realize this was considered canon in the series, and I skipped it. I didn’t play this game until 2021 and am just now understanding how truly [i]WEIRD[/i] some of these “Side Stories” in the RE universe can really get.

RE:R takes place between the events of Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5. This is right after the formation of the BSAA, the group Chris Redfield runs within RE5. This game's main characters are absolutely long-time franchise staples Chris Redfield and Jill Valentine. However we meet so many new characters it’s absolutely insane… and every single one of them are out of this universe [i]quirky[/i]. Like, this is Deadly Premonition: Resident Evil edition. In fact, this entire game is like a B-movie, cast and all. Like these people are straight out of Twin Peaks or something. You’ve got Jackass, super computer nerd, Jessica, who tries to be overly sexy by pretending to be stupid and wearing a wetsuit with only ONE pant leg. I mean this is a cast that even Suda 51 would be proud of.

So in RE:R a terrorist organization known as Veltro has attacked the, [i](now hear me out)[/i] Floating city of Terragrigia. Yes, that’s a thing that happened in this universe filled with monsters and zombies. There was a floating city built in the Mediterranean Sea completely powered by solar energy provided by a laser/satellite orbiting the planet. This terrorist group released a bunch of B.O.W’s onto the Aquapolis and the city was destroyed by turning it to ash and sinking it with the space laser. Yep. So, now, one year later some ♥♥♥♥ is going down. Weird slug creatures are washing up on “The shore of the Mediterranean” as if that’s just, ya know, a spot that exists. “The shore”. The Terrorists seem to be back in action with a new virus called the “T-Abyss” virus. So Jill and her new BSAA partner Parker head off to a cruise ship that is basically a super fancy and absolutely massive floating Spencer Mansion and laboratory disguised as a ship. Because of course. And this is where the majority of the game takes place. Contact is lost with them and Chris and his new partner, the worst character ever created and absolutely completely terrible [b]Jessica[/b], head off to find Jill. They fly to the Mediterranean Sea and begin searching. Yes, they don’t have coordinates or anything, they literally just take a Helicopter and try to find them in the 945,000 square mile Mediterranean. Jessica even has a line where she says something like “This is like an ocean, I thought it was supposed to just be a big lake”.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

This is where the game differs from the standard Resident Evil formula. This game is a third person shooter with light horror elements. Told as episodes and chapters, it is split up into about 15 minute sections. You won’t find [i]many[/i] creepy dark rooms or standard RE environs here. Remember, this was a 3ds game, so expect long metal hallways and generic rooms. That doesn’t mean there aren’t some gorgeous set pieces and well crafted sections, but they are the exception in this title, rather than the norm. 

The weapon and item system in this game is completely different than any other RE game. You can find weapons lying around of which you can carry 3 with you at a time. Ammo is found via a scanner device called the “Genesis”. This is also how you find health items. By defeating enemies and scanning them you get experience, that when it reaches 100%, you get a health item. You can also find them lying around the area but you’ll get most of your healing by scanning enemies. It’s weird… This entire game is weird.

The enemies are all Lovecraftian monsters in this game with the exception of the good ol’ Hunters who:
[h1] DO SICK ASS BACKFLIIIIIPSSSS [/h1]
[i] AIR HORN BLOWS [/i]

Seeing as this is a new T-virus strain known as “Abyss”. You fight a lot of barnacles and weird cthulhu type creatures throughout. Seeing as it takes place on a boat, the entire theme is completely nautical, of course.

[h1] Performance [/h1]

Game ran fine on 1440p for me. I had some issues getting the game to register mouse input on the menus both in game and out, but was able to get used to where to click to get it to work. It was a slight annoyance. I had no bugs other than the dumb-as-barnacles enemy AI that would constantly get stuck on walls etc… The game has very little in the way of video/graphics options, and even at max it looks like an uprezzed handheld game. If graphics are your thing, or you’re coming from RE2 or RE3 remake, then man this game is going to hurt your eyes…

[h1] Summary [/h1]

With all that said, I actually quite enjoyed this game. This game made me laugh many, [i]many[/i] times and I was quite entertained throughout. “But isn’t this supposed to be a horror game, Yorith?” You bet your ass it is… but so is Army of Darkness.

[b] Overall Score: 6/10 [/b]
[b] Why not just skip it? [/b]: RE:R is canon and will put a smile on your face if you like things a little… abstract.
[b] But… [/b] This is not your normal RE game. If you take video games seriously or if quirky and silly characters blasting Lovecraft monsters doesn’t quite perk your interest, then go ahead and skip it. You aren’t missing much more than a good time here.
 
Thanks for reading [i](if you did)[/i] and please let me know if you found this review helpful!
Cheers!

This is purely a review of the campaign, I'm a series vet and I've only played and beat this game once, having picked the highest(Infernal) difficulty.

Starting with the bad.


   The beginning of the game had the least thought put into it, it's really unfun to play, tedious and unbalanced. The early chapter gunplay is dreadful since your guns can't be upgraded yet. The early enemies are bulletsponges, they don't respond to hits and their design is just a dull gray goop-man. Furthermore, early on you're forced to use a dodge system that's broken and unintuitive, pulling off 10 sequential parries in Dark Souls or 10 dodges in RE3 is easier that pulling off a single dodge here.

   More over the game overall suffers from very poor communication, a lot of information simply isn't given to the player resulting in trial and error as well as frustration and backtracking.

   Another thing is the dreadful voice acting, Jill, Chris, the main antagonist, and a few other characters all have the personality of a piece of cardboard, the voice actors were given no direction resulting in awful performances. Even when characters are about to die they're as stiff as a stone. Not to mention the boring and unengaging dialogue writen for said characters.

   Lastly the game has one of the worst mechanics ever seen in Resident Evil history. 90% of items such as bullets and upgrades are invisible and can only be seen after being revealed by a tool called the "Genesis". Using it is mandatory, else you're gonna miss out on almost all the ammo and vital upgrades for your weapons. It all comes crashing down when you realize such a mechanic is pointless, the game wouldn't change at all if the items were visible from the start. And since the Genesis majorly slows you down you end up exploring each area once, and then again at snail's pace looking for items you "missed". I am not lying when I say my 14,5 hour playthrough could have easily been an 6-8 hour one if not for this stupid mechanic.



As for the good, while this one will be shorter, that doesn't mean the game lacks it.


   From chapter 3 on wards, the game becomes really, really good and hell of a lot more fun. The game really starts to shine when it deviates from including fan service and starts immersing you in it's original content. The setting of the game(ship), the new characters, custom weapon parts mechanic, all original and full of personality. It's a shame the new cast gets benched so often so the series veteran characters can be put in the spotlight.

   The game's gameplay loop also becomes more engaging when the game finally gives you some options. With the weapon upgrade system and the limited resources you have on your hand it's great fun strategizing and overcoming gravely difficult scenarios. Who would have thought giving players freedom of choice in how they want to survive would be fun?
 

While the early chapters made me want to quit and never touch the game again, I'm glad I forced myself to play through this game to find a shining gem that's crusted in rubbish.
It's not the best, but after working through it's kinks I had great fun with the game.

Right off the bat I have to say that controls in this game are overall dreadful. It's not an issue characteristic to either k&m / gamepad control scheme, but rather to the sheer sluggishness of characters' movement. It's really hard to dodge or strafe out of harm's way (as a matter of fact, I do not like how tough dodging is, for me it worked only by accident). Dodging is pretty much a QTE sans the button indicators, and strafing is so slow that it is almost useless. That said, I can understand that above issues probably stem from the game's origins as a handheld product, and I still appreciate that it was converted for PC and I had the pleasure to play it, for the reasons which I will be stating further on. It's a Resident Evil game, cheesy, fun action-horror - which is enough for it to be worthwhile. Seeing the setting of the game, and the not-so-intuitive map, I was a bit afraid of tedious backtracking, but it never was excessive or confusing. Capcom certainly know how to design fluid (no pun intended) levels, packed with action and some nice set-pieces. If a game is fun to play, it is easy to look past its sluggish controls and dated graphics. RE:R has fun inventory management system with numerous upgrades, and an ok variety in weapons. I also liked the character dynamics, this is one of very few games where I actually preferred to have a partner present because they require no protection from the player and are quite likable. Speaking of level design, it was mostly fine, but I did not like the 'swimming' levels (ever since Super Mario, I do not enjoy water levels). Another thing worth mentioning, which is always Resident Evil's forte, are the boss fights. There is something about how Capcom designs bosses, that makes every encounter unique and exciting. All in all, even if it is one of the worst Resident Evil games, it is still a good game in its own right.

I am fairly new to the Resident Evil series. I remember playing the RE3: Nemesis demo front to back when Dino Crisis was released, and then playing only a little bit of Code Veronica X on the PS2. But it wasn't until this year that I finally sat down and started to make my way through the series.

I had already made my way through several of the best RE games. The graphics, though dated, still held up really well and did not look clunky. The cinematics were top notch and intense. There were several moments my jaw was to the floor. 

It has been years, and I mean years since I played a video game that made me care about every character in the game. Where I felt angry and sad because of moments in the games story. And where I actually felt as though I truly saved the world after going through hell and back. And it was the first time in a decade when I played a game from start to finish in one sitting. I could not put the controller down because this game was that good.

The games story is obviously like any other RE game. A virus infects the world blah blah blah. But the way it was executed in Revelations was beyond impressive. It felt fresh and it felt new. The pacing of the game was really good. And I appreciated the recaps between the games episodes.

To sum it all up. Resident Evil: Revelations in my opinion is the best Resident Evil game I have played thus far. Will my opinion change as I finish the rest of the games? Most likely. But will I forget about how incredible this experience was playing this game? Absolutely not! This is the best game to get someone into the Resident Evil franchise.

[h1]B Movie[/h1]
Resident Evil: Revelations is like a “B Movie” Resident Evil game. The dialogue is comically poor at times, with hit lines, such as “Me and my sweet ass are on the way!” That said, Revelations really grew on me throughout my playthrough. I honestly wasn’t enjoying it all that much in my first few hours, but as the story fleshed out, and I grew more comfortable with the combat, I honestly enjoyed my time with it quite a bit.

[h1]3DS Relics[/h1]
Resident Evil: Revelations was originally a 3DS game. While it’s been ported to PC and modern consoles, there’s a lot of design decisions that make it obvious this game was originally designed for a portable console with severe hardware limitations. 

Doors. Doors everywhere. I can only presume that the levels in this game were designed with the 3DS’s limited memory budget in mind. Each area of the game is divided up by an exorbitant number of small rooms and hallways. If the sheer number of doors doesn’t bother you, then then the doors slamming in your face certainly will. 

There’s a significant amount of backtracking in this game, which is exacerbated by the number of small, cordoned off hallways, which oftentimes feels like a maze. So, it’s fairly common to walk through a door, only to quickly realize it’s the wrong direction, turn around, and be unable to leave until the door has completed its closing animation. You’ll have to wait, click the door again, wait for the opening animation to complete, and only then can you exit. This is comically bad when the story is telling you to hurry to an objective and your partner walks through a door in front of you...and then [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3B4YHJ3V6hk]♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ closes the door on your face[/url]. This also happens underwater. It’s hilarious for all the wrong reasons. 

[h1]Gameplay and Sound[/h1]
During the first few hours, combat was honestly not very satisfying at all. Enemies felt too spongy, and there’s not a satisfying gooey explosion sound when enemies die, like in Resident Evil 4, 5, and 6. The gun sounds are also pretty weak and low quality. The guns just lack any bass or “oomph.” They sound very toy-like and are just unsatisfying to use. Good sound design can often hinge on subtle effects, and this game is just missing that. 

However, I really grew to enjoy the game’s gun upgrade system, which really improved my experience with the combat over time. Guns are upgraded by finding Weapon Parts throughout the levels. The Weapon Parts offer upgrades like, 30% damage increase, %20 capacity, 10% fire rate, etc. The Weapon Parts can be swapped in and out of weapons at will, which gave some thought to which weapons to give each upgrade. After installing a few upgrades in my weapons, enemies felt significantly less spongy, and I started to actually enjoy the combat. 

An addition to the game that’s pretty central to gameplay is the Genesis, which is this Batman Detective Mode™ gun that you use to scan enemies and your surroundings. Apparently, some ammo is so microscopic that it can’t be seen until the world’s greatest detective™ reveals it. I honestly wasn’t a huge fan of this addition. 

Another change that Revelations makes that I’m not extremely fond of is the health system. In lieu of a health bar, the screen becomes increasingly bloodied and the colors fade to gray. Green Herbs will now always put you at 100% health. However, the game limits you to holding 5 Green Herbs at a time. That’s a fair trade-off, I suppose, but in my opinion, it’s an overall inferior system compared to previous RE games.

[h1]Visuals and Ultrawide[/h1]
“Pretty” is not a word I’d use to describe this game. The textures and 3D models in this game can be very poor at times. For example, [url=https://i.imgur.com/sBystiO.jpg]take a look at this vending machine[/url] that pops up in the first half hour of the game. 

The game has a strange green hue to it that I wasn’t very fond of. So, I opted to use a ReShade preset for my playthrough. The [url=https://sfx.thelazy.net/games/preset/9806/]one I picked[/url] had a bit too much bloom for my liking, but it was an overall improvement, in my opinion. Here’s a [url=https://i.imgur.com/2O8PSc0.png]before and after comparison[/url].

As an ultrawide user, I was disappointed to learn that this game does not support 3440x1440. There are community fixes for 2560x1080, but even the [url=https://www.wsgf.org/dr/resident-evil-revelations/en]WSGF page for this game notes that attempts to use 1440p ultrawide will result in a crash[/url].

Aside from just my personal preference for ultrawide resolutions, one of my primary complaints with Resident Evil games is the overly narrow FOV. I was able to use Flawless Widescreen to adjust the FOV with Resident Evil 4, but for this game, I had to live with Jill taking up 30% of the screen, which is unfortunate.


[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Resident Evil: Revelations isn’t a numbered Resident Evil game for a reason. It’s a side story that doesn’t really have any lasting impact on the overarching franchise narrative. The dialogue can be pretty poor at times, but the story, while tropey, gets fairly interesting. The gameplay is fun, but poor sound and level design results in unsatisfying gameplay.

Resident Evil Revelations (ReR) is an action focused Resident Evil game. Yes, I think it is still considered a Resident Evil game, just that it has a lot more stuff going on. There are still some genuinely scary moments here and there, and the concept is faithful to its roots - the usual ridiculous puzzles and architecture, finding key items at very odd places (hell there is a [spoiler]stupid screwdriver taped beneath a toilet seat cover[/spoiler] like what?), and very very unfair enemies - all present like its predecessors. I'm not a die-hard RE fan so I'm not gonna say things like this is not a true RE game or whatnot. I think fair is fair and this game is a pretty solid horror action game. Still, I consider myself an RE fan and I think this game is a little too easy. Not that the enemies are easy to kill (I only cleared easy and normal modes so far), but there isn't much thinking to do because the game progression is quite linear. The general play area is smaller in comparison and there is very little backtracking required to complete the main campaign. The game pretty much tells you exactly where to go at every turn and your map pin-points your destination. Your only real difficulty perhaps is ammo rationing (at least in the first half of your first playthrough) and beating some truly annoying boss fights. But let's talk about what I absolutely hate about this game shall we?

1) Strafe movements - I'm glad that this game has strafe movements (something which RE2 Remake did not implement well enough imo), but the character moves TOO DAMN SLOW while strafing. It really makes no sense. The characters are trained soldiers and they should be able to side step faster than this LOL. Especially when there is one particular type of enemy who will aim and shoot some sort of projectile at you, you gotta aim fast and fire to stagger/kill it or you will get hurt. The thing is, the projectile moves in a straight path and side stepping would actually be a solution, but the character strafes so damn slowly you gotta stop aiming (if you're not fast enough) and run away to dodge it. Also, strafe movement is a basic tactical movement when turning corners and the slow speed is just uncalled for. 

2) Too many characters - In this game, you not only play as Jill and Chris, but you also play as many other side characters which honestly I did not care for one bit. And since their stories are part of the main campaign, you do have to play through them in order to complete the story. This then becomes a chore because these gameplays do not affect the actual main event that you're here to play, but just fillers for more action shootouts. I wish this game had an episode selection function so that I can choose what I want to play and what I don't want to lol. 

3) Walking-through-the-door animation - This game was released in 2012, so I have no idea why going through doors require some sort of mandatory animation especially when its purpose is not to load maps like classic RE1. Is simply going through doors too advanced for 2012? This I'm not sure, but if it's not then I cannot understand why it is as such. This is a stupid move because you cannot open a door and look into a room before entering - the moment you press the key to open a door, you automatically walk through it via an animation. The game knows this, and there is one room where an enemy is placed to get you before you can react after the walking-through-the-door animation is complete. This is just pure nonsense. RE is not exactly known for very fair enemies, but this one takes the cake. The worst thing that can happen to a game is when you have to take a mandatory health plunge and you have no control over it. Also, when you have a partner and he is ahead of you...when he goes through a door and you're not fast enough to "open" the door at around the same time, you gotta wait for it to close before you can open it LOL. I am glad that RE7 and RE2 Remake is not like this, so kudos to Capcom!

4) Lasers - I'm not gonna go into too much detail here to prevent spoilers, but if you've played this game before you'll know what I'm talking about. It is the most ridiculous thing ever. There is literally no solution to this other than to get hurt and then succeed through trial and error. I believe that while a game can go all out to be challenging, it should always be fun for the player. I cannot imagine anyone spending money to play a game for any purpose other than to have fun (unless you have some specific reason to do so...my sympathies). This crap is not fun at all; it is just pure annoying and a hassle to go through. 

5) Unfair enemies - I know I kinda mentioned this earlier, but it deserves a spot on its own. I am generally quite okay with the type of enemies here. Not the best, but not the worst. HOWEVER, there is a particular segment in this game where the clock is ticking very fast, and one particular enemy can kinda move faster than you. If it grabs you, you gotta shake it off. The issue here is, a few of them might gather around you and grab you RIGHT AFTER you shake one off. There is no cooldown time where the enemy cannot touch you after getting caught by one; it can literally grab you right after one lets go. This does not make sense at all, because in this scenario you may not die by the enemies, but you die anyway because you have run out of time. Plain ridiculous. 

In summary, ReR is a solid game in its own right. It is a considerably chill RE game with its own unique set of challenges. The gameplay is quite linear so even non-experienced gamers can play through this easily. If you play your cards right, the enemies are also generally very easy to defeat once you get past the starting phase. Some boss fights are truly annoying, but which RE boss fight isn't? Recommend for casual RE fans or anyone who just wanna chill with some action horror, but honestly, why come here when there is RE2 Remake?
