Imediately it becomes apparent that the game is episodic. Every episode is made into smaller parts. Everything is scored and timed. Like speed runs was a thing.
This is mostly a game where you play as Jill Valentine. Original Resident Evil Jill. She sure has changed. Or maybe the resolution just makes her body parts pop more. Eyes up here buddy...
But don't take me wrong, she is not a damsel in distress. She opens her own doors.
We also get to see Chris Redfield again, also from the first game, although not from the start and not much before later in game. There are several other side characters like Parker, Jessica and Raymond. You shift between some of them through the game, which is nice when changing pace.

The game has you investigate some new strange virus (T-Abyss) infested sea creatures, that appear after a terrorist attack on a US/EU mutual island in the mediterranian sea, Terragrigia, by a guy named Veltro.
This investigation leads you to a ship called The Queen Zamaria. You then start to search through this ghost ship to try and piece together what is going on. You spend most of the game on this ship but do also see other places.

I played the game with controller, and never tried the Mouse/Keyboard combo, so I can only judge the games mechanics based on the controller. This was mostly fine, although a bit clunky. Worst part was the dodge mechanic that I never mastered during this game. It had to be timed within a certain attack window on top of pressing direction button and A-button. I might have dodged 7-10 times during the game, mostly not on purpose as the A-button also was used for a special melee attack on downed opponents.

The game is very action heavy, and puzzles are not existing at all. I really love the first 2 games, and I really can't see any of those games in this game besides from the chracters used, the lingo and the Hunters. Rarely did I feel any tension or sacry moments. Only the first 2 episodes gave me a little tingle once in a while, but it quickly wore off when facing 150 enemies before the first 3 episodes out of 12 were over (I got the achievement to prove it).

There is an inventory management system, but nothing like the first games as it was only used to stash weapons. You could hold 3 weapons at any given time, and the rest went to the inventory. When you found new weapons you could only swap it with one of your existing weapons, but still that weapon went to the inventory.
To not make you too powerful the game limited the amount of ammo you can carry, and let you expand on that during the game. 6 types of weapons/ammo, handguns, large handguns/Magnum, assault rifles, rifles, shotgund and rocket launchers. Although rocket launcher ammo was not something you picked up, but you could have 1 launcher left over from a boss battle. I believe I had something like 12-13 different weapons using those types of ammo at the end. Most of them are real world weapons like G36 or PSG1 etc.
It was also possible to collect secrets that could better your weapons with mods.

There were a few different enemy types, but most were boring. Goo-puddle, Goo-man, adv-Hunter, Camo-Hunter, wolves, big wolves, huge-arrow-blaster, cleave-man, Messy-Goo-Man etc. Most of them are very slow moving. But that is needed when you get attacked by 3-6 enemies at a time and they all are bullet sponges. On normal difficulty you can take 4-5 attacks before dying and you can carry 5 heal-ups at a time.
Most boss battles were horrible. I had 2 somewhat good encounters. The first one, but he was just a ginormous bullet sponge that could kill me in one swoop while a continuous horde of other minions kept coming until the big died. And the other was the last one (I died 3 times). Last boss was just ridiculous, but I suspect that my lacking ability to dodge properbly made that one more difficult than it needed to be.

The story there is bland at best, with only a few scenes that peaked my interest.

Resident Evil Revelations is the result of a port of a glowup of a Nintendo 3DS game that's emulating the style of a console game. Let's break this down:

The game is in the style of Resident Evil 5. It's a third person, over-the-shoulder action game with some extremely light puzzle elements. 

But it was made for Nintendo 3DS, which isn't as powerful as a home console, so there were compromises. No large maps with a lot of enemies. The most you'll usually see at a time are 3. Most fighting takes place in corridors. Also, since the 3DS has a gyroscope, there is a first-person "scanner mode" that will reveal hidden items like ammo and health.

Then it was given the HD treatment and released to Xbox 360 and PS3. Since these systems don't have touch screens and gyroscopes, that stuff had to change. But also it doesn't seem like much was added.

And now it's on PC, so it can be played at much higher resolutions than a 3DS was capable of. 

The action is okay, but it's still a Resident Evil so it's a good idea to hoard ammo and health, which makes the scanner necessary. The problem is that the scanning is real tedious. It's really just corridors with enemies and then looking around in scanner mode to pick up items. It's just not a whole lot of fun.

It's also not very revelatory. It takes place between Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5 and doesn't really add much to either of those games. It's just a side story. Also, it pulls the same plot trick twice, which is really unforgivable. 

I only finished this because it's not a difficult game and it didn't frustrate me. I wanted to play some Resident Evil and that's what I got. It's just not a good Resident Evil.

[i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i] is a mind-bogglingly dumb game, but I'll be damned if it didn't kinda get its hooks in me by the time the credits rolled. I dunno if that's necessarily an endorsement, but it makes for an entertaining time, at least. Just... don't buy at full price.

Set in-between [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] and [i]5[/i], the player steps into the role of several BSAA agents as they investigate a potential bioterror attack in the Mediterranean ocean. For most of the game, that means navigating returning franchise heroine Jill Valentine (along with her shockingly charming partner, Parker) along a series of misadventures on an abandoned cruise liner, now inhabited by all manner of terrible fish monsters. It's these moments that the game positively shines. With the over-the-shoulder combat of [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] and the tense resource management of the early titles, the game really hits its stride for the middle part of the game, where you explore the Queen Zenobia in search of answers.

It's a rocky ride though, and part of why I'm so hesitant to recommend the experience is the frankly baffling pacing of the games first few hours, a vestigial (and episodic) organ leftover from the game's original release on 3DS. Instead of constructing a single, tight narrative on-board the ship, the plot feels the need to grow into a sprawling tale of political manipulation, intricate conspiracies, and aspirations of global geopolitical influence... with a plot containing all the depth of a kiddie pool. There were multiple occasions later where it felt less like I was playing a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game and more like I was playing a horror knock-off of [i]Metal Gear Solid[/i]. With unnecessary flashbacks that should've been treated as prologue, a plot taking place on two separate continental plates, and more side-characters than you'd care to shake a stick at, the game often feels unfocused. And that's [i]before[/i] dwelling on when the game chooses to be an action game over being a survival-horror game.

But I finished the game in one weekend, and save for some sequel-bait cliffhangers at the end, I genuinely enjoyed myself, and I have to wonder why. I think part of it might be the aforementioned Parker. Despite being a bit of cliche, the game actually did a decent job of making  me care about him, which felt like a natural consequence of the really tight-pacing of the later parts of the game. For as bloated as the plot feels, its odd mix of high melodrama and cartoonish pomp did prove kind of entrancing. Part of it might also be the novelty of seeing the game preserved; this is a solid port, and seeing the game survive past its initial release on handheld has a real charm to it.

At the end of the day, there are much better [i]RE[/i] games out there, and you shouldn't play this before those. If you haven't already, check out the other [i]RE[/i] games on Steam, since most of the mainline series is already here. But for all my misgiving and doubts, I liked this game enough as a popcorn affair to give it a tacit, lukewarm endorsement. Will this win hearts and minds, being remembered as the unsung classic of the series? [i]Hell[/i] no. But if you enjoy the series and are looking to scratch that survival horror itch? Sure, it's worth the dive. (Just, [i]please, [b]please[/b][/i]... don't pay full price. Get this on sale, or else play one of the other games.)

[h1]It's one of those "meh" Resident Evil games[/h1]
[i]That being said, I gave a thumb up because overall the positive stuff outweighs the negatives[/i]

[h1][u]PROs[/u][/h1]

🟢 [b]Functional combat[/b]. Bonus points because you can dodge attacks akin to good ol' RE3. Also, you can modify weapons which is a welcomed addition.

🟢 [b]Interesting bosses and enemies[/b]. Some designs are gruesome and spectacular, others feel pretty lazy. As a rule of thumb, if you're fighting the bosses then it's always pretty fun, with some rare exceptions.

🟢 [b]Hidden collectibles[/b]. Because seeing numbers go up is always a good thing and generally it makes my pp go up too.

🟢 [b]The main setting is pretty cool[/b]. Although you'll switch between maps as the game progresses (which to be fair can be quite disorienting and I didn't like that aspect very much), the main level is pretty cool. Resident Evil: Dead Aim did the ship thing way better than Revelations but hey! At least it's not a darn city again (it's a good concept but it becomes monotonous after a while).

🟢 [b]Raid mode[/b] is a clever way to get more replay value by recycling levels and put a bunch of enemies in it, arena-style. It's like The Mercenaries but slightly more entertaining.

[h1][u]CONs[/u][/h1]

🔴 [b]The Genesis[/b]. Seriously, what were they thinking. It ruins the pace like nothing else and the idea behind it isn't really that appealing... But now I'm getting ahead of myself; what is the Genesis, you may ask. To simply put, the Genesis is a gadget that lets you scan your surroundings. With this tool you can, most importantly, find hidden items (which makes the survival aspect way more trivial since now you pretty much have double the items in the map... Oh wait, Resident Evil isn't a survival horror anymore, what I'm talking about). So yeah, have fun walking two steps then using the Genesis. Rinse and repeat.

🔴 [b]Uninspired plot[/b]... Although you should take that for granted for todays standards and for the newest entries in the series overall. To be fair, there's way worse so no need to be too harsh about it.

This game spent 90% of it being so bad it was funny. Originally a 3DS port, we now get this mess of a game faithfully restored for the PC. Without fixing any of the elements about it that were necessary for the 3DS but just are kinda stupid for the PC.

The cons:

- Jessica feels like the student intern who they accidentally handed a gun. Her one personality trait is being jealous of other female characters.
- One of the characters is literally nicknamed "Jackass" and he wears bullets on his head. He's introduced like halfway through the story and we play as him like twice total and we're supposed to care about him despite him being... well... a jackass. His only personality trait is finding his female coworkers attractive.
- Oh, and the game forgot that a keyboard has more buttons than a 3DS so the dodge button is doubled with the move forward button. So you have to read the enemy's attacks and then walk into them to dodge their attacks. If you time it right, no problems. If you time it wrong? You get smacked in the face. If that bothers you, don't worry! The "turn around on the spot" button can also be used as the dodge button. So when an enemy attacks you, instead of walking into them and getting smacked down you can [I]turn around on the spot and get hit in the back[/I]. Well I'm sold! It's not like the keyboard has enough buttons that they can just make a designated dodge button or something. 
- Why do they even [I]have[/I] the "turn around on the spot" button?
- Your running speed is your walking speed and your walking speed is somehow even slower. 
- That unbelievably slow walking speed? Any strafing and backwards pedalling has to be done at that speed. So no backing away and shooting. It's turn around (with the mouse because that's quicker and doesn't give you idle time like the "turn around on the spot button") and run away and lose track of your surroundings because the FOV is pretty bad and you can't keep track of where the monster you're running from is. I get this might be part of the Survival horror experience, choosing "fight or flight" and not "both", but in boss fights in enclosed arenas? You can't actually get far enough away to get to shoot more than maybe two shots before you've got the boss on top of you, and if you want much more you have to go into a corner where you start spamming the forward button in the hope you dodge one of their attacks.
- Because they just copy and pasted the 3DS data over to this one, things that could be animated instead are replaced by text descriptions of the thing you're looking at [I]which don't really line up with the thing you're looking at[/I]. Such as "it's covered in blood" appearing in text when the model very clearly doesn't have any blood on it.
- Oh, and the final boss is just [I]not fun[/I]. The main portion of the fight involves having three illusions come up and you have to wait for the real one to reveal itself and shoot it. The problem is that because you back up so slowly, you can't ever have all three of the illusions visible at once. And it reveals itself about one second before it unavoidably damages you. So unless you already happened to be looking at the one that is about to become real, you get hit and miss your window to damage the boss. The concept was good, but because of the FOV and terrible movement the final boss fight just felt like RNG. And that's not a fun way to finish the game.

I could put up with the other stuff because there was strategy to it. There were interesting things happening. The characters that weren't stupid were interesting enough for me to care about. But the final boss fight is so stupid and would easily be fixed by actually adapting the 3DS version of the game to include a better FOV. But nope. We get the RNG bonanza as the final fight.

The game does have good things going for it, I was a fan of the scanning mechanics and pulling a "can I scan this monster while it runs at me because I really need more health and fast?" 
But overall the game was more pain than it was worth. Or at least the final boss was. And seeing as that's the last thing you walk away from, it's the thing that sticks out the most.

Resident Evil Revelations is probably the most forgettable game in the whole series.

The story is very flawed, as a lot of characters do a thing or two and never appear again in any other entry. In fact, the entire story arc bears nearly zero consequences to the series. The script is overstuffed with clichés and phrases that are cheesy, but not in a funny way like 1990s-2000s RE. Chris and Jill barely have a personality, every villain is predictable, and the provided comic relief is straight-up bad.

In the gameplay and graphics departments, we have to cut this game some slack due to it having originally been made for the 3DS. However, even by more relaxed standards, RE Revelations just feels like an ad-supported zombie game you'd play on your phone. The FOV is low enough to make anyone have motion sickness, and downgrading the game to use Widescreen Fixer is practically mandatory. Gun models are low-resolution and bland, as is the sound. The aiming and shooting mechanics are a watered-down version of the ones in RE4/5/6. Enemies are mostly reskins from the same installments. Scanning the map for items via the Genesis is slow and annoying. The list of problems could go on.

The only redeeming features of this game are some parts of soundtrack and the Queen Zenobia cruise ship, where most of the story takes place. The hallmarks of old RE are still there: a claustrophobic atmosphere, coupled with exploration and backtracking. Other than that, it's a bit difficult to recognize the DNA of the series in this installment. I would not recommend this game to non-fans of the series, let alone at full price.

I'm giving this game a cautious thumbs up, because it lays the foundation for the story of "Resident Evil: Revelations 2", which I consider to be a good game, even if it is overpriced and sold in such a way as to function as a cash-grab. 

This game isn't very good, however. I didn't really care for it - that said, it works. And it is an older game and ported from some other platform, so a lot of flaws can be excused and I will not unfairly judge a title just because it doesn't quite compare to contemporary titles designed to run on a more powerful platform. 

If you're a fan of resident evil and looking for another title to beat, or perhaps considering giving RE:R2 a try, I recommend seeing if you can make it through this title first - but if not, RE:R2 is playable on its own and you can safely skip this.

After the action-packed Resident Evil 5, Resident Evil Revelations looks back to the series' roots for an experience that many old-school fans will recognize. Revelations adapts the pre-rendered titles' defining traits to the modern RE, bringing back the series' name to a more grounded state, and actually knows what it wants to be this time: a survival-horror game that focuses on the atmosphere. Revelations reinforces this in the earlier hours of the campaign, where the player is greeted by distant eerie sounds, dark corridors, and the occasional jump scare that's done so effectively due to tension build-up. Some of the scariest parts of the game are the paths leading to the bosses because you can hear their cries echoing the hallways, either laughing from the thrill of the hunt or desperately crying for help. The tension does slow down during the latter half of the game, but the way leading there has been consistent in tone and quality.

Revelations uses an episodic structure to move the plot forward. This was done by the developers because "the game needed to be suitable for playing on portable hardware,"[web.archive.org] regarding the the original 3DS release. The 12 episodes featured in the game contain different scenarios from the perspective of three playable characters and their partners, all contributing small pieces of information and some backstory for the grand finale. While the game starts and ends exactly how a Resident Evil fan expects it too, this has got to be the most complicated series entry to date because there are a lot of character motivations to factor in, and the most important plot points are shown so poorly, with little explanation on why things happened the way they happened; Revelations isn't as straightforward as the games before it so some time is needed to fully grasp the story.

Overall, a good game and a great entry to the RE franchise. It retains the B-movie feel that the rest of the series is known for, and the gameplay combines the best of both worlds to deliver a solid experience. Definitely a must-have for the RE fan.

Okay; I've played this enough to give it my thought. Well, this game is far from what I expected. It is... well, it is VERY GOOD! Definitely not the best game ever, or best RE, but for a handheld console port spinoff, it is surprisingly polished and hefty in content.

First off, let's get this out of the way: don't expect a super in-depth customization system or inventory like RE4. Also, don't expect massive, well-thought scenarios like RE4/5/6. In this case, this game shows its humble portable console roots. the game is pretty basic in design, but yet it manages to pull it off so smoothly that in some cases you'll feel you're playing a full title. However, props for the cruiser ship design. It is really well done!

Gameplay is surprisingly great! If you play these game chronologically, you'll play it after RE4. And boy, do you feel the difference. The controls in Revelations are like what a good shooter should be. Mouse for looking/aiming, WASD for moving and strafing. A little bit sensitive, but with just some minor adjustments, this game feels like heaven compared to RE4's tank controls. You'll be getting 95% and above accuracy with mouse acceleration OFF and auto-aim OFF (thank god for these options!). Commands are pretty basic, and very intuitive; what you would expect from an OTS RE.

To call this game a pure action RE would be unfair. The game has a really good horror atmosphere in some places, making it feel like a genuine classic RE. Backtracking, fetching emblem keys, etc, it's all here! Just replace a spooky mansion with a drifting sea cruiser.

My only complain would be the story and characters. So far, I still don't know what's going on? Some terrorists with a new strand of the T-Virus threatning people. Also, characters seem a bit over-the-top for a RE game. They downright look straight out of a Metal Gear Solid game.

Graphics are pretty impressive! I did not expect the game to look this good, being a Nintendo 3DS port. You can notice there is something "flat" or bland about the textures, but at first glance it doesn't look that different from RE5/RE6. It supports higher resolutions without a hiccup, and the game is capped at 120fps when unlocked. And so far it has ran like absolute butter for me, with no stutter, crashes, or frame drops whatsoever.

Music is fantastic, as well as the sound design. Again, very surprising for this game's origins.

All in all, if you're like me and only stuck to the main RE titles 0-7, you have to give these a try. they are worth adding them to the good old RE collection. Storywise they might not offer that much, but Revelations are solid enough games to be worth playing (and really enjoying!). Also, if you're getting it for single-player only like me, get them on a sale. Not that they are not worth it, but the game has a more multiplayer focus, which is where gameplay hours are piled up mostly.

Can't wait to try Revelations 2!

This is one of those games that makes me wish Steam had a “Mixed” option.

Resident Evil Revelations came out after Resident Evil 5, but it plays very differently. Instead of leaning fully into action, it shifts back toward survival horror. Slower pacing, tighter resources, and noticeably less fluid controls. That change isn’t necessarily bad — it just depends on what you’re looking for.

Rather than the usual Mercenaries mode, this game (and its sequel) features Raid Mode, a separate mode where you run through stages defeating increasingly powerful enemies. It’s a cool idea and adds replay value, but it doesn’t fully replace the chaos and replayability Mercenaries fans might be expecting.

My biggest issue is the unlockable weapons. There are barely any truly special unlocks, and the only infinite ammo weapon is the Infinite Rocket Launcher. Unlocking it is a serious grind, and even then, you can only use it for about 70% of the game. For a series known for fun post-game rewards, that’s disappointing.

Overall, it’s pretty cool — solid atmosphere, decent survival horror vibes — but it doesn’t offer much beyond that. Not bad, just not particularly memorable either.

It's hard to explain what this game is. On one hand, it captures the general claustrophobia and lavish set designs that have been ravaged by a virus. On the other hand, its story, dialogue and overall voice-acting really kill the vibe. The earlier Resident Evil titles (Zero and the original, more specifically) have some cheesy voice-acting, but they're still quality titles.
The gameplay (especially on mouse-and-keyboard) feel...well, there's a difference between so smooth it's comfortable and so smooth you can barely control it; this game definitely hits the latter. Even turning down the general sensitivity makes the menus and aiming feel annoyingly sensitive. The dodge mechanic is an interesting idea, but the controls for it (again, mouse-and-keyboard, no point of reference for controllers) are really clunky, along with most other movement. This largely isn't a problem until you encounter the Hunters (the big lizard things, for those who don't know) and Scagdeads (the big ugly things with chainsaw arms), which can instantly kill the player with little warning.
The story tries (emphasis on "tries") to be suspenseful and dramatic like a TV series, even going as far to add recaps between chapters. These are largely unnecessary, and really just repeat information you learned about ten minutes prior, trying to be like a TellTale game. Granted, while the dialogue and story do make an effort to be good (and that effort does show), the voice-acting really kills it. The dialogue tries to be witty and either dramatic or funny, but the voice-acting shows little effort.
Overall, the game feels largely well-designed, especially with the locales and soundtrack, but there are so many little bumps that make this game hard to take seriously. Overall, it still earns a 7 out of 10 because there are some very great parts that make this game fun. It's more the finer mechanics and poor voice-acting quality that lower the overall likability. Is it worth full-price? If you're a die-hard RE fan, sure. Is it worth it on sale? Probably. It's a great way to kill time, but not much beyond that. 7/10.

The problem, however, is that the developers at Capcom were in their scrap age(the opposite of a golden age). Given that this game was made in the same time period as DmC Devil May Cry, Capcom knew that they had to ♥♥♥♥ up this game too. Ergo, they hid the game behind the label Raid Mode and forced the players to play what is the absolute worst excuse for a Resident Evil campaign since 6. It's more or less the same narrative structure of "HEY GUYS LOOK AT THESE CHARACTERS YOU RECOGNIZE AND A BUNCH OF NEWCOMERS WE'LL NEVER HAVE SHOW UP AGAIN" as RE6 but with somehow even worse gameplay. No, Capcom, the "enemies dropping nothing with VERY few exceptions means you gain nothing by fighting enemies OoOoOoOoO THIS IS A HORROR GAME AGAIN BETTER RUN" idea does not at all work when you still use the RE5 game design of "implying you won't get punished just for running away LOL"

However, to compensate, they added a dodge function! Wait, no, sorry, that's wrong. They added a dodge ability. See, it doesn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ function due to what I can assume to be the world's most spastic RNG dictating if you can have it work or not. The game itself says "press A and then up or down on the control stick to not get hit" and next thing you know, you're doing your damnedest to figure out how this barely-function feature works... and then you're somehow able to do it by just repeatedly going left. And then that stops working and 
you're once again trying to figure out how this abominable dodge can even be used.

So you take the original Resident Evil trilogy's "low supplies, and game designed to give you a way to swooce out" design, then mix it with the post-4 era's "game encourages you to shoot those infected SOBs up and use your kick/punch of death after you shoot the right parts of an enemy, and gives you a far more generous amount of supplies as such" design, cut out the latter parts of both groups, and expect you to endure it for Raid Mode. It's just Final Fantasy XIII levels of "you have to play all this garbage if you want the fun," except it's arguably even worse because you get taunted every three chapters by the drip-feeding of new levels. This WILL burn you out and just make it worse to go back to the campaign, might I add, so don't take the bait.

In short, Resident Evil Revelations is a great game, but sadly the devs labelled it Raid Mode and forced us to endure the absolutely abhorrent campaign, which somehow goes from RE's usual "cheesy, kind of bad, but amusing" narrative to "just stupid" to unlock every level.

Revelations is okay.
I know a lot of people heralded this game as a return to survival horror and it's ...really not. At all.
The game is a bit spooky at first with some really, really gross monsters which is awesome and things start out really tense but it doesn't maintain this atmosphere at all.

The game has two major problems, it's trying to be the old RE games with the boat where it's tense and scary, with the mystery of where did Chris go?? But ALL of this falls apart both gameplay wise and 'story' wise. 
Chris's location is straight up told to you, you find out by suddenly getting a cutscene and gameplay where he's located so you know he's fine and that Jill and Parker are wasting their time. So the story is moot and absurd. Story isn't RE's strongest but character's and some motive usually are enough to drive you along but even the supporting characters are either flat or awful. 
Parker's fake accent is so awful it's distracting, Quint is an annoying cliche, Keith is unmemorable and the bad guy may as well laugh manically the moment you see him, you know who it is as soon as it starts. No twist is surprising or impressive. 

So, why does the gameplay fall short then? So like I said it plays it off trying to be survival horror, giving you this scanner to try earn herbs and such. The scanner slows things down and I feel hinders the gameplay. It adds nothing & feels like they're dragging it out. Also this survival horror gets thrown out the door when you play as Parker in flashbacks gunning down dozens and dozens of hunters while you're on a man made, scifi island. Then you go to Chris and he's getting some action-y bits too, same with Keith and Quint. Jill is the only one who gets any real horror but not a lot of the survival aspect. 

So, anyone who says this game is survival horror or a call back to the good old days is talking out their a$$. You're trapped on a ship as Jill but you don't get that feeling of trapped since you're constantly playing as other people elsewhere in the world. 
You don't feel trapped because of the other characters, you're not really strapped for supplies nor do you have to really manage an inventory & you don't feel like you're accomplishing anything because you know Chris is fine and this is answered, EARLY. It's not even a spoiler, it's straight up done in the first 15 minutes. 

So, why am I recommending the game then. 
Well if NONE of this is a factor for you and you liked Resident Evil 4,5,6 and you're not looking for something super scary, this game is alright for that. There's variety in the areas, some characters carry the feel of the game and it's overall pretty fun. 
It's a little rough visually as it was a 3DS game but they've done enough to enhance it to where it's good looking. It'll also run on some really low end hardware, I had it running on my old Surface Pro 4 (low end as in the intel GPU isn't anything you want to rely on for gaming) and it was around 60fps on high/720p settings. So, you intel GPU gamers, drop your res to 720p in most games and you'll be fine for the most part. 

Just don't go in expecting Resident Evil 1-3, it's not that. It's not survival horror. It's a spooky shooter with a awful story but will entertain you throughout the game.

[h1] An underrated RE game [/h1]

In a time when RE games were shifting away from its original concept and getting worse with each release, this game was an unexpected return to the original survival horror the series is known for. The game was originally released on the 3DS and because of that it’s pretty straight forward, no side-quests, no multiple endings, it’s much simpler and easier than the other titles I’ve played, not necessarily a bad trait. 

The great thing about this one is that it combines elements from the original horror focused games (1,2,3) and the action focused ones (4,5,6). In one episode you’ll be in a room without weapons with a monster chasing you and in another one you’ll be in a turret section shooting everything in sight. It mix things up pretty well, they don’t feel forced and the game maintains its focus. Classic Resident Evil mechanics are still in this game, inventory management, storage box, the ability to avoid enemies and the puzzles.

80% of the story happens aboard a cruise ship and that’s where you’ll experience the survival horror aspect of this game, the ship is filled to the brim with monsters, not the run off the mil zombies but new creatures known as “Ooze”, basically the same thing gameplay-wise, the difference is that [spoiler] they don’t really look human and have some maritime characteristics because of the virus’ origins  [/spoiler]. The creatures in this game are very creepy and unsettling, specially the bosses. The ship looks run down and depressing, it will make you uncomfortable, its corridors are dark and narrow, similar to the mansion from the first game, giving you that claustrophobic feeling and setting the “survival horror” atmosphere. The place itself is huge, you get a decent variety of environments, from the ship’s machine room to its luxurious hall, there’s even an underwater segment. The way you survive and fight also change with the environments, you won’t get strong weapons till later in the game so this part is mostly the classic: “Should I kill or avoid them?”. The story bits that happen out of the ship are usually more action oriented, having to kill most of the enemies you’ll have better weapons and more ammo. 

The story is divided in episodes, it goes back and forth among the characters and timelines, shifting perspective and tone.  Almost everything that take place on the ship will have you play as Jill Valentine, some episodes will have you play as Chris, Keith or Parker, those are the more action focused ones. Set before the events of RE 5, It’s the same great conspiracy with multiple twists and intrigues plot we all love, it works like a prologue, explaining the BSAA and what Chris and Jill were up to. The dialogue still has some cheesiness to it but that’s part of Resident Evil.

There are a lot of main characters in this game, and I mean A LOT, classic and new ones, sometimes you’ll get lost by so many names. Most of the levels you’ll have a partner with you and you’ll get to see their relationships play out, they’re all compelling in a way, even the fan hated Jessica. I really enjoyed Jill and Parker chemistry.

The game features a Raid mode, you play it solo or with a friend, you choose any character from the game to play as, even some bonus ones if you have them unlocked. It’s an action oriented mode where you’ll have to complete levels from the main story as quickly as possible, the only mission here is to kill as many enemies as you can and get to the objetive. There’s a level system and a shop that you can use to unlock stronger weapons and completing objectives unlock new characters. While I’m not a big fan of these action modes I had fun with Raid, mainly because of its co-op and the ability to play with characters you like , it gives the game replay value.

The only real issue I had with this game was the camera and the fov, they’re bad, had to install another program to fix them.

[b]  This game is often forgotten whenever someone brings up the RE series, while not a masterpiece it’s a gem and if you enjoy the series you should definitely play it. [/b]

[b]Resident Evil Revelations[/b] is an extremely solid entry in the series, so much so you don't necessarily notice it being a 3DS port beyond less complicated geometry. Has great atmosphere, very classic RE in some regards, and has a pretty decent story that furthers builds on the post-umbrella lore while still be contained enough where no prior knowledge of the franchise is necessarily needed to understand. Gameplay is tight, especially if you get the dodge mechanic down (which is pretty fair and balanced). Bosses as expected aren't spectacular though the final boss is above average for Resident Evil, I'll just assume those who complain about it haven't figured out the dodge mechanic after 7 hours. Raid mode is also great, amongst the best side-content in the series, offering a sizable amount to do post-campaign.

Playing this on PC, you can tell it was made with the 3DS in mind, especially with the new genesis scanner to make full use of the two screens on the 3DS and the fact that the scale of this game has been cut down from previous games. This works well however, as it makes this the first resident evil game since RE4 to return to a more atmospheric and horror focused setting that would set the groundworks for all future installments. One of the best parts of this game is that it is very much a self contained story, meaning that people new to the series will not need to know much about the overall lore in order to enjoy the game.

I don't know about this one. It's definitely more an action game with ammo scattered and often hidden about than a more traditional RE game.

It tries to remember the Spencer Mansion through locked doors and keys named after things found on ships, as well as a sprawling, continuous map where sometimes you need to backtrack to find optional rooms. This is good.

What isn't so good is how you need to scan the environment because there is more ammo laying about than you realize, but you need to fill a loading bar first. In addition, you can scan enemies to slowly work your way to getting a green herb to basically appear out of nowhere. The game can also rely on it's dodge mechanic a bit too much, and I never quite figured out how to do it consistently, and some of the game's bosses have infinite spawns of enemies that like to come out of the vents and blindside you, since the FOV is zoomed in a little too close for my liking.

The only thing of item management you really need to worry about is if you come across a new gun in the environment. Jill can carry any three guns on her person, and if you find a new one in level, you need to leave one of those guns behind in favor for the new one, or backtrack to an item box and store a gun to make room. Other than that, you have a separate inventory for ammo to where you may have your maximum capacity of 60 handgun bullets filled up, but you can still carry 20 rifle rounds, 20 magnum rounds, 5 herbs, and 35 more shotgun rounds. You don't really need to worry about having space for keys or whatever notes you may encounter.

Something about the atmosphere is off. Some of the sounds are ok, but I think it's a little too bright for a derelict ship out in the middle of an ocean. I haven't really been put on edge all that much, and the monster design just doesn't really do it for me. It's like they are trying to be the Regenerador from RE4, but they die easily.

All an all, it might be a perfectly playable game if you aren't thinking of it like a Resident Evil game in the classic or more modern remake sense, but it's still a package I found myself feeling nothing for.

Resident Evil Revelations is probably the worst Resident Evil game I have played (I haven't played them all, but I am getting close). Similarly to RE6, it doesn't feel like a Resident Evil game or a survival horror game at all. At least in 6 you had some segments that were a little scary or you were tight on ammo. In Resident Evil Revelations, you almost never run out of ammo and never did I ever feel threatened by the enemies to which most of them I don't even know the names of because this game is so forgettable. 

 Firstly, let's talk about the story and how all over the place it is. So, a terrorist group threatens a city on the water called Terragrigia, then is destroyed to cover up later events. The B.S.A.A. are working to solve the riddle behind the attack while another group named Veltro are supposedly behind it when another government group named F.B.C. are actually behind it. Also, a different strain of the T-Virus is made called the T-Abyss and like many of the other games, the goal is to weaponize it. However, instead of being straight forward, two identical boats are made for testing it as well as the infection in Terragrigia. But the boats were a cover for a plan to destroy the evidence of the testing of the T-Abyss and Veltro actually doesn't exist anymore because it was a cover for your boss to lure out the main antagonist Lansdale. You don't find most of this out until later because there is a mole in the team and there are three pairs, Jill and Parker, Chris and Jessica, and Keith and Quint. That sums up the story which I should mention takes place on two boats and a couple sections in a snowy wasteland and one on the beach.

  Which brings me to my next point, the characters. It took Capcom years, but they FINALLY made a Resident Evil game in canon that takes place on a cruise ship!

A pretty darn good one too. Makes a good companion piece to Resident Evil 5, and is essentially a prequel to that game as a sort of pseudo origin story for the BSAA. The pacing is . . . interesting, as the game's narrative is geared toward short bursts of play (since it was originally for the DS) and so most of the segments are short, with you hopping between a section where you play as Jill on the big boat with continuity (in items and game progress) between her segments, and then another section where you play as a rotating assortment of other characters in the BSAA in different locales and times solving the big mystery going on that the gang has to eventually solve. It all comes to a fairly satisfying conclusion, and honestly, it's at least on par with the franchise in terms of story telling.

The gameplay is solid all around. Essentially a culmination of the "Action" REs up to that point (4 & 5) but you also get Jill's dodge mechanic from RE3. But placed in a more traditional RE 1/2 setting with limited resources, essentially proving that the REmake 2 formula worked before that game ever released. Nothing in the way of truly ludicrous puzzles though, the most you're going to have to handle are some simple rewiring mini-games. The interesting addition to the gameplay here is being able to customize your guns with mods, and eh, it's alright I guess.

The enemies here are a nice twist on the formula too. The aquatic theme to them makes them stand out from other Biohazard foes quite well, and it's pretty obvious that the standard Ooze enemies became the gameplay inspiration for the zombies in the REmake 2, with a fair amount of health and a LOT of sway on their heads. The final boss is a bit BS though, that dude has WAY too much HP compared to a normal RE final boss.

Also the Raid Mode is an interesting replacement for Mercenaries, with a time attack run through levels you've already beaten with remixed enemies. It has a decent progression system to it, but I don't think it has the staying power of mercenaries modes in prior games because it doesn't have that sense of random chance those did in RE 4, 5, & 6. It's more about perfecting your run through a level with little in the way of variance. Also very little was done to make the later Raid Mode levels different from their respective story levels, so you're still going to have to do story objectives in a bunch of them and get lost trying to remember where you have to go if it's been a minute since you played the campaign, so they tend to get a bit tiresome.

TL;DR - The game cruises into a completely solid entry in the RE franchise. It's nothing too exceptional but it's enjoyable enough. Probably mostly for those who like RE 5 a lot though. Or who just want to see Jill in a wetsuit from behind for a few hours.

(Good action game, but does not feel like Resident Evil)

============

Review:

Resident Evil Revelations is similar to the action games of the series (4-5-6), it's a shooter and not a survival horror game.

Graphically.. well, you can just see it's a port from a handheld console - with quite sloppy graphical improvements.

The level of detail varies - it mostly looks like a PS3 game, but some places (especially terrain textures and details) look more like they're from a PS2 game. The main character models and the ship areas look mostly alright - but side characters and other areas like the beach, buildings and snowy areas look quite dated.

It's like they were told to make the port look better on PC, and some things most likely do - but others were probably nearly untouched. So sloppy work would describe this well.

For a game released in 2013 graphics of "PS 2.5" are not good. Both Resident Evil 5 and 6 were released before this, and they look better. Hell, you can pick just about any game from that era and they will look better.

Graphics are not that important to me - but the lack of consistency in the detail is what bothers me. It should either look like a PS2 game in every place, or a PS3 game in every place.

It feels like a really half-assed job that the level of graphics just changes between the areas - it makes it feel like a cash grab.

The monsters are also just not scary - I get it that they tried to go with the oceanic theme, but the game would've been scarier with the typical zombies lurking in the ship.

Sound-wise it's alright - nothing exceptional but it works just fine. The music fits the oceanic theme well, but does not create that dreadful, oppressive feeling that Resident Evil is known for.

============

Instead of a typical resident evil game - it is divided into short episodes, much like a TV Series. It even has those "Happened Previously" cutscenes that shows some highlights of the last episode you played.

You play different characters in different episodes - which works in the TV Series system of the game.

Again this system points towards the handheld console roots - because it's well designed for playing one episode at a time. Handheld consoles generally don't have much of a battery life, so you'd play an episode and call it quits there, let the device recharge.

So it's sort of brilliant design from a handheld console point of view - but does it work on the PC?

Well, actually it does. Especially if you don't have much free time, the system works well - because you can just play one episode every now and then, and the cutscenes remind you where you left off.

The Raid Mode is a nice little bonus after you've finished the main story. It essentially eliminates all the story elements - there's no cutscenes, no key items or such. Just short missions in the same areas as the main story, enemies and weapons have levels and you level up as you play.

============

But it just does not feel like a Resident Evil game - the only thing that even remotely gives this feeling is the keys and doors that they unlock.

It's a good game, but a mediocre Resident Evil. When you see the name "Resident Evil", you have some kind of expectations - and this game just doesn't meet those expectations.

That being said, if it was named differently I could've forgiven more of the flaws. But it's not bad even as is, it's just in the lower bracket of RE games.

If you're a fan of the action-oriented parts of the series (4-5-6), then you'll probably like this one too.

But if your cup of tea is the survival horror parts of the series, then this might be a waste of money.

============

The Good 👍

+ Solid Action Game
+ Raid Mode

The Bad 👎
- Inconsistent Quality of Graphics
- Does not feel like a Resident Evil
- Not Scary

Resident Evil Revelations was originally released for Nintendo 3DS in 2012 between Resident Evil 5 and 6. This HD version for Windows was released a bit later in 2013. So the game is about four years fresher than Resident Evil 5.

Let's begin with the graphics. Simply put they are outdated - especially the textures. In some places they are more accurate. So those looking for better looking experience than for example Resident Evil 5 will be disappointed. 

How about the gameplay? Well you can feel the 3DS haunting in the background. The narrow field of view (FOV) together with clunky controls may cause motion sickness for sensitive people. At least turning off the mouse acceleration made the aiming easier. Otherwise there is no big difference comparing to Resident Evil 5. 

As already seen from the thumbnails the game takes place in marine world. This gave a huge opportunity for the series - imagine all those scary zombies crawling in shipwrecks and stuff. The result being ill-tempered fishes and hungover janitors that seem to have swollen some sort of rake and they are trying to shoot (or at least hit) you with it. Hilarious and sadly not too scary. 

The enemies also seem to have only one dying animation so don't expect those heads to explode. Actually the enemies are just melting on the floor. They also tend to get stuck very easily.

The game is at least as arcade-like as Resident Evil 5. Instead of that tiny bit of horror there is humor and even flirting. There is only one type of herb so obviously there is no combining any more. To get more herbs you can collect them or cook some sort of antiviral from the corpses by examining them with a device called "Genesis". By using that device you can also reveal secrets and collectibles. 

One reason why I bought this game was a statement that it would be closer to original Resident Evil problem solving style - with those distinctive keys and puzzles. Excluding few exceptions - NO. 

The gun upgrades are a bit different - you don't simply upgrade your weapon until it is at its max. You can make your magnum insanely lethal of course - but instead you can make it faster with that high damage etc. Bogies in this game are pretty weak so it is not entirely bad idea to put that damage to more general purpose weapon.

How about the plot then? As said this is a spin-off.  There are naturally some references to main plot but nothing in particular. All the characters are new excluding Chris and Jill. I didn't like the actual plot, it was a bit too "ambitious" and lot of big things seemed to happen in a very short period of time (with its ion cannons and blowing cities and ships to smithereens). But I really liked how the story followed different persons at different time and how it all entwined at the end. 

Even though I was "a bit" disappointed with the graphics and the marine setup... and pretty much everything - the game was "ok". Resident Evil 1 & 2 are in my top 10 or 20 all time list and even Resident Evil 5 was a jolly good game too. So I may have just hoped too much. So if you are looking for Resident Evil(ish) adventure and you get it for a cheap enough price - just go for it. Knowing it is not that beautiful it probably should be and it is pretty far from the original horror theme.

[b]Resident Evil Revelations[/b] is another unusual installment in the franchise featuring familiar faces, mechanics, and themes. However, it also features some outright unwanted conflicts following the narrative, characters, and purpose as with other failed attempts. The story follows Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield, working within small groups, uncovering a mysterious outbreak haunting an abandoned ship that gives more answers than they bargained for. But their journey doesn't come without nonstop chaos and deceits leading them into further endangerment.

When Revelations shines, it delivers the horror as players are dragged further into the ship and understanding the impact of the viral outbreak. It returns previous features with some additional twists but only enough to give players advantages during fights and investigations. However, they've introduced a particular tool entirely used to scan objects that would greatly benefit players seeking extra outlets to feel immersible and truly like a detective. The game also offers a vast collection of items, characters, and modes to explore by the most devoted fans and newcomers.

However, Revelations is a mess. Not mechanically but by storytelling since it introduces some of the most unresolved, convoluted, and ridiculously written content in the franchise. Despite being set between the events of two specific installments, the half-witted writing channeled Resident Evil Survivor but made that story seem more plausible. Additionally, half of the characters are either outright expendable or boring compared to notable alumni from previous installments. It's a shame because after they're introduced players are expecting more thrills but actually obtain more questions and unsatisfying results.

It's the type of game from a beloved franchise that expects hardcore fans to know what they're getting into but fails to take itself more seriously and attempt innovation. Outside the story, there's plenty of creative ideas that often makes the experience feel genuine. But entirely ignoring the story makes it a mere third-person arcade shooter that probably would've benefited this game better than telling a disjointed story with forgettable characters and terrible twists. It's nothing new but shouldn't be a reoccurring flaw within the franchise especially when not properly utilizing characters and subplots.

The game offers plenty of replay value but the bland story otherwise ruins what should've been a better game. Without following the lore of other installments, and ignoring the asinine storytelling, it's a fun game challenging players to utilize methods to eliminate hordes of new foes. But that visioning isn't fair and equally the storytelling should be just as enjoyable as its mechanics. After completing the story, players could still replay solo or with other players to compete with scores and skills. However, the fun only lasts as long as the modes allow until they realize there could've been more done.

This also, for me at least, is the first game that puts you almost entirely against a new, unique type of B.O.W, in short fish people or as I call them Grunts and Brutes since they look strikingly familiar to the Amnesia: The Dark Descent monsters...and before anyone goes there I'm not saying anything is stolen, cloned or copied! Its just what I see...Amnesia DID come out a good year and a half to 2 years before Revelations so I could understand any light inspiration if it was the case. The game takes part mainly on a giant ship with many floors and rooms to explore or return to when you have the necessary means, which is often a good idea in Resident Evil games due to there usually been some sort of high damage weapon waiting for you or in this case some rare mods.

The story is fairly standard, nothing special...secrets, betrayals, cloak and dagger here, mystery sprinkled there. Revelations isn't necessarily the best Resident Evil game ever made, but it's still among one of the better ones in my opinion.  A lot of that is owed to it's reworked controls that mime Resident Evil 4 and 5, but remove some of the more irritating aspects of those games.  You can move while shooting, for one, and switching around weapons is much more straight forward.  Melee attacks are also significantly iterated upon, and they actually work really well even on their own in Revelations.  Guns are also interesting: the game doesn't have a whole lot of them but there's a modification system in place that makes them customizable, which is I find to be a rewarding mechanic.  Beyond that, the game's map is fairly small, and a lot of areas are re-treaded as you proceed through the game.  Oddly enough, even though the game is divided into a number of rather short "episodes", the map never shrinks outside of specific events, so it's actually kind of open to exploration as you find keys to the various doors.  It eschews the usual mercenaries mode for a thing called "raid mode" which are basically all the single-player chapters with the story elements stripped out, crammed full of tough enemies, and playable in co-op.  It's simple but entertaining, and the same gun mod mechanics are even more present with different "rarities" of guns and mods being rewarded for faster runs on tougher difficulties.  You unlock different characters for raid mode just like in the mercenaries modes of other games and they have some slight differences among them, mostly just damage bonuses for particular weapon classes, but some do have novel attributes.  It is worth noting that this game is a port of a 3DS game, and it shows a lot.  The character models and most of the environments look passable, I'd even say that the lighting looks pretty nice, but there are some areas where it's really apparent the game was designed with the 3DS in mind.  Environments aren't especially detailed, and if you examine various elements of them closely, you'll find a lot of very simple geometry and blurry textures.  It's also rather short; I beat the campaign on normal in about 9 hours.  I'd recommend hard for most people who've played a Resident Evil game before, in retrospect.  Additionally, several touch-screen interaction elements have been removed from this PC port, so occasionally you get to watch Jill unscrew a panel or cut open a door with no input from the player for 4-5 seconds.  Still, these issues don't interfere with the game-play much, so they're not a major issue.  I could recommend Revelations to anyone who enjoys Resident Evil games as a solid entry with a good amount of content that's surprisingly replayable.  It's a good game with some novel ideas you don't see in other entries, just don't expect the prettiest or most complex game in the series.  $30 still might be a bit much for it, to be honest, but it goes on sale fairly regularly and it's usually a really steep discount when it does.

Final note: Under NO circumstances should you use the "classic controls" the game offers in it's menu.  They're awful and actually make certain actions entirely impossible.

[h1]The Good[/h1][i]Campaign reminiscent to the original games in the franchise.[/i]

The presentation of the game’s campaign was refreshing to experience, given that the previous Resident Evil games (5 & 6) were more action oriented.

Revelations provides a tense atmosphere that’s been absent since Resident Evil 4, as you explore the areas with so much air to mystery, little provisions to assist the player and different enemy varieties that can provide a challenge, especially the first boss. It’s safe to say that this game will certainly keep players on guard.

[h1]The Bad[/h1][i]Campaign has no option for Co-op.[/i]

What took me by surprise when first playing this game was the fact that there was no option for Co-op in the main campaign. Personally, it was a real bummer, as I was looking forward to playing this with my friends.

As I played through the campaign, I couldn’t help but notice and realize that for the part, you play as one character while having another one tag along, or two in the rare event, to support you. It goes without saying that not having Co-op was a missed feature to have, since it was first introduced on Resident Evil 5.

[h1]The Ugly[/h1][i]Raid mode has Co-op, but isn’t really impressive.[/i]

Revelations features an additional game mode simply referred to as “Raid Mode”. It’s basically an arcade run for the campaign stages with more monsters, power-ups, bonuses and so on.

I have two problems with this game mode. The first is the incredible irony where Raid Mode has a Co-op feature available (I’ll stop with the Co-op now…). The second is that it’s not at all impressive. Going through the campaign stages with the tense atmosphere replaced with an arcade environment to get the best score and best time breaks the immersion of what I liked about Revelations.


While I have some obvious problems with Revelations’ features, I can still recommend this game for the enjoyable campaign. I’d recommend getting it on a sale, seeing as I like half of the game and not the other.

Being that this game has been out for quite some time, I'm going to compare it to Resident Evil 2 Remake, as this game is probably going to be something fans of re2make would seek out after completion. 

The biggest problem with Resident Evil: Revelations is the label... in no way, shape, or form is this a survival horror game. Maybe it is moreso survival horror than re4, 5, and 6... but regardless, it still isn't survival horror. Not even remotely close. There's no inventory management. You switch and reload weapons on the fly, while moving and running. You can heal yourself with a single button - WHILE being attacked... this is an arcade shooter at best. 

I guess the only distinction it would have with survival horror is the clunky controls. The camera follows you explicitly, so you can't look over your shoulder like in re2make. This makes for stiff gameplay. There is a dodging mechanic, but it seems to work more on luck than anything else... in my time I could very rarely reliably do it. 

To push it even further from survival horror, this game includes physical attacks that seemingly do more damage than the magnums/revolvers in the game. If you score a few headshots on an enemy, you have a chance to stun them, and then have a free pass to go up to them and do a fully charged physical attack that hits like an RPG. You may not realize how powerful it actually is until you play the raid mode (which displays health bars)... shooting a hunter with a shotgun once (that does maybe 1/5th damage, depending on circumstance) then punching it as Chris is enough to kill it. It's pretty ridiculous. 

When the writers went into the board room, they must've burrowed it in their brains that a story with twists is the only way to go... the story of this game has so many twists, it gets a little annoying after a while. Twists can be a great plot mechanic, but not when literally every plot point is a twist. That being said, I did really like the way the story was told out of sequence at times. 

Campaign play is split into chapters and subchapters, as you switch between characters to navigate the story. The settings range from the ship with the ooze enemies - which majority of the game is played on - to snowy mountains with dog enemies to a city and office building with hunter enemies (my favorite section). It's some varied gameplay, but you spend so much time on the ship that it does get a bit stale after a while. It is a huge sigh of relief when you can enter the mountains and fight the dogs, or walk down office corridors with your gun raised ready for hunters to attack. As far as scares, there are two bosses that are quiet creepy, but the rest of the game is fairly tame; although I found the hunter levels to be as tense as anything. Unfortunately though, majority of the campaign is played the same... enter a room, pull out your scanner, scan for bodies/handprints/etc, kill enemies, repeat. The scanner gameplay was really a drag... you pretty much have to play the game with three strategy guides open to get all the secret items with the scanner if you don't want to completely waste your time. If you care about achievements and other things like that, anyway. 

The campaign also comes in three difficulties; easy which should be skipped if you've ever played an over the shoulder game before, normal which is the base gameplay, and then infernal mode which is seriously questionable. Each narrow corridor is filled with nearly double the enemies that are so bullet spongey you have to end up dodging (or, attempting to) the majority of them... some of them literally take 50 bullets to put down! While sure, it's difficult... I can't find a mode like this fun at all. 

The game truly shines - as most reviews say - once you enter the raid mode. That's when it drops the appearance of attempting to be a survival horror game, and fully embraces its arcade shooter instincts. In raid mode, you run through certain sections of the campaign mode and complete bonus objectives, such as defeating every enemy, not taking damage, and completing the stage at a lower level than what is recommended, all the while purchasing weapons and upgrades from a shop after the stage. Very arcade-like. What's notably missing is a "retry" or "restart" button, especially in stages that are incredibly difficult to avoid damage... instead, if you mess up, you either have to complete the stage, or quit the stage and go through 3 or so loading screens to try it again. It's fairly annoying. Another complaint about raid mode that might be strange is that it's entirely too long... you "have" to play through each stage 3 times - at 3 difficult difficulties, at least - to 100% complete it. It takes many hours. There is a co-op mode, but I really struggled to ever find someone to play with using the in-game options. 

Graphically, and in general, you can really tell this game is a port from the DS. I'm not exactly sure why they didn't use the usual model for Jill. The movements are sometimes weird... running diagonal for example looks very strange. There are so many assets and animations reused from re4 and 5. This all makes the presentation look cheap.  

Overall, it's not the best game I've ever played, but also far from the worst. I don't think it's worth the $30 price point and would definitely wait for a sale. I might play it still from time to time going forward to try to nab more of the raid mode achievements, but I'm not exactly sure it's worth any more of my time. I'm hoping Revelations 2 is better than this game. I'm not exactly sure why this game has so many rave reviews... I must be missing something. While I still recommend the game for fans of Resident Evil, I have to give this one a barely passing grade of 60/100.

Bought this during the sale. Was the only RE game I didn't own, so "when in Rome". It's an ok game I guess. It's definitely not bad, but I have my criticisms of it.

The Good:
Characters

The Bad:

Too many "Wave enemy" sequences

No treasure hunting

The writing and voice acting of this game definitely reminds me of the older games, in that they both are kind of cheesy and not well done. A couple spots where you just have to laugh, even though the voice acting and writing don't portray a funny moment. It's just so poorly done in some spots, and the voice actor for your BSAA handler was by far the worst voice acting in the game. He is so lifeless, and forgettable. Playable characters were alright for the most part. My two favorite characters, Parker and Keith. Good chemistry, and both voice actors did a great job voicing them.

Mechanically, the game is good. The shooting mechanics work well, nothing more needs to be said. I didn't really get the hang of the dodge mechanic as the game really doesn't help explain how it's used, other than that I had no real issue here.

The setting of the game, I liked the idea of the huge ship. Definitely a more unique setting, and new to the game. I thought it worked well. The problem is, you don't spend all your time there. You have the copy/pasted snow areas, which I didn't like. I mean you literally visit the same snowy mountain area where a plane crashes two different times with two different sets of characters. I felt like there should've been more focus on the ship, and they should've been more creative setting up flashback parts of the game. They just felt rushed and very bare bones. Not a lot of depth in them at all.

Enemy variety in this game, honestly, is terrible. You spend most of your time fighting against the same enemies over and over again. The basic mutations in the ship and the wolves. I feel like they could've made far more enemies. I also felt like there were some half assed "wave defense" sequences. Like the one in Terragrigia for instance, you sit there and fight nothing but hunters the whole time. Zero variety there.

Lastly there is a lack of weapons in the campaign in your first playthrough. I know you can unlock certain weapons by playing Raid, and you get one after starting a New Game+, but other than that you don't find a lot playing the campaign.

My main gripe with the game: The Genesis
This mechanic is the WORST. Reason being, you're constantly using this to scan areas which can get really annoying really fast. You can chose not to scan anything, yes, but there are a lot of times where you will use a ton of ammo because of the aforementioned "Wave Defense" areas in the game. Basically forcing you to scan every inch of the game in search of bullets. I do like that you gain healing items when you scan enemies, but I feel this tool is more of a pain in the ass over anything else. I got annoyed using it before I even finished the game.

There's also a complete lack of the puzzle element RE games are known for. Like none. I didn't understand that. 

Not a terrible game, but it's not that great either. I know people tend to love the Raid mode, but I haven't really touched it that much yet. As for the main story, this game is OK at best. Not a bad game, but also not a great RE either.

Resident Evil Revelations isn't a very interesting game. I've finished the game a few times, once on the original 3DS playthrough and once on the first home console port. It follows an episodic format, and it makes use of this to jump around the timeline of the game's plot with different characters and locations. This is an interesting technique, though it doesn't fit the game very well, and there's a strange dissonance associated with episodic cliffhangers and particularly 'previously on' scenes in a game you're experiencing most of it in one sitting. It worked slightly better in the sequel where the episodes were actually released individually. 

This is a survival horror game, though ammo and health is fairly plentiful thanks to a device (the 'Genesis') you're given that picks up freebies in the environment and gives you health for scanning enemies. Item boxes are back but they're mainly for swapping out weapons, and item management in this game is very superficial. It's not as if you need to make a decision between carrying a healing item, an extra weapon or ammo. 

The setting is fairly interesting - a luxury cruise ship called the Queen Zenobia, though we've had a ship as an outting before in RE Dead Aim and Gaiden. The gameplay as a whole feels very stale, and this is probably where Revelations falls hardest for me. It has puzzles and some backtracking which fans of classic survival horror (i.e. the original RE games) will cozy up to, but there's a lot of chapters which are extremely linear segments where the player simply shoots enemies. These action sequences are the weakest because of Revelations' unsatisfying combat. 

With the combat, most of the weapons aren't very fun to use; even shotguns and rifles fail to give that delectable headshot pop. Enemies are generally acquatic-themed, though none of them are especially fun to fight or terrifying. The game introduces a dodge mechanic, but it's unintuitive, unreliable for some people and usually unnecessary. The melee system seen in 5 was scaled back to just a single, chargeable melee attack for when enemies are stunned. It helps the game feel less like an arcade African adventure, but it does scale back on the enjoyment you could get with the previous system. 

The game is strongest when you're given time to explore some of the ship's admittedly beautiful environments. I overall do not recommend this game if you aren't already a fan of the series and must at least try it out of obligation. It's done much better in its sequel and the main series. If you'd like to try out horror-styled Resi games on Steam, try the remasters of the gamecube games.

[h1] Campaign and Core Gameplay[/h1]
The game's main campaign is fun to play and the story is interesting to keep you playing and figuring out the case of the Queen Zenobia. You get the returning characters of Chris and Jill while introducing new characters like Parker and Jessica.
I enjoyed the look of the enemies of being aquatic on the ship and familiar enemies on missions out of the ship.
You collect weapons and parts throughout the campaign to increase your arsenal and completing some challenges give exclusive weapons that will give you an edge on your enemies. It gets more difficult in the later stages and makes you learn what weaknesses to go through areas with ease.

[h1] Raid Mode [/h1]
Going through the episodes unlock missions for the next game mode, Raid Mode. Raid Mode can be played Solo or Co-op.
This is a replacement for Mercanaries mode where you go through the campaign's stages in a more linear way facing enemies and obtaining bonuses along the way. There are 3 different difficulty stages in total to increase more chance of rewards with challenge. You also have a Trinity bonus challenge to obtain if you beat the stage with No Damage, Lower Level, and Genocide objectives. You unlock more playable characters throughout other achievements you accomplish in Raid mode with have different stats with weapons which you pick your preferred character.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
It's a great deal to get this game on sale with the Complete Addition to get some starter weapons and DLC characters. I've enjoyed every minute of this game and hopefully you enjoy it too

Set on a ship that is swaying in the middle of the ocean named "Queen Zenobia", Jill Valentine tried to find the whereabouts of Chris Redfield who reportedly lost.  As we know Jill and Chris were formerly fellow members of S.T.A.R.S.  and is a survivor who survived the Raccoon City incident in 1998. When Jill arrived at the place where Chris was held captive.  It turned out that it was just a trap made by the Veltro organization and Jill was captured by them.

 GAMEPLAY:
 The gameplay is a blend of elements of survival horror and action.  As we know that Resident Evil 5 is the first game of the Resident Evil series that has an action genre, not a survival horror like the previous series and then resumed with Resident Evil 6. In the gameplay section Jill places more emphasis on survival horror elements, but in part  Chris emphasizes the elements of action.  I could say this is a perfect blend.  And this Resident Evil Revelation is also the first game in the Resident Evil series that can shoot while walking.  As we know in previous Resident Evil games like Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5 it can't run when we're shooting.  And this is a good step that Capcom made.  Also in Resident Evil Revelation this is the first game from the Resident Evil series where the gameplay can swim.  Also new features such as a tool called "Genesis" that is with this tool we can scan enemies and also be able to track the presence of hidden items such as ammunition, herbs, and so on.

 ENEMY :
 For enemies in this game unlike classic Zombies because of infections from T Virus like the classic Resident Evil game.  But here we have to fight new enemies of infection from the T Abyss virus, of course this makes the enemies of the Resident Evil series increase, in addition to classic Zombies, Lickers, Ganados, and so on.

 CONCLUSION:
 Resident Evil Revelation is one of the best (but not perfect) Resident Evil games to be played by fans of the Resident Evil series.  With interesting storyline, good gameplay, scary enemies, awesome graphics, and more.  A combination of survival horror elements with perfect action.  I say one of the Resident Evil games with the best horror elements, apart from the latest Capcom game, the Resident Evil 2 Remake which was just released last January.

 My value for this Resident Evil Revelation game is: 9.5 / 10.

RE: Revelations is a pretty well done game that, despite feeling a bit outdated (date of this review is March 2019), is still fun to play.

There isn't really much to say because there isn't much from the game that really stands out. It's a third person shooter with some horror elements, as a lot of other games in the RE franchise. But despite not bringing anything too new to the table, it's still a fun game that plays mostly well, apart from a few frustrations. You go around exploring the scenario in order to reach the next objective while fighting enemies on the way, finding ammo and custom parts for your guns on the way, besides a few new weapons occasionally. The custom parts are what keep the game fresh for the most part as they improve stats for each gun and sometimes also grant some special features like burst shots or ability to charge a shot.

I found the story to be a bit too convoluted as they tried to pull a lot of twists throughout the story, but I think for a game with "Revelations" in the name, that was to be expected and the story wraps up somewhat well by the end.

The voice acting is pretty bad, but it didn't really bother me for the most part, it's something that I got used to after a while.

Frustrations in the game mostly come with how bad the map is and sometimes you don't really know where to go or what to do, plus the first part of the game (exploring the ship) also feels way too confusing to explore. Some enemies can feel annoying when they're constantly dodging around and attacking you before you can react, plus dodging doesn't always work as intended.

I didn't play raid mode too much, just a few solo rounds to get a feel of it. It seems interesting although levels feel short, but it looks like something that could be fun to play with friends as you can play as different characters with different abilities, level up and purchase guns and custom parts that are actually very different from the ones obtained in the main game.

Recommended even at full price. It's not the greatest RE game, but it's a good one nonetheless.
