Resident Evil: Revelations is a survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom.
The game follows counter-terrorism agents Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield as they try to stop a bioterrorist organization from infecting the Earth's oceans with a virus. 

Gameplay is a mixture of old and new RE games in one.
It combines exploration, level design and survival from older games, with a modern touch of newer RE games such as improved camera, movement controls and combat.
 
Game is seperated into episodes, each includes a series of scenarios you will have to complete to progress. In most of them you will play as Jill aboard a ghost ship in the Mediterranean Sea, but from time to time you will step into boots of other characters in different locations. As you make your way through the ship, you will have to check every room for items, solve "puzzles" and fight with different types of enemies. Each character can carry 3 main weapons, plus set of grenades and a knife. Valentine can also upgrade her weapons, using parts collected while on her escapade. From simple ones like more damage or faster firerate, to increased crit chance or stun, most of the upgrades is helpful and combining them will depend from what weapon you use and your preference. 

Like in most of the RE games, you have a decent variety of firearms. From shotguns and pistols, to sub-machine guns and rifles. There is around 2/3 of them each, some of them have weaker base stats but more spots to upgrades, some are better from the start but have less places for upgrades so it's quite balanced. Beside that, you can carry herbs to heal yourself, and ammunition to each type of a weapon. To increase the amount of ammo you can carry, you will have to look for weapon cases.

One of the new features in the game is device called Genesis. Genesis is a scanner, which you will use to scan rooms for items and parts! You can also scan enemies, gather enough data to get a herb, and you can scan handprints. Handprints are basically ingame collectibles, that will unlock weapons if you will find enough of them. Oh and since this is RE game, beating a game and doing specific challenges, such as beating a game on specific difficulty, or without using herbs, will unlock new costumes and characters, which are always a good reason to play the game again. So game has a replayability. 
When it comes to levels, most of the areas is unlockable in a good old RE system of finding a key which is hold by the biggest enemy in area. Although often you will get a key thanks to story. Beside that, you will also have to defeat enemies in specific areas, get to a location in time, or fight a boss to progress. Objectives are simple indeed.

I've had few issues.
From the start, dodging mechanic. I guess it's because game was ported from 3DS and they had to somehow put those mechanics so they can work on PC, but I hate to shake my mouse like a moron when enemies grab me. Plus the dodging itself is based around proper timing rather than QTE system of RE 4/5, which I prefer personally. And because most of the locations (especially on ship) are quite tight, even dodging an attack can fail thanks to animation, as Jill might swiftly move pass the enemy to kiss a wall after which enemy can still catch you. 
Animation is especially weird with one specific boss fight, where to "dodge" Jill does a spin, often ending up being pushed by that enemy into a wall, but not taking any damage since you hit that right timing to "dodge". I'm not an expert, but if I still get pushed into a wall I didn't really dodge an attack, did I? 
Boss fights are lazy. You either have a bullet sponge boss fight or "shoot a spot" fight. Lack of variety and challenge.
Puzzles. Lack of them, and the one puzzle that is in the game is just bad. Game tries to fix that by putting a simple minigame which, while appreciated, is not enough. 
And something personal. After each episode game tries to shove this "Previously in RE: Revelations" thing like it's some sort of a TV show.
It's not needed since episodes are quite short so you can easily remember what is in them, plus story is not that complex as the game tries to sell it so I don't really see a point of that being in game. 

As for a Resident Evil game, voice acting was better than expected, which was quite shocking to me. It's still on level of "decent" though, but your ears won't bleed when listening to dialogues it so I count that as a good thing.
Rest of the audio, from enemies to soundtrack itself, was good! 

No issues with performance! 

Game features second gamemode called "Raid Mode". It's an action-oriented mode with rpg elements where you revisit locations from main game and need to complete them again. So you basically play a game again, but without cutscenes, as character you choose. Mode copies everything from main game, like collecting and upgrading weapons, and adds RPG elements such as level progressing and weapon rarity. You can play that mode solo or with a second player in coop! 
Overall concept of a mode is great, as I enjoyed upgrading my character, getting new weapons and playing with friends, but later on it becomes painfully grindy, and "difficulty" is just adding more waves of waves of enemies, making episodes really long, even longer than in main campaign! 

Solid campaign with good survial feeling, decent combat and emphasize on exploration plus grindy secondary mode put together make it for a interesting game that shows you can combine old and new. 7/10!

Pros:
- A very strong and atmospheric main setting, with Jill Valentine being aboard an abandoned cruise ship to discoever a new virus.
- A decent amount of weapons, enemy variety and weapon modification, with aiming similar to that of resident evil 4.

- Ran at a near consistent 60FPS on the highest settings with little to no bugs.

Cons:
- Most of the new characters, such as Parker and Jessica are very bland 
- Several times in the game you take control of another character away from the cruise ship. In these moments, you are given too much ammo and these bits simply don’t hold the same atmosphere as the cruise ship with Jill.
- An overall mundane and average story
- The bosses range from being gimmicks to bullet sponges.

Overall, a decent game that is worth playing, but does have a few flaws holding it down. Buy it while it’s on sale.

[h1] Experienced on the Oculus Rift with Vorpx; Xbox One Controller [/h1]

So this review will focus on playing this game in VR. I used Vorpx and an Xbox One Controller. I used the default settings from Vorpx and made zero changes to it. The default setting is not full VR, but instead an immersive 3D gameplay view, in other words, it looks like you're playing on a giant 3D screen. 

This setting can be changed, but in my opinion, the game is best played this way. The game ran smoothly for me. I experienced zero crashes or any major issues. The only minor issue is something common in 3D games ... the reflections (mostly water) don't translate well in VR. Luckily, this happens only a few times during the whole game.

My complete playthrough took a little over 13 hours. I did try the game for a little bit in Non-VR (on my desktop monitor) and the difference was very noticeable to me. I would not want to play this game outside of VR after having experienced it in 3D VR. The game just looks amazing in VR. You really get a sense of all the little details they put in the world and how well the characters are modeled. Jessica looks especially ravishing in 3D.

The experience reminded me a lot of The Wolf Among Us (using Vorpx), except it had less technical issues. I enjoyed the game a lot. I like the Resident Evil series, but I'm not a huge fan. The cinematic scenes are just really fun to watch in VR, even if the story can get a little hokey at times. Even the start up menu looks excellent with that eye looking at you. This is one of the best experiences I have had with Vorpx (after several disappointments).

[b]VR Rating 8/10. Yeah, it's not as good as native VR, but it still looks amazing and this game is better than most VR games out there. If you have a VR headset, you owe it to yourself to test out this experience in VR.[/b]

I absolutely love almost every single entry in the Resident Evil series and Revelations is no exception. When this game came out, I had been kind of bummed out by Resi 5, Resi 6, and Operation Raccoon City and this game was a MASSIVE breath of fresh air that I still absolutely adore today. I love that there are parts of the game that take away your weapons, I love looking for items with the scanner, and I love the episodic storytelling. And most importantly, it still looks fairly good despite being a port of a Nintendo 3DS game. They really pushed that tiny handheld to the max with this game and it shows. 

If anyone is curious what the game looks like on modern hardware, I've started uploading a new series for Revelations that you can check out on my Youtube channel:

Resident Evil Revelations is a game that really exceeds beyond what you'd expect from a port of a 3DS game. The story is pretty good, the setting and atmosphere are really great, and the gameplay is surprisingly fluid and challenging with a 5-star upgrading system to boot. 

The new enemies you fight come in a variety of interesting forms that really makes you think on your feet with each encounter. Also the boss battles you face are really creative and intense with no one boss fight being too similar to the last.

The environment is also probably one of my favorite in the Resident Evil series. The cruise ship creaks, rolls, and rain plasters the windows as the game goes by. The ambient sounds really set the tone and the music score, although nothing to write home about, still manages to work well for the game.

If there was anything I could say negatively about the game would be the segments of the game that take place outside of the ship. Although those segments aren't exactly terrible, in comparison to the ship segments they really stand out like a sore thumb in terms of quality.

Overall i'd rate this game a 7.5/10. Though I sing praise about this game, it's quality is obviously that of a portable game for sure. Still 100% worth the asking price on Steam.

This was the first RE game I enjoyed since RE4, and I enjoyed it quite a lot, which was a very pleasant surprise after how much I loathed RE6. Revelations smoothed out the few rough spots of RE4 such as being able to move while aiming, while not completely screwing everything else up like other RE sequels. Aside from the short campaign, somewhat bland personality compared to RE4's wackiness, and the overly streamlined/eliminated inventory system, it's basically everything I wanted since RE 4 came out all those years ago, plus more thanks to the addition of Raid Mode. It would have been nice if Raid Mode didn't simply recycle the already minimal amount of ground the campaign covered, and it could have been better balanced in terms of how some challenges go from nightmarishly difficult alone to a total cakewalk with a partner, but it's still an excellent addition to the package.

Overall, I'd recommend it to any fan of Resident Evil or third person shooting, and especially anybody who felt RE peaked at 4 and has been disppointed ever since - with one big caveat. The latest console versions have a bit more content that this version lacks and shows no signs of ever getting. So if you want the most complete experience, this isn't the version to get, unfortunately. Which is extra frustrating since this is the version that offers the best possible aiming thanks to mouse and keyboard support, so there's really no perfect version. Not to mention that it's a bit insulting that Capcom can't be bothered to give us PC players the same updates other versions got, despite being fine with taking our money. But I guess I shouldn't be surprised at devs punishing people for buying a game sooner than later, that's par for the course these days. It always pays to wait.

Anyway, mostly this is a great game, but I can't truly fully recommend this specific version until it gets all the content other versions have, so I'm giving it a thumbs down for that reason alone until there's an update.

Resident Evil Revelations / Biohazard Revelations is a low grade unpolished zombie shooter based on the Resident Evil series. It tells of the time before Resident Evil. This was released in 2013. The objective is to get whatever character you're playing to solve the mystery of Teragrigia, Queen Dido, Queen Zenobia, Queen Semiramis and the T-virus Abyss

Gameplay-wise, it's 3rd person view. Press C to use the Bio Scanner. Right Click to aim, Left Click to shoot. G for grenade. You have handguns, rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles and rocket launchers, the standard items. 

Monsters come in standard shambling zombies, frogmen, blade zombies, spike shooters, huge saw arms, zombie fish, mouth full of teeth fish. There are a few boss monsters which are more interesting to play against.

Conclusion, Resident Evil Revelations / Biohazard Revelations is unpolished. It was hastily done with little polish. You can see it in the design of the decor, the scanner doing nothing but scanning dead bodies, etc. If this was done back in the 90's, it would still be acceptable. However, standards have been raised. This is more of a RE spinoff used to get money.

Resident Evil Revelations is a sorta-survival-horror/action game. Came out after RE5, takes place between RE4 and RE5. Plot is stand-alone. It was released as 3DS exclusive at first, before being ported to consoles and Steam, enhanced up.

And well, not really feeling like writing it out this time. Only going to say that it's like modern (pre-RE7) gameplay style. But it's not focused on melee or crowds, so you get to stun enemies into melee-able state on heavy damage. It also has a partner in main campaign, despite not having coop there. They are near useless, devs played too safe there. No one attack them and they deliver minimal damage. But this time you also can modify your weapons with parts that you find. I mean, modify stats a bit, putting modifiers into slots.

You also explore stages a bit more by itself. It's more linear than old RE but it still got something going. Such as puzzle minigame that devs quickly forget that it exists. You find ammo and stuff. You also still don't manually apply any items. There is now a scanning mechanic, which feels like a random gimmick. Rooms have items hidden in random spots without any reasoning, so at times you pull it out and look around the room. Not sure what's fun in this, but it does occupy me for a bit. And then you can scan enemies and after few scans you get a free heal. That is more interesting, you often have to scan enemies before they die.

Resident Evil Revelations is another Capcom cut-off game because of development cycle. It is one of the two shortest Resident Evil games along with Resident Evil 3 Remade (both 8 hours or less). As a result, it doesn’t keep consistently good quality and the story doesn’t do much justice to the largest cast of characters (even more than Resident Evil 6) in the series. But at the end of the day, the experience is not bad.

Unlike its action-packed predecessor Resident Evil 5, it goes back to the series root to be a horror game. The beginning that sets in the dark cabin has one of the best horror atmospheres in the series. There is something about the claustrophobic environment that makes it genuinely unsettling and scary, but as the environment opens up, the atmosphere doesn’t quite keep up. Some scenes here and there still feel scary, yet most of them fall flat and aren’t quite as good as the beginning.

Different from Resident Evil 5 copying Resident Evil 4’s control system, the control got revamped this time. It is the first Resident Evil game that you can shoot while walking, but it remains a fair amount of sluggishness. You can view it either as a good thing if you like the tension from the tank control, or as a bad thing simply since it is sluggish. The shooting, however, is problematic, probably because it is originally a 3DS game. It is inaccurate and feels off, as you can feel there is a force pulling your crosshair. I turned the assistant aiming off (default is on) so it is less being dragged and more acceptable yet shooting still feels stiff and inaccurate.

As for level design, it doesn’t have a consistent difficulty. Some levels are very brutal even at easy difficulty, particularly in where you first meet the chainsaw dude. It is not a good experience to get into the awkward situation of running out of ammo very soon but still having hordes of enemies chasing your butt who don’t go down easily.

For the story, it is okay, however, there is no necessity to have such a large cast of characters, since some characters feel very redundant (such as Keith and Quint) that don't really do much to the story. Keith and Quint's session has a very abrupt, inconsistent story tone to fit their characters. It is not good for storytelling either, for switching between four narrators. I suspect Capcom originally had a bigger plan for the characters (but got cut off midway). Anyway, I would prefer a more compact story, and I wonder if Capcom will ever do anything more to these characters since the ending is kind of a cliffhanger.

If you're an older gamer with only a little time to play, this is a great pick.

Resident Evil Revelations is a pretty enjoyable game to be honest!

I played this game on normal difficulty and got through the campaign in about 8 hours.
Besides the campaign, you get a second mode called Raid Mode, which was surprisingly enjoyable too, but I'll start with the campaign (No Story Spoilers):

Graphical Options are fine. The game looks good for a 3DS port (Not so good, when you are outside and it's bright, but that's rare!). But you can't choose Ultra HD Resolution, which was a bummer, but let's be real, it's a 3DS port and Full HD looks fine :)
Controls are full customizable and the game has Gamepad support.
So let's begin!

In the campaign, you mostly play as Jill, but there are many other characters and depending, which chaper you are in it, you play another one. I believe, you can play as 4 different characters in the Main campaign.
You are ALWAYS accompanied with another, AI controlled person, which I personally didn't like, because I like to be alone in Horror Games most of the time, but that's just me. Your Partner never get's in your way, but to be honest, doesn't do much other than talk with you, giving you directions in some cases and shoots Enemies (But deals almost no damage!)
It's not like in RE5 or RE6, where your Partner plays a huge role, here he or she is just there, because. 
The game could live well without a partner on your side the whole time, in my opinion.

Overall I loved the atmosphere. 80% of the game, you are inside a Ship, walking through claustrophobic corridoors, machinery quarters and also quest or even entertainment quarters. There is a healthy variety to explore. The whole ship is also completly open to explore, after you've been through 1/4 of the game.
That means, there is also some backtracking involved, and even side objectives, but the game always gives you one direction to go to conplete the main objective. It's up to you, to follow it and complete the chapter to carry on, or take a break and explore the ship.
The Game also has you swimming and diving in some parts, which I thought was pretty cool, because the controls work fine under water, so no problems here.

Combat works like in Dead Space, it's third person, but you can move while aiming. I never had a Problem with the controls, they were super smooth and aiming in tense Situations was perfectly doable. I never felt out of control.
My only criticism has to be with the dodging. Maybe, I'm just bad at it, but sometimes it just didn't work, so I rarely used it in my playtrough, because it felt unreliable. To explain it, you have to press W or the "Walk forward" button right as an enemy wants to hit you. Sometimes my character just didn't want to dodge, but like I said, maybe I was just bad.
There is one situation in the game, where dodging was really important, and I had a bit of difficulties with it.

You got your typical weapon sortiment: Pistol, Shotgun, Machine Gun, Sniper, Magnum. So nothing special here, if you've played a Residen Evil Game before.
You are also able to customize your weapons with extra damage, bigger magazines or a special weapon class ability, etc.
Throughout the game, you finde customization parts and rare parts, if you pay attention and look around.
But how it works, you pick your 3 weapons of choice and put all your best Parts into it (You can unequipp your parts without loosing them or paying something). Nothing too deep to consider here :)

Ammunition on normal dificulty was always almost available for me. I killed every Monster I encountered and rarely was out of ammo. You CAN however get out of ammo if you are lazy to search for it!!
There is a Game Mechanic involcing a Scanner. In almost every room, you can find hidden Items and/or Ammunition or even collectibles. You can only see them, if you use the Scanner. If you use it frequently, you won't get Out of Ammo. It you ignore the Scanner, you can get out of ammo pretty fast.
You can also Scan Monsters to get Healing Items.

Your Enemies in this game are bloated humanoid "Zombies" I guess (They called them Zombies in the game). Their actual name is "Ooze", because they are slimey and oozy :)
If you've played the most recent Resident Evil 7, they reminded me heavily on the "Molded" with how they moved.
You get many varieties of Enemies, most of them look a bit samey, but each variation has their own special abilities, like projectiles, armored bodyparts, stronger attacks, etc.
There are also other enemy types in some chapters, but mostly encountered in those specific chapters.
No enemy was really a huge problem, except the Hunter (That Frog/Lizard like monster you've seen in other RE Games). They come in huge numbers and are fast, so if you have a slow weapon, you're kinda screwed.

I don't want to say too much about the Boss Fights in this game. 
They are all enjoyable and some are even pretty difficult to be honest, even on normal difficulty! 
I'm talkiing about the first Boss especially. The developers tried to recreate the First Chainsaw Fight in RE4 and I think they accomplished to recreate that feeling at least. But he was definately the hardest boss for me and from what i've heard from other people. It was tense and kept you on your toes. Still enjoyable!

After 8 Hours, you will be done with the Campaign. You've now unlocked all Levels for Raid Mode (You unlock them throughout the Campaign)

Raid Mode is surprisingly enjoyable!
You replay all the different Scenarios from the Campaign, but with different enemy locations and different variations special to the Raid Mode, they are the same enemies, but some are faster, stronger or get more health. They also vary in their height and I think I even encountered a Mini Boss variant of a normal enemy (It was like an enemy with a name)
A name you ask? Yes, and every enemy has a healthbar over it's head now, like in an RPG Shooter. You can also level your character up, your weapons have different levels and deal more damage, the higher it's level is. 
You can find rare and epic weapons with special abilities and customize them.
You can choose between all characters from the Campaign and also the non playable ones. Each character has it's own perks, like being better with pistols, or shotguns, or auto health regeneration etc.

So the goal of the Raid Mode is to level up your character to proceed the Stages, in which you find more and more difficult enemies, the further you get. There are 21 different Stages to complete. For each completed stage, you get BP. With BP you can buy new weapons, customize-parts, ammonition etc.
You get a special reward if you complete a stage without getting hit or killing all the enemies in one stage.
In each stage, your goal is to simply reach the end, like in a mini dungeon. You kill enemies and find loot. All the loot you find isn't stage specific. What I mean with that is, you use it for every stage. There is no ammo pool for one specific stage. You've got a Inventory with contains all your loot and ammo and that's what you have when you enter a new Stage.
So you have to be economic if you don't want to spend all your BP just on ammo each time.

Overall a really well done Mode, which I didn't expect I would have so much fun with.

So thats Resident Evil Revelations for you! I hope, I could help you getting a better picture of what you can expect from the game :)
It's totally worth the price and one of the better Resident Evil Games out there!

Overall I am a little bit torn. The gameplay itself was fine. The controls, as expected, very fiddly and hard to master.

This game originally came out for the 3DS back in 2012. Back then it was an amazing technical achievement. Obviously now, on a high-end (or even a low-end) PC, those graphics are not quite as superb. That said, they still hold up remarkably well.

Revelations is a weird RE side story. The game takes place in 2005, shortly before the events of Resident Evil 5. You follow S.T.A.R.S. veterans, Jill Valentine and Chris Refield, as they attempt to solve the mystery reoccurence of a terrorist organisation called Veltro. A year prior, this organization was responsible for destroying a floating city in the Mediterranean known as Terragrigia. The main weapon this time is the T-Abyss virus, a water-soluble form of the T-virus, capable of rapidly infected anything that even touches contaminated water. The story is both simple and extremely convoluted (so, standard RE fare). The voice cast is pretty top notch, but the physical acting of the characters is often over the top, which adds to the cheese of the game. Along with Chris and Jill, you will occasionally switch between four other throwaway characters as the story is told out of order. 

The game features 12 levels referred to as Episodes. They even have their own recap when moving between levels, which is weird since the game was not episodic. Each episode has between two and three stages to it. These stages are uneven in their pacing. Some stages have you cover twenty minutes or more of back tracking and monster dodging / killing, whereas others are little more than hall walking simulators. You get graded on each stage too, meaning that there are some stages that you would have to work at it to avoid getting an "S" ranking. 

All that said, the gameplay in general is very good. The characters are as responsive as they were in Resident Evil 5, and bosses offer up a variety of challenges. Things aren't completely perfect, though. Running is determined solely by left stick pressure rather than left stick + A, so there will be many moments when dodging a tough enemy, where it feels like you are just barely getting out of the way. Dodging is equally unintuitive. I pulled off most of my dodges on accident. Weapon variety is good and will leave you feeling plenty powerful through most of the game (though rarely too powerful). Enemy variety is equally interesting. The game does not feature zombies, but instead has what are called the ooze. Their form is reminiscent of the molded from RE7 (indeed, the molded may even be considered a callback to RE: Revelations). The majority of the game takes place on a cruise ship, which is a nice change of pace. Water plays a huge part in the game and there will be multiple moments where you have to swim around underwater. This is kind of a pain, but isn't overly terrible since there are not too many enemy encounters underwater. 

Game pacing is a tad strange. There is at least one point in the game that feels like the end, only to discover that the game continues for another couple of levels. As such, it can make the relatively short game (my initial run was 11 hours) feel like it's dragging.

Lastly, the game features a Raid Mode game, which is basically a dolled up version of Mercenaries. As with Mercenaries, Raid Mode greatly increases the replayability of the game, allowing players to earn new weapons and costumes for speedy and efficient runs. 

All in all, RE: Revelations was a nice surprise back in 2012, and it still largely holds up. While the story may not be that entertaining, the gameplay makes up for it. A worthy purchase during a Steam sale.

[h1]Resident Evil Revelations's handheld roots don't hold it back one bit[/h1]

[i]They were posed with a question. How do you break up a game like Resident Evil to make it work and feel like a full fat RE game. But make it easy to commit the time to play it on the go or portably?[/i]
Their answer was arguably a brilliant one that works very well as a portable game and still holds up just as well if you play it on modern consoles or PC sequentially.
Keep the standard chapter structure introduced in RE4, but break each one into smaller chunks. Introduce quick segments each time you restart and at the end of each to recap the story so far, and set up the next episode.

What's also interesting is the fact this was released the same year as Resident Evil 6, developed separately and in the transition to better 3rd person contols they each went in different directions. (While also offering classic'ish controls)
I am of the opinon that Revelations executed it's control changes far better, and the game plays better as a result. Overall the game itself is executed better. It's not as ambitious as RE6, but it doesn't falter because of it either.
Some have said RERev is more like Classic Evil games than RE6, and in some areas this is true. But overall, it's still just as much as action focused while achieving better balance and not removing key elements of the series or making them almost entirely optional.[spoiler]Having to hunt for tedious collectible medallions while the game is trying to keep the pacing tight. This really detracts from the immersion it's trying to create with the story, keeping key character,world and story information segregated from the main game where it should naturally be part of the flow of the game as in past RE games. With readable notes and documents you discover. RE5 had separate files that simply unlocked as you progressed through the game. But it still had lots of in game documents to read as you went that keep the most important stuff in-game.[/spoiler]

The PC Port is overall very good with some unfortunate design decisions and limitations that limit the game's potential to be enjoyed in the future.
And the game looks gorgeous with the only real downfalls being massive banding that was dithered on the 3DS,low bloom resolution, needing higher resolution textures and maybe some geometry improvements.

Not as polished as Revelations 2 (for obvious reasons) but still an enjoyable game with a creepy setting.  Some of the bosses (one in particular) can be a pain to defeat but even today, this game still holds up as an enjoyable entry into the Resident Evil franchise.  It has its flaws to be certain, but nothing we haven't seen in this series before.

Despite what the title might imply, Resident Evil Revelations doesn't provide any grand perspective on the series as a whole, but rather takes its place as a spinoff side story to the franchise.  It uses the same shooter style controls of Resident Evil 6 (although Revelations came out first).  Almost the entire game takes place on board a derelict cruise ship called the Queen Zenobia, with multiple teams of characters investigating the resurgence of a terrorist group responsible for a massive bio-terror incident a year prior.

The story itself is very cheesy and over the top, but I feel like that's par for the course when it comes to Resident Evil.  The game is full of plot twists and dramatic cliffhangers at the end of each episode.  The tight pacing does make it a fun ride, and if you go into it knowing that it's going to have its fair share of corniness, you'll enjoy yourself.  It's like a silly broadcast television show.  It won't change your life, but for all its stupidity it still ends up being a fun time.

As I said before, it uses the same shooter controls that Resident Evil 6 does.  And in a strange twist, the added mobility actually makes the game feel less tight at times.  In RE 4 and 5, the game was clearly designed AROUND your limited movement, making each fight feel tough, but fair.  At times, Revelations pulls out the cheap "spawn at least six bad guys at once" and watches as you struggle to manuever your way around them.  It doesn't happen often, but when it does it can be frustrating.

Another complaint I had was with the Genesis gun.  This device allows you to scan enemies and objects, allowing you to find hidden caches of ammo and supplies.  But that's literally all it does.  The only pupose scanning enemies has is to fill up a percentage in order to earn a healing item.  It feels like a missed opportunity to provide some background info on enemies and how to beat them, especially when some of the bosses are really vague when it comes to having special weak points or not.

Overall, Resident Evil Revelations isn't a standout title in the franchise.  But if you're looking for more RE action and this one is on sale, you could do worse.

Considering its a more "streamlined" experience then the other Resident Evil games I've played, I actually rather enjoyed Revelations. Calling it survival horror is something of an exaggeration, but the term hasn't meant anything in years anyway. I maintain that the "horror" of the early games was the shoddy controls and jump scares. It certainly wasn't the writing. Regardless, Revelations manages to have a sense of tension that is absent from many of the numbered games post-RE 4.

At the same time, I've gained an apreciation for the series over time. The over-done tacticool suits, the nasty guns, the disgusting mutant enemies, the satisfaction whenever you turn up so much as a box of handgun rounds or a single herb. I  also enjoy its efforts to construct a sort of "strangereal" universe, a world that is sort of like ours but different, with a story of an ongoing struggle between elite agents of a global anti-bioterrorism force and increasingly deranged villains with increasingly flimsy justificiations for releasing mutagenic plagues ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ everywhere. It's silly, but they're trying. Harder then they try with Devil May Cry, anyway. Or Megaman. Or pretty much any other Capcom property. Nice going there, guys.

Revelations plays like a diet version of RE 4. Its lacking the ridiculous action-movie presentation of 5 and 6, and also the campaign coop that made those games more enjoyable, though there is a seperate online "raid" mode I haven't yet tried, as there aren't many people playing it at this point. Gone is the obnoxious money-based upgrade system of 4. Here, you need only ferret out upgrade parts which can be equipped and unequipped from your guns at any of the conveniently placed weapon storage boxes. There's no grid-based inventory either- you can carry three guns and a limited quantity of ammo for each, but you can expand that by finding ammo cases. You can also carry up to five green herbs, which here function like first aid sprays, healing you to full. 

The episodic structure means gameplay is spread neatly into compartmentilized chapters like the old days. The load times are very fast and the game runs quite smoothly, though considering it was a 3DS game, anything less would be absurd. Aiming and shooting feel pretty good, considering this is the first Resident Evil I've played on PC. I never quite got the hang of the dodge mechanic, but that's par for the course in my case. If nothing else, its a more competent PC port then I'd expect from Capcom after Lost Planet 2 or Dead Rising 3.

Series regulars will definately want to check out Revelations. Aside from that, if you like third-person shooters, "survival horror" games or anything with gross enemies and even vaguely creepy atmosphere, Revelations is worth checking out, especially at its typically low sale price.

Resident Evil Revelations is an attempt to blend the action of Resident Evil 4/5/6 with the claustrophobic areas of Resident Evil 1/2/3.

As such, the game is tonally all over the place. About two thirds of the campaign have you playing as Jill Valentine, now a BSAA agent, the S.T.A.R.S. officer from Resident Evils 1 and 3, and at first these are ambiguously creepy, with dimly lit, cramped corridors, and flickering lights, but towards the end, these levels lose sight of that survival horror vision slightly, with timed escapes and gatling gun boss fights. That said, the final chapter returns a little to the survival horror of the earlier chapters. The game is a bizarre mix of different Resi styles here: tank controls are gone, but there are also fewsections on a par with the tense action in Resident Evil 4, and backtracking and tight geography are both brought in from the earlier Resi games. It doesn't work as well as it could have, but the level design and enemies do enough to create a tense atmosphere early on, and when Jill's sections decide to dial up the action, the Queen Zenobia is populated by enough varied enemies to stay interesting and fun. The game succeeds in its aims here.

The other third of the game sees you take control of several side characters, including Chris Redfield, and these sections are far more focused on action than Jill's. While enjoyable enough, Jill's side of the game is superior to this often dull gameplay. The problem is the game isn't built as a pure action title, unlike Resident Evil 6, which delivers no shortage of exciting action, and the action sections highlight this. Jill's story works when it introduces action due to the tension of its limited ammo and its enemies, this portion of the game hands out ammo in an attempt to make shooting fun and throws hunter after hunter at you. with more enemies, it could have been much better, though Jill's side of things makes up for this dreary side-game.

The highlight of the game is its enemies. It opens with some blobs on a beach, and overrelies on zombie dogs and hunters in some sections, yes, but every other enemy is inspired. The main enemies Jill faces are the Ooze, grey, faceless abominations that limp around due to their twisted physiology, and these are later joined by Scarmiglione and Scagdead, as well as a number of disfigured bosses. The final boss in particular is a joy to fight.

Revelations also introduced the Raid Mode, a series of action-oriented levels with RPG elements. Thankfully, these often take after Jill's campaign, with limited ammo and a variety of deep sea terrors to face. It's a blast.

Revelations is worth your time in the sale, a good game, if very flawed, with a well realised location and incredibly designed enemies, let down by some weak shooter sections.

The episodic format used since RE4 returns, though it has a different purpose here, being used to swap perspectives and dispense story cutscenes at pivotal moments in the plot, rather than just cutting the action into even chunks.  However, the online co-op gameplay introduced in RE5 has been dropped, which greatly benefits the game's environments and pacing.

RE:R makes several efforts to return the series to the survival horror genre.  The physical combat and character movement speed have been dramatically reduced back to pre-RE4 levels, which forces you to think about your placement in combat scenarios and use your weapons rather than dash and punch everywhere.  Even normal enemies can be threatening if you're in a tight corridor and don't have the right weapon/ammo.  The inventory system is pretty streamlined, such that you can carry only 3 weapons at once, but all key items and all types of ammo, with a limit on the amount of each type of ammo you can carry, and a limit of 5 restoratives, which are all full heals.  The environments are also much less linear, with locked doors and many optional hidden items and weapons which makes exploration rewarding.  Flavor text describing examined environmental objects also returns, which is a wonderful series throwback that adds a little more immersion to the experience.

As for what doesn't work, RE:R adds a Metroid Prime-esque scanning feature to scan enemies for additional restoratives and environments for additional miscellaneous items and occasional plot advancement.  This was probably a feature designed to work with the initial 3DS launch, but here it's really clunky and out of place.  There are rarely any indications on where scanning would be beneficial, so you are encouraged to just pull the scanner out every few steps and check again, which is tedious and immersion-breaking.  This mechanic could have been a good opportunity to get players looking down the scanning scope too often with surprise enemies/scares, but the game never takes advantage of this.  Thankfully, the scanner is required only rarely to advance, so you can choose to mostly ignore it.  The excessive items it gives you also tends to make the game a lot easier than necessary.  There's also dodge commands and melee finishing moves that are kinda finicky and unnecessary, but those are less obtrusive.

RE:R is probably the first Resident Evil since 4 I can simply recommend as a solid good game instead of a mixed bag with some good in it.  Check it out if you like classic Resident Evil, it doesn't quite make it all the way there, but it's pretty close.

They apply boost to the gun only if it has any avalible slots to add said upgrades. Some guns have 5 slots while others may have 3 or 6. Each part has a number tied to it, the higher the number the more boost the gun gets.

      A new mode called raid mode. Raid mode plays like a basic kill all enemies and get to the finish line game mode. It is available in co-op and has rpg mechanics. Through playing the player gets exp that levels up their level rank. The higher level the player is the higher level weapons they will find in the stores or better chance of beating a stage. This mode is not entirely stressing survival since guns can be bought from the in game store with BP, resident evil currency gain through gameplay of either raid or the campaign. Not to mention the player can always restock on ammo and herbs from the store between selected missions. 

Con:
      The story teeters between boring and being a chore. The story is boring because of how uninteresting the plot is and at the end there is no real conclusion. It is not nearly as in depth as other resident evil games like the original where the motives of the main villian is clear at the end. The story also becomes a chore when playing as a totally new character without any equipment or ability to upgrade their guns makes playing these segments a pain to deal with. Especially when something really interesting happens to one set of characters and when this rising action of the plot is here it takes a long time to get back to it because it is time to play as another set of characters you dont want to play as. Not because they are bad characters but because I rather be playing as Jill than those two dudes in the snow storm. They are great characters with loads of good communication but being locked in these segments with no choice of my arsenal really bogs down the pacing and the thrill.

       Enemies are a huge disappointment. The enemies look really interesting and borderline cool but the issue is their weakpoints are visually hidden. The early enmies you face apparently the weak point for them is its arm. Shooting them with enough damage in the arm will cause them to be stunned so the player can perform a melee attack. Basic knowledge of how enemies work from other games like resident evil 4 or 1 is always aim for the head. Basic weak point but never in this game.

       Wow a new mechanic lets force it down the players throats. The new mechanic is the ability to dodge an incomming enemy attack. That is really cool but it is technically very flawed. The main issue is the way to dodge is not entirely clear as to how to preform it. There is a tutorial early on in the game but what is the issue is that the dodge sometimes works when it wants to. Many times I tried to dodge either for practice or survival in a tense situation and it would refuse to give me any leway in unfortunantly I end up taking the hit. The mechanic is very flawed and yet they focus the whole game around it. They intentally limit the ammo that can be found throughout the game to make the player focus on using the dodging which was a horrible move on the developers part. None of the other games had dodging other than resident evil 4 with it's button prompts mainly on boss related enemies. I understand that resident evil is very much a survival horror game but revolving the game over a mechanic that is very fickle is lazy and all around bad game design.

        Previously on revelations. Get use to that small sentece there because the game very much enjoys saying it and recaping the story even though you did not turn off the game and just experienced said moments. I get the idea that they were trying to go for but ultimately an odd design choice. If it exist to recap moments for a player that turned off the game then it makes sense but the recap happens after every chapter.

       infernal mode is awful. What infernal mode does is that it adds more enemies and changes the damage modifies. Lazy work there developers and again it is designed to focus on the mechanic of dodging so you know that this is going to be a huge flawed design for a difficulty. It would help in the the secret unlockables ment much in making the harder difficulties more reasonable but that is not the case. What is the main focus is on weapon parts and how well one can dodge. 

Conclusion:
         This game was very interesting at first glimps. It had very nice close quarter combat on the ship and an interesting plot but then shifts focus. It is like trying to teach a child with ADD. Not to mention the bs designs like invisible laser trap maze because that is fair or how about hunters that are invisible and are very good at dodging. It is not fair designs in the game and breaks the game's flow. There is so much bad with the game but the one part that really connects it all together is the horrible dodge mechanic. It is way to unpredictable to be remotely a reliable thing to do in the game let alone make it the main focus of how the game is going to be structured around. Needless to say if those who read the review and are not sure what i think about the game, let me say I think this game is bad and dont reccomend it at all.

Paul Eiding, the voice of Metal Gear Solid's Colonel Campbell, plays Clive R. O'Brian and he's awesome in anything he's in. Clive O'Brian is pretty much the same character as Colonel Campbell as well so I really enjoyed his character. Having owned this product on DS and Xbox360 i feel confident enough to review it here with my current play time. I have probably 50+ hours invested and simply needed to test out the controls. 

This is one of the better RE titles in recent years. Up until RE7 fans of the atmosphere in older RE games were kind of left out in the cold. So the setting, the pacing and the distribution of ammo were all very welcomed by the oldschool community when this game released. It was very much the first sign that survival horror just might come home to stay this time! Since RE6 had happened just weeks before... let's not go there... 

Graphically the game is passable. Nothing special here but this was a hand held title at one point so keep that in mind. Regardless of the aesthetics, the atmosphere shines! 

The sound is fantastic as usual. RE has always been known to have great sound, from the bloops and beeps of the menus, to the sound of enemies lurching near. The music is always top notch with this series so it goes without saying that it's AAA stuff. The main theme has a creepy, yet classy, almost regal tone to it to reflect the setting that most of the action plays out in. 

Controls are a bit iffy for PC players. I'm not a fan of aiming with the mouse in this game at all. It feels floaty and just isn't responsive. Not sure if this was a design decision to increase tension but it doesn't work with a PC players mentallity. You can't handicap our aim, you just can't. The controller works as you would expect and i honestly prefer it with this game... yes... i know... i mean this is kind of a shooter after all, not in the traditional sense but you get my point i'm sure. So a controller is NOT on the top of my list of prefered methods to get my game on. 

The story is pretty decent, but i mean this is RE, you're here to love the characters more than the story because you already love Jill, but you need to meet Jessica lol. But seriously, the characters in these games are always entertaining and the story is servicable. 

The gameplay is well balanced, it does feel like you move way too slow, but you adjust to it. It's just because you're most likely used to twitch style shooters and faster paced games, they take it down a notch here to ramp up on the fear, and it does work. It just takes some time to begin to work it's magic on you, but once you get an enemy behind you, breathing all freaky like and sh@# you will understand why your sprint is more like a crawl. Pacing is well done with action sequences broken up very well by exploration and puzzle solving? can you call it that? Idk... but stuff is in your way and you get it out of your way and proceed. Bosses are fun, sometimes frustrating especially on higher difficulties! 

All in all, as RE games go i would say this is one of the best in the latter installments (post RE4 era) but we would have to wait for RE7 to truly bring back that oldschool formula, albiet in first person. Still... as oldschool RE fans we take what we can get.

[h1]Short version: 85%[/h1]
Revelations is a great mix of classic survival horror atmosphere and modern third-person shooter gunplay, combining the best of both worlds with only a handful of the drawbacks. As a bonus, it also has a strangely addictive additional looter game mode.

[h1]Long version:[/h1]
Resident Evil: Revelations was the game many older RE fans dreamed of, where the classic survival horror aspects of the early games meet the modern, user-friendly mechanics of the later ones.

The level design is an obvious callback to the early Resident Evils. Not only this is the third RE game placed on a ship, but also it manages to evoke the old RE1 atmosphere with some posh, spacious rooms and many narrow corridors with their infinite possibilities of running into a blind corner.
The controls are a variation of the third-person shooter style from RE5, but simplified to fit Revelation’s handheld roots. On PC, it is fast, responsive, and easy to learn, but it has some tricky mechanics (like dodges), which may be difficult to master.

The quintessential RE experience is not complete without some low-grade writing, and this is where RER1 went all-out. The conspiracy-ridden plot, goofy characters, and especially the cheesy dialogue and hammy acting create a perfect B-movie feeling, even if some may feel it too stupid sometimes.

Like in most old RE games, the campaign is short (3-7 hours), even if it offers some good replay value with a challenging difficulty option and a nice weapon upgrade system (where you have to search for additional parts instead of using a store).
Still, this would have not been enough for that final score, and this is where Raid mode comes up. It is an additional game mode, replacing Mercenaries, where the goal is to complete small combat stages for experience, money, and random loot drops. It is practically a Diablo/Borderlands style looter minigame with some addictive mechanics, offering dozens/hundreds of hours of additional fun (and quite some mindless grinding towards the end).
Gameplay is fluid. Zombies look like crap though; couldn't get past how silly they looked.

I will evaluate the game under 6 criteria: Story, Graphics, Optimization, Gameplay, Game lifespan and Sounds/Soundtracks.

[list]
    [*][h1]Story[/h1]
The story of RE Revelations is located between RE4 and RE5. The main protagonists are Jill Valentine and Chris Redfield. A terrorist organization called Veltro has deployed a new virus and your job is to stop and Veltro and the virus propagation. Let's say it right now: the story is weak. They tried to add some suspense with an episodic scheme but it does not really work and you won't really care about what is happening or the characters themselves. Some of them even seem to have been designed to be used once anyway and are completely uninteresting. The "aquatic" ambiance is however kind of refreshing, but doesn't add anything really consistent to the story apart new monsters designs.

[b]Story score: 11/20[/b]

    [*][h1]Graphics[/h1]
It's a port from the 3DS. They revamped some textures but a lot of them looks like they come directly from the PS2. However, the 3D models are generally well done and their animations too ( for a  3DS port ) and the lighting is nicely used. It's far to be "Crysis 3 level" however it's watchable. The level design is very closed and "corridor based", telling you clearly you have to go from point A to B; if you are kind of clostrauphobic, this game is not really for you :-p ^_^.

[b]Graphics score: 14/20[/b]

    [*][h1]Optimization[/h1]
The game will run pretty well on a 5/6 years old hardware PC. On my laptop ( i7-4600 with a radeon 8500HD ), it runs rarely below 60 fps. The game is slightly buggy though, and if I never had any return on windows, I'm however constantly obliged to edit the ini configuration file to launch it, first on windows mode, then I pass on fullscreen via the game menu. I have never find a solution for this issue. I also had the same problem with Resident Evil Remaster HD. Guess it must affect the laptops with dual GPUs ( and with AMDs discrete ones ? ).

[b]Optimization score: 13/20[/b]

    [*][h1]Gameplay[/h1]
And there, you hit the first real force of the game. It's a real pleasure. In campaign mode, the aspect search/exploration is reinforced by the genesis ( a kind of environmental analyzer ). The weapons customization is back ( they dropped it in RE6 ) and is nicely thought. The characters are perfectly responsive and the implicit QTE for avoiding enemy damage is a very good addition by the devs. You cannot handle more than three main weapons and the ammo is kind of limited, but it is really not a problem when you know how to use the melee attack.

[b]Gameplay score: 17/20[/b]

    [*][h1]Game lifespan[/h1]
Another force of the game. The campaign mode won't really last more than 6 to 8 hours. You can try the higher difficulty levels for a challenge ( the hell mode is really not a piece of cake ). The real time monger will be the "Raid" mode, where you will spend a lot of your sessions, especially if you have a friend to play with ( the campaign is solo only ) and if you like achievements. The DLCs are more cosmetic than anything else and won't really add any value in this domain.

[b]Game lifespan score: 19/20[/b]

    [*][h1]Sounds/Soundtrack[/h1]
The soundtrack is not that great ( it's not bad either ) and the only score that I can remember is the one from the last campaign level of the game. The sounds in general are well chosen and I didn't notice anything wrong with them.

[b]Game Sounds/Soundtrack score: 14/20[/b]

[/list]

[b]Overall score: 14.6/20[/b]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Resident Evil Revelations doesn't bring anything interesting or new on the table story wise but if you want a RE with a solid gameplay and a good play lifespan, this one will satisfy you.

This game begins with great promise, hinting at a game which recaptures the spirit of the original Resident Evil with the over-the-shoulder camera of Resident Evil 4. It sets everything up perfectly - a bioterror attack leads the protagonsits of the original game to investigate a derelict cruise ship. Early on, these cruise ship segments are fantastic and a lot like the original RE mansion - an isolated and claustrophobic setting, a big key hunt, a large environment to roam around and slowly piece things together, narrowly dodging enemies instead of trying to fight them, and lots of atmosphere (complete with odd camera angles - the rocking ship replaces the fixed framing). There's even a moment where you can drain water from a dirty bathtub - what better tribute could there be?

But it seems the devs didn't want to make the excellent game they were hinting at with this early crusie ship sequences. They were seemingly trying to strike a balance between appeasing fans of the classic RE games and fans of modern 3rd person action games. These deeply atmospheric cruise ship segments are constantly interrupted by generic and bland linear 3rd person shooter segments at other locations, preventing the atmosphere from ever fully taking over. Unfortunately,this is the side of the game that ends up winning - before long, even the cruise ship segments become brief, linear snippets where you're running away during a countdown, or quickly swimming through flooded areas, with constant cutscene interruptions - any atmosphere the game had early on is completely eradicated. What hinted at becoming a one of a kind game becomes a dime-a-dozen generic action shooter. And if all of that doesn't kil the mood, the awful generic hollywood action soundtrack certainly will (don't let the rather nice title theme get your hopes yp about the music).

Part of the problem is their experiment with the game's format - it's divided into 12 episodes, each lasting a mere 20-30 minutes, leading to a very short game (my final clear time was a mere 5hr40min). It has more of a story than any RE which preceded it, which is nice on one level, but it also means you can never really get immersed in the setting as you're constantly getting pulled out of the game by cutscenes and scene changes (and every scene is so brief - they rarely exceed 15min). The story is classic RE and quite enjoyable (of course involving a secret lab, though it doesn't have an appearance by Wesker this time), which makes it all the more frustrating that they chose to deliver it in such a cinematic and fragmented way. Every episode is also preceded by a recap, which would have been fine if there wasn't a pointless recap every 20-30min, futher pulling you out of the game. Having the protagonists from the original game doesn't help much, as they're hardly recognizable here.

On the plus side, the PC port is excellent. Unlike REmake, RE0 or RE4, I was able to run this at native resolution (1440p) without a single slowdown - quite surprising as this game is much newer and the graphics are much better than those titles. Many have complained about the controls, but I didn't have a single issue with them, which is a first for Resident Evil on PC. It's too bad the best RE port I've experienced so far was wasted on the worst title.

[h1]General gameplay and difficulty modes[/h1]

[i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i] is an action horror game. And unless you set the game's difficulty to hard, it plays very much like a third-person shooter, too. You see, on the hardest difficulty, you'll want to dodge the monsters as much as possible to conserve ammo, whereas on easy and normal difficulty, you can kill everything that moves.

If you want to tackle the hard mode but you're not a masochist, I recommend you play the game on easy or normal mode first and then start a 'new game plus' for a hard mode run. 'New game plus' means you start the game with the weapons and the weapon upgrades you gathered in your previous playthrough(s). That way, hard mode is a bit more bearable but still very challenging. 

During the campaign you can collect 16 different weapons. With the exception of one special weapon, all weapons belong to one of the following categories: handguns, machine guns, shotguns, rifles and magnums. Each of these categories of weapons requires a different type of ammo. 

While playing, you collect various weapon upgrades that can increase damage, fire rate, critical hit rate, ammo capacity, and so on. At one of the 'weapon boxes' you'll find scattered throughout the ship, you can select up to three of your weapons to carry with you and apply upgrades to your  weapons.

There's a limited supply of grenades to be found in the game. Grenades come in four different types and can be a real lifesaver in difficult situations.

You'll collect 'green herbs' and use these to fully restore your health.

A short while into the campaign, you'll get a scanner. You can use this scanner to find hidden items or to scan monsters. Scanning a number of monsters automatically yields a green herb.

[h1]Raid mode (solo or two player co-op)[/h1]

By playing the campaign missions (on any difficulty), you'll open up missions for the game's raid mode. Raid mode is meant for two players but you can play the raid mode missions solo, too, if you prefer. In raid mode you need to go through one of the zones from the campaign but the monster placement is different and the monsters sometimes have special 'skills' like increased speed, defense or offense. 

In raid mode, your character gains levels from 1 to 50, allowing you to tackle more difficult raid mode missions. The weapons also have a level from 1 to 50, reflecting their power. Adding improved weapons and unique weapons to the mix, raid mode has a huge amount of weapons to find or buy.

There's a shop in raid mode where you can buy weapons and upgrades. The currency is called BP. You collect BP by playing through both raid missions and campaign missions. This is the only way the campaign mode has an impact on raid mode.

[h1]Story and settings[/h1]

The theme of [i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i] is bioterrorism. Terrorists use bio-organic weapons, meaning mutant monsters and viruses that cause such mutations. 

You'll mostly play as Jill Valentine, who belongs to an organization that combats bioterrorism. She teams up with a guy called Parker Luciani to look for her former partner, Chris Redfield, aboard the 'Queen Zenobia', a cruise ship that's adrift.

Sometimes you'll play as another character for a while, like Chris or Parker. Those missions are either flashbacks or events happening elsewhere at the same time as the events on board the Queen Zenobia, and they are set in a wintry landscape or in a building. Although these side missions add to the story, they do break the main storyline each time, which is both a good and a bad thing: you're eager to continue the main story aboard the Queen Zenobia and would rather see how events unfold there, but the side missions do add a welcome variety of settings and atmosphere.

The Queen Zenobia is an impressive location. Its narrow corridors and small quarters add to the claustrophobic feel a horror game should have. Its larger rooms, like the huge hall and the brightly lit casino, make for an interesting contrast with the smaller, darker spaces. And then there are parts of the ship that are flooded, adding a different kind of claustrophobia to the mix.

[h1]Gameplay mechanics[/h1]

Most of the time, you'll be accompanied by an AI-controlled partner. These partners are very weak though, dealing almost no damage and rarely attracting the monsters' attention. So the point of these partners is up for discussion. On the one hand, they often help further the story and they're welcome company in an eerie creepy setting. On the other hand, being alone in an eerie creepy setting does improve that scary, lonely feeling horror games usually aim for.

Each room is a seperate game area. This means that monsters won't follow you through doors. It also means it's harder to retreat if you run into trouble in a small room.

The game has a few situations in which it uses 'quick time events': when a monster knocks you to the ground or when a monster grabs you. The former requires you to mash a button and the latter requires you to shake your mouse left and right. I really disliked this mechanic as it breaks the flow of combat completely. Maybe it's less of a nuisance if you play using a controller.

There's a lot of backtracking involved in the game. You'll revisit most parts of the ship several times. But the game does try to keep things interesting by adding new monsters or by allowing you to unlock a door you couldn't unlock before, leading to some loot or to new parts of the ship to explore.

The half a dozen boss fights in [i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i] aren't extremely tactical but they're challenging and lots of fun. Also, some of the bosses look, sound and behave genuinely scary.

[h1]Graphics and sound[/h1]

This PC version of [i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i] is a port from an early 2012 3DS game. Although the game's graphics have been polished and upgraded for PC, this still shows. Human faces and expressions look mediocre, and shadows are below par. But on the other hand, the graphics are detailed enough to make the monsters look at least a bit realistic and scary. And the backgrounds and the lighting on the ship often look relatively nice, all things considered. 

The music is great. Not in the way that you'd want to listen to the soundtrack when you're not playing [i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i], but in the way that it fits the game's atmosphere perfectly. The music is subtle and quietly in the background when you're exploring a creepy place, and it gets symphonic and bombastic when you're in an epic fight against a boss or running for your life against the clock.

The sound effects are impressive. Basic things like the guns firing sound more than okay to me, but especially the ambient sounds and the monsters' sounds are great.

The voice acting is top notch. The main characters' voice actors deserve the highest praise for adding a lot of personality and emotion to their characters despite the fact that the material they had to work with was pretty thin.

[h1]On Steam's Extra Features[/h1]

[i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i] has 13 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 7 while running the game.

The 50 Steam Achievements are challenging. There are only about 5 achievements you'll get just for playing through the game. There are a few collectibles achievements that require your attention throughout the whole game (or the use of a guide, of course). There are some challenges in the literal sense of the word, like 'kill 3 monsters with one grenade'. And then there are quite a few achievements for raid mode. Most of these can be achieved solo but some do require a partner, so co-op play is necessary if you want 100% completion.

On an interesting note, some achievements yield in-game rewards like additional guns or upgrades, so even people who usually don't bother with achievements may want to not ignore them completely in [i]Resident Evil: Revelations[/i].

I've come to learn that Resident Evil: Revelations is not a suitable introduction into the series. As someone unfamiliar with the franchise - apart from the films - there's the matter of being thrown between various timelines and characters with little exposition. Because of this I have almost no familiarity with each character's history or purpose throughout the game, so how can I be expected to care about their situation or understand the chemistry between each other when I don't understand their significance to the story? All I know is that Conan O'Brien's long lost brother, Raymond, makes several appearances.

I did enjoy the game as whole but there were many issues I couldn't look past. For one, the disjointed story, as if inspired by the film Memento. The controls are quite sluggish; turning can be slow, as is aiming, even though the mouse sensitivity is comfortable for all other situations. Dodging may as well be avoided at all times, it's more of a gamble of whether it will or won't work. There's also the matter of an extremely tight and claustrophobic Field of View, please use a program called Widescreen Fixer to solve this as it works really well.

The main missions consist of backtracking, being a semi-Metroidvania layout where further areas of the overworld will become unlocked over time, providing new additions and upgrades to the player's arsenal. The pacing is kept fresh as various secondary and tertiary characters will become playable in their own unique settings, serving to expand on the story, although each mission does not last long.

It soon became clear that many enemy encounters are only difficult due to how claustrophobic the area can be, with its small rooms and corridors, rather than how menacing the enemies behave, and the difficulty is only increased further by the poor controls. An impending sense of doom that I'd once experienced with a game like this is soon lost after making the unexpected discovery where enemies would not continue chasing me through multiple areas. The boss battles can be difficult when ammunition becomes scarce, the way I adapted to this was to try avoiding all conflict with the basic enemies in order to conserve resources in preparation for the real battle ahead. As I mentioned earlier, enemies will not chase the player through closed doors.

The most frustrating part of the game, story wise, is the amount of red herrings the writers threw my way. There are more twists here than found across M. Night Shyamalan's entire career, unfortunately none of them are as subtle.

RE: Revelations really feels like some wasted potential, especially without local campaign co-op. The writing is poor and the enemies are more a nuisance than they are threatening. As this is my first impression of the series I must say I'm left unimpressed, it's pretty much on the borderline of a negative recommendation.

Combat and exploration are enjoyable, the visuals hold up well, and the mission-based structure gives a nice rhythm to the gameplay. It’s not perfect—some levels feel repetitive, and the story isn’t as compelling as other entries—but overall it’s a quite enjoyable ride.

Resident Evil: Revelations is a decent survival horror outing. Not a series-defining classic, but scary enough and fun enough to keep fans entertained.

Resident Evil: Revelations is a continuation of the action / survival horror hybrid that started in Resident Evil 4 and, in this case, was originally developed for the 3DS. As such, though the visuals have been brought up roughly to a Gamecube-era RE game, the environments are more limited and closed than its predecessor. While you can still leap off of high points, hurdle over some rare obstructions, and aim in first person, a lot of the environmental interactivity is relatively limited. In general it's "Resident Evil 4 Lite: Boat Edition".

Similarly, weapon upgrades are just discovered in the course of the game. In general, the weapon layout isn't going to have many surprises for RE veterans, though there are some nice new improvements in the latter half of the game. The emphasis is largely on action this time - though there's keys to find and some pointedly simple puzzles, for the most part the focus is on aiming and shooting baddies. Shooting enemies remains satisfying, though sometimes feedback on the enemies part is lacking - it wasn't until late in the game I realized you could tell if an enemy was dead or not by whether or not the crosshair is lit. I probably wasted a decent chunk of ammo firing at slowly-slumping, melting enemies where it just wasn't clear I'd already finished them off.

Though it has some tension, the horror is generally absent this time around. While not as enjoyably schlocky as RE4, it does have some fairly ridiculous moments that stand out. The new fish-hybrid enemies aren't particularly frightening, and mostly it just feels you're fighting pale piles of goo without much personality. The bosses are solid, but fall more than a bit into frustration due to their ability to soak damage even on normal.

The big change is Genesis, a first-person scanner akin to Batman's detective vision (in Arkham Asylum) or Eagle Vision in the Assassin's Creed series. This lets you find hidden items (and a set of collectibles), and scanning enemies regards you with extra health kits. It's a bit of a misfire, because though the extra health kits come in handy and it can increase tension early on when you're scanning just to get that extra kit, it doesn't do anything interesting like reveal new weak points or at least give you a library of scanned monsters.

The boat environment is kind of a mix of neat ocean liner nods and boring grey hallways, and the forward motion of the game keeps it from ever developing too much personality. Though there's backtracking, it's relatively mild. Having Jill return (along with her prominently featured third-person butt) as the main character is welcome,  given the treatment she had in Resident Evil 5. You'll regularly swap out to a few other characters for different chapters, including series mainstay meathead Chris. The plot is pretty much just interesting enough to keep you going but its twists and turns are generally predictable for a series veteran like myself.

In general, it's a decent little side game for the series, nowhere near the best but also nowhere near the worst. It does just well enough to hold together on its own and to earn a recommendation, but not a ringing one. If you've already experienced Resident Evil 4 and would like a little more in that vein, this is probably worth your time more than Resident Evil 5 or 6.

Resident Evil Revelations is a solid port of a 3DS game. The graphics look acceptable; there are some muddy textures on doors, but that is not a bad thing given that it is a port. Controls are a bit awkward, but that is due to game play mechanics. 

Game play wise, this game plays like Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 5. The notable difference is that in this game, the player can move and shoot which is a welcomed change. The best aspect of this game is the game play. Fans of Resident Evil will like this game. The enemies are disgusting looking and the game aims for a classic Resident Evil type of feel. 

Unlike RE4 and RE5 alternative game mode, Mercenaries, Revelations has a new mode called Raid Mode. Raid Mode is fun, but to can become a grind fest. Raid Mode puts the player in certain maps from the main game with an objective. The objective can be get from A to B or eliminate enemies. Enemies health bars are visible and when the player shoots the enemy, numbers pop out. There are different weapons and upgrades to get in this mode that are necessary to progress and prepare player for the difficult bonus stage. To remedy the monotonous grinding, Raid Mode can be played online with another player. 

Overall, Resident Evil Revelations a solid port and game that fans of the series most likely will like.
